#8039. The Busy Mom’s Guide To Gift Shopping On Budget

Amazon and Alexa for Shopping make it easy to get it all for less.

Amazon knows how hard moms are working, and they have some ways to lighten the load. When you shop through Alexa for Shopping — Amazon’s personalized agentic shopping assistant — it all becomes way less stressful and way more affordable, and you might even get enough time back to finish your coffee before it gets cold (can you imagine?).

With everyday low prices that meet or beat other retailers across a huge selection of products, from affordable private-brands that help you save without sacrificing quality to the name-brand finds your kids have been asking for, Amazon makes it easier to find gifts that fit your budget.

Here are a few ways to use Amazon to get all the gifts you need — and stay sane while doing it.

Alexa for Shopping is Amazon’s agentic shopping assistant, and it’s really something else. It combines knowledge of the hundreds of millions of products across Amazon with info from across the web, and applies all of that to your personal shopping history and preferences. In other words, it knows all the possible gifts you could get on Amazon, and it knows you.

You can use Alexa for Shopping by asking it questions, like “What are the best toys for 5 year-olds?” or “What are teenagers asking for this year?” or even “What are some premium and more affordable brand options for a red dress and matching headband for my 3 year-old daughter’s holiday outfit?” It will give you ideas (including taking your shopping history and preferences into account) and then share a list of products to look through. So whether you’re gifting your own kids and just need some fresh ideas when you’re drawing a blank, or shopping for an older niece who lives five states away and have no clue where to start, you get tailored advice that helps you land on the perfect thing.

Budgeting during the holidays is not for the weak. Between finding the perfect gifts for your kids, your mother-in-law, and your spouse, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of holiday shopping and discover more things you know they’ll (or you’ll) love along the way.

The good news? Amazon’s prices consistently meet or beat other retailers, so you’re already getting low, competitive prices when you shop on Amazon. On top of that, Alexa for Shopping is a great tool to help you stay on track. First of all, you can use it so see up to a full year of price history for any product you’re interested in. Once you have that information, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to let you know when it drops to the right price for you. And even better, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to turn on auto-buy so it can complete your purchase using your default payment method when the item reaches your price target.

That saves you time (who has the bandwidth to keep checking back every day?!) and helps you know that when you do hit “buy” (or have Alexa do it for you), you’re getting the thing you want at a great price. And if you do that for all of your holiday shopping, you’re setting yourself up to spend less this season. That can be a huge relief at such an expensive time of year.

Bonus: the savings aren't just about gifts. From stocking up on groceries for the holiday feast to getting extra household essentials for overnight guests, the season comes with plenty of demands. With everyday low prices on fresh groceries and household essentials, plus fast free delivery, you can get the things you need at great prices that help your holiday budget go further.

A large part of the mental mom load is figuring out which [insert kid-related item here] is the best one. From onesies to bikes to pimple patches, there are so many things to choose from, and it takes time to figure out what’s actually right for your kid.

Alexa for Shopping takes that stress off your plate, too. Once you’ve found a few options that might work, Alexa for Shopping’s got you: it can show you side-by-side comparisons, highlighting the differences in features, price points, and even the reviews. Instead of digging through details, you get it all laid out and can quickly make your pick. Goodbye, overthinking.

We all know that holiday magic is really just... moms. But Amazon and the features built into Alexa for Shopping sort of feel like their own kind of magic. With Amazon, you can create a holiday season your kids will always remember, and make it look almost effortless. When you can do that without overspending or screaming into the void? We think that’s beautiful.

(And heads up, the savings go even further with Prime thanks to free delivery, exclusive deals, gas discounts, and more. But we digress.)

The best kind of holiday magic isn't just finding the right gifts at the right prices. It's getting a little time back for yourself, too. And honestly, moms deserve that kind of magic most of all.

Amazon and Prime deliver billions in savings every year — averaging over $1,000 per customer for 100+ million customers. Learn more about how Amazon makes the holidays and everyday life more affordable for families here.

#8038. These 7 Fall Cleanup Mistakes Could Ruin Next Year's Garden – Here's What to Do Instead

Some well-intentioned fall gardening chores can damage plants, weaken bulbs, harm wildlife, and rob you of next year's blooms. Here's how to avoid them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Have you ever cleaned your house so thoroughly that you tossed out important papers or other things you need? Well, the same can be true in the garden. A tidy garden isn't necessarily a healthier garden, and some common fall cleanup habits can actually compromise next year's flowers.

Yes, fall cleanup is as important as spring cleanup, but there is more room for error. At this point, plants have buds or seeds that will turn into flowers in springtime. The foliage is still storing energy to keep the plants alive through winter. Prune wrong – or make any of a dozen wrong garden moves – and you’ve set up problems for yourself and your plants.

So which autumn cleanup tasks are actually bad for your garden? I'm here to help you avoid the fall missteps that will keep you from getting a spectacular display come spring. Here are the key fall garden mistakes to watch out for – and what you should do instead.

Most spring-blooming shrubs bud on old wood. These include some of your favorite perennials, such as azaleas, lilacs, forsythia, and magnolias. If you go wild pruning in fall and chop these shrubs too, you'll cut off next spring's flower buds.

This doesn’t kill the plant, of course. The shrub will still grow healthy green leaves, but you will get very few or no blossoms when spring arrives. You’ll have to wait another 12 months to see most of those flowers.

Instead, prune spring-flowering shrubs that bloom on old wood immediately after the flowers fade. This allows them plenty of time to develop buds that will fill your garden in spring. For clean cuts on woody stems, use a sharp pair of bypass pruners, such as the Felco 8 pruning shears, which can cut branches up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick.

Summer-flowering bulbs, corms, and rhizomes use their green foliage to make food and store energy for their next flowering cycle. If you cut back the leaves of summer-flowering plants such as lilies, gladiolus, cannas, and crocosmia too early in fall, you risk depriving them of the energy they need. As a result, they may produce fewer flowers next year, or even fail to bloom altogether.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fortunately, this mistake isn't usually fatal, but it can weaken plants and affect their flowering performance. Instead, leave the foliage in place for as long as it's green and healthy, then cut it back once it naturally yellows and dies. However, frost-tender plants such as gladiolus and cannas may need to be lifted after frost damages their foliage, rather than waiting for it to die back naturally.

Tender plants such as dahlias are a little different – wait until the first frost blackens their foliage before cutting back the stems and lifting the tubers for winter storage, where necessary. Don't leave the tubers in freezing or waterlogged soil for too long, though, as they can rot.

Once lifted, store bulbs, corms, and tubers in a cool, frost-free location. Ventilated storage crates, such as these stackable, collapsible crates from CleverMade, are ideal for keeping different varieties organized while allowing air to circulate. Gladiolus corms can be stored dry after curing, while dahlias and cannas benefit from being packed in a suitable material, such as vermiculite (available on Amazon), to prevent them from drying out.

A thorough fall cleanup might leave your garden looking neat and tidy, but it can also strip away valuable food and shelter for wildlife. Many perennials produce seed heads that feed birds through the colder months, while their hollow stems and dead foliage provide overwintering habitat for beneficial insects. Cutting everything back in fall can leave these creatures with fewer places to shelter when they need them most.

Instead, leave plants such as coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, asters, and ornamental grasses standing through winter. Their seed heads provide food for finches and other backyard birds. If your garden is short on birdseed-bearing plants, you can supplement this natural food supply with a nyjer seed feeder, like this easy-clean feeder on Amazon, which is particularly attractive to goldfinches.

Standing stems can also offer nesting habitat for native bees in the following growing season. Wait until spring to tackle the cleanup, and even then, consider leaving some hollow or pithy stems standing at a height of 8–24 inches (20–60 cm). Cutting the stems creates openings that certain native bees can use for nesting, often in the following year. It's also worth leaving some fallen leaves in garden beds, as these provide overwintering shelter for butterflies, moths, and other beneficial insects. However, you should still remove diseased foliage to prevent problems from spreading next year.

Soil structure is important. If, in a flurry of fall cleaning, you dig or cultivate your garden beds too aggressively, you are actually destroying that natural soil structure. More specifically, that type of aggressive digging disrupts the habitats of beneficial earthworms and microbes. It also damages the delicate fungal networks that nurture the plant roots.

But that’s not all. When you do a lot of heavy tilling, you also run the risk of bringing up weed seeds into the upper soil, where they have a wonderful time filling your empty garden beds. Over time, repeated tilling can also break down the soil's natural structure, making it more prone to compaction, especially if you work the soil when it's wet.

Instead, choose a gentler alternative. You might layer on compost or straw right on top of the soil, allowing worms to do the work for you as they pull down food. Alternatively, install deep-rooted cover crops (like Tin Shed Seed Company's No Till Cover Crop Mix) or just loosen soil with a garden fork. Push it straight down, then just wiggle it a little.

The very word “smothering” should give you pause. If you pile on so much mulch that it smothers the plant crowns, it blocks sunlight, traps excess moisture, and keeps oxygen out of the roots. These conditions can lead to stem rot, fungal diseases, and plant death.

Instead, apply several inches of mulch (no more than 2 inches) to regulate soil temperature. Keep the mulch about 3 inches (7.5 cm) away from plant crowns. For that matter, keep it away from trunks too. A small hand rake, like this Ames one from Home Depot, makes it easy to redistribute mulch that's piled up too close to stems without disturbing the plants.

You may have heard that healthy leaf litter can decompose over time, providing nutrients for the soil. It can also shelter wildlife.

But leaving diseased foliage provides a reservoir for problems – like bacteria, pests, and fungal spores. If that happens near vulnerable plants, rain or wind can splash these pathogens onto healthy new growth. That means that the garden can be reinfected with powdery mildew and black spot.

Instead, clear fallen foliage from vulnerable plants (like roses) in fall, but dispose of it properly. Never put it in the compost; instead, bag it and put it in the garbage – these Kraft Lawn and Leaf Bags will decompose with garden waste. Then, lay down clean mulch.

With so many fall garden jobs competing for your attention, it's easy to overlook tender flowering plants that need protection before winter arrives. Dahlias, fuchsias, and tuberous begonias are all vulnerable to freezing temperatures, and forgetting about them until the first cold snap can put next year's flowers at risk.

If frost has already struck, don't panic. A little damage doesn't necessarily mean the whole plant is lost. However, the next step depends on what you're growing. Dahlias can be left until the first frost blackens their foliage, then cut back and lifted for winter storage in colder climates.

With other tender perennials, avoid rushing to prune away frost-damaged growth, as leaving it in place temporarily can offer some protection to the stems and crown. Instead, move containers somewhere sheltered or use frost cloth to protect plants from further cold. If you're using plastic covers, keep them from touching the foliage and remove them once temperatures rise to prevent overheating.

This versatile plant cover is ideally used for protecting crops from frost and pests, but can also be used for other plants.

These zip-up plant jackets protect shrubs and small trees from frost and feature drawstrings for a secure fit.

These heavy-duty planter dollies make it easy to move large pots indoors or to sheltered outdoor areas.

The best rule for fall cleanup is to keep it selective. Stripping garden beds bare is thorough – but very short sighted. So hold onto the reins before letting the autumn garden tidying run away with you.

As a final reminder, be sure to leave some seed heads and stems standing. They can make the landscape more interesting in winter, while providing food for birds and shelter for beneficial insects. It makes your garden more eco-friendly and welcoming.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole tackle the controversial topic of scruffing, while also sharing some fun comparisons between cats, dogs, and toddlers. Instead of treating scruffing like an absolute taboo, the hosts break down why understanding a cat's specific boundaries can make quick vet visits or home care way less stressful for everyone. Dr. Karyn brings her cat, Sirill, onto the desk to show why a timid pinch fails, how a solid hold gives cats a sense of security, and how to quickly test if your cat is way too sensitive for the technique.

Get the real scoop on scruffing catsâincluding why total bans ignore harm reduction when you just need to safely pull out a thorn or trim nails in a pinch. Dr. Karyn breaks down the biggest mistakes pet parents make, explaining why delicately pinching a bit of skin only annoys your cat and how a full-hand hold actually provides better control and stability. Youâll also learn how to check your catâs tolerance before even trying a hold so you never accidentally upset a sensitive pet.

Plus, the hosts chat about research comparing how dogs, cats, and toddlers help others, debating whether cats are truly selfish or just super selective about their time. From winning over shy rescue cats to comparing dogs to needy toddlers and cats to moody teenagers, this episode offers a relaxed, relatable look at living with felines.

Rethinking the Scruffing Debate: Dr. Karyn and Nicole discuss how complete anti-scruffing rules miss the mark on practical care. They explain that learning safe restraint acts as harm reduction, letting you handle fast tasks like pulling out a thorn or trimming claws without having to resort to full sedation.

Test Sensitivity First: Before going in for a hold, Dr. Karyn recommends checking the neck area with gentle pets and tickles. If a cat flinches or pulls away (like her cat, Zelda), you should never try to scruff them.

Skip the "Pinch": The most common mistake people make is grabbing a tiny pinch of skin, which just annoys the cat and provokes a fight. Proper restraint needs a full, firm hand on the scruff so the cat feels secure and can't wriggle free.

Never Pick Them Up by the Scruff: The hosts emphasize that while a hand on the scruff helps keep a cat grounded, you should never lift or carry an adult cat this way.

Altruism in Pets vs. Toddlers: The conversation turns to research comparing toddlers, dogs, and cats. Studies show dogs and kids will help out even without a reward, while cats generally step in only when thereâs something clear in it for them.

Earned Love Feels Extra Special: Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how dogs offer constant, people-pleasing affection, whereas a catâs love feels like an earned privilege. That conditional nature is exactly what makes it so rewarding when a quiet cat finally comes over to snuggle.

#8036. If Life With Dogs Were a Movie, These Would Be the Outtakes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Meet Dave Coverly, creator of the popular cartoon panel, âSpeed Bumpâ, which appears internationally in hundreds of publications, including The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, and the Detroit Free Press. His work was named âBest in Newspaper Panelsâ by the National Cartoonists Society in 1995, 2003, 2014, and 2021. He is also the principal cartoonist for Bark (formerly BarkBox) and illustrator for Ranger Rick magazine.

We sit down with Dave to learn the story behind his charmingly wry comic, and find out how, 32 years down the road, inspiration in the ordinary keeps his content relevant and relatable.

The path to becoming a professional cartoonist always starts in childhood â pretty much every kid likes to draw, right? And I was no different. But as kids get older, they tend to get more particular about how good their drawings look, and thatâs where frustration sets in. They tend to move on to other hobbies. Where a cartoonistâs path diverges from that of wiser, more sensible humans is that we love the process of creating more than we chafe at the frustration. Believe me, there is frustration. One misconception about artists is that we do it because it comes easy to us, but the general truth is that most of us put in long hours because we want to be good at what we already love.

I taped rejection letters to the wall above my drawing table for motivation. At the time, though, my panels didnât have a title, so when my breakthrough finally happened, I needed to name it. I submitted a list of possible titles to Creators, and Speed Bump was the unanimous choice. Fortunately, that was my top choice, too. Iâd like people to perhaps slow down just for a second when they read my work since Iâm rarely going to hit you over the head with the joke.

My second favorite title was The Wide World of Stretch Pants.

Animal humor has always been a part of my work. I was slightly obsessed with Ranger Rick magazine growing up, and spent loads of time drawing the critters they featured. I discovered thereâs something inherently funny and absurd about talking animals, not to mention itâs the most fun way to trigger the imagination. What would a giraffe order at a restaurant? What does a dolphin dream about? That was how I discovered how much fun cartooning was â and that the crazier you make it, the less perfect it needs to be.

Iâve always had a dog until very recently, and had two hilarious knuckleheads as a kid: Shag and Tigger. They were actually father and son, and I didnât need a DNA test to prove it â Shag got out one day, and the neighborhood kids on bikes came by to let me know he could be found down the street at Queenieâs house, where they were in the front yard together. Letâs just say Shag was living up to his name. Then Queenie begat Tigger.

I grew up in a small lake community, but Shag was found by my grandpa just living on the streets of Detroit. He was pretty feral â Shag, not my grandpa â and impossible to train, but also a total sweetheart. They slept in the garage, and in the morning weâd often find him sleeping on top of the car. Tigger, on the other hand, preferred to sleep behind the toilet. And he wasnât a small dog.

In any case, I believe these two funny mutts had as much influence on my work as any other cartoonist.

Great question! Cats and dogs are obviously very different, but they have one really big thing in common: their own unique personalities. Thatâs what makes both perfect for cartoons â most of us already treat them like little furry people anyway, right? Itâs just their behaviors that set them apart.

Dogs tend to be goofier, cats tend to be cooler, and they show affection in their own ways, too. Pets generate a lot of material because almost everyone knows a dog or a cat. Even if they donât have one (or many) themselves, the odds are a reader will recognize why the cartoon is funny (hopefully!).

One of my most popular cartoons is a sign that says âBeware of Avant-Guard Dog,â and the dog in the yard is wearing black and a beret and holding a sign simply saying WOOF. The idea started as a pun, but I think one of the reasons readers seem to like it so much is that it plays against type. The dogâs sensibility is quite cat-like, making it even more absurd.

My new book is a full-color collection of the âbest ofâ my dog cartoons from the last decade, and thereâs only one cartoon per page so that they can be seen in a larger format, which was important to me. I put a lot of effort into the art and the details, things that are often lost when the cartoons are shrunk down to an illegible size, so I wanted readers to be able to fully enjoy that aspect of the cartoons. Also, the friend who colors my panels, Ron Raff, is a genius, so whether you think the jokes are funny or not, youâll see that they look gorgeous and consistent throughout!

It was difficult but fun to choose which cartoons made the cut, too. Some are simply personal favorites; others were chosen based on readersâ reactions and how much love they got online. Feedback is extremely helpful, by the way â sometimes it feels like Iâm drawing these alone in my belfry studio and tossing them into a black hole, so hearing from people which ones they liked really makes my day.

There are two aspects to dog cartoons: The first and most obvious is that they really arejokes about dogsâ behavior in general â how they eat, how they might react in different settings, why they lick themselves, bathroom habits, etc etc. Thereâs a lot of material there! The second aspect is what generates even more material, and thatâs when dogs are reflecting human behavior, or simply behaving like a human.

Many of the dog cartoons are really about us, and heaven knows people will never stop providing fodder for jokes. Dogs â and animals in general â are a good buffer between the joke and the point of the joke. A good example in the book is a dog shaking a toy in his mouth, and a woman next to him is saying, âBad dog! Drop Mommyâs voodoo doll! Bad dog!â In the background, her husband (presumably) shakes back and forth like the toy. At some level, the cartoon is about the coupleâs relationship, right? But itâs framed by a typical and humorous dog action weâve all seen before. Just not with a voodoo doll, haha.

I would say simply that our question is also the answer: love. I try to approach my cartoons the same way I approach dogs in real life; from a standpoint of love, affection, admiration, and a little bit of gratitude that they exist.

There have been too many to count over three decades! I drew a cartoon years ago of a man walking his dog in heaven, but the leash is attached to the dogâs halo. A few weeks later, I received a card in the mail from a woman whose dog had just passed awayâ¦only a month after her husband. She said she cried with happiness thinking of the two of them like that, and it made her heart feel lighter. How incredibly moving is that? I think of that often: when I share a cartoon, the reader brings their own life experiences to it and then weâve made a two-way connection. That connection is my favorite part of the gig.

My only hope is that my cartoons help people simply see the world in a different way for a few seconds. I want them to laugh with others and not at others; see that absurdities are universal and that when we recognize ourselves or others in a cartoon, weâre really just acknowledging that weâre all connected.

And then I hope they cut them out and slap them on their fridges.

The best place to find all my work and links is my site: www.speedbump.com, and anyone should feel free to reach out, follow, etc on Instagram (https://www.instagram.com/speedbumpcomic/) or Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/davecoverly)

If youâre a skywriter, aim for the west side of Ann Arbor. Iâll look out the skylight in my belfry studio.

November can feel like the end of things, but if you put these cottage garden and prairie favorites in the ground this month, you can enjoy beautiful early flowering displays

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November often feels like the end of the growing season in many backyards. Annual and perennial borders have likely died back for the year, and deciduous trees and shrubs stand have lost their leaves. Yet while the air is getting fresher, you can still work a little magic in your cooling soil. Because as it turns out, this month is a prime time for sowing some classic hardy flower seeds.

Many pretty cottage garden favorites, native prairie wildflowers, and pollinator staples actually need a winter chill to thrive. In nature, wild flower seeds drop from seed heads in late fall, settle into the cool earth, and take part in a natural winter cycle known as cold stratification. Exposure to freezing and thawing breaks down the tough seed jackets of key annual and perennial flower types, prompting the embryo to awaken as soon as spring conditions become favorable.

Sowing these flower seeds in November gives them a big head start. Seeds planted now establish strong roots. This means healthier conditions in spring, with sturdier stems, superior drought resistance, and prolific displays that can bloom a month ahead of spring-sown counterparts. By taking advantage of these planting conditions now, you lay the groundwork for an effortless explosion of color next season.

Keep in mind your USDA hardiness zone, your local climate, and weather conditions before deciding on specific plants and a sowing strategy. Successfully sowing flowers in November comes down to matching your plant variety with the right late-season sowing technique. There are a few primary approaches you can try with these flowers, depending on your region and weather. In mild winter climates (zones 7-10), you can try fall sowing (directly outdoors) so seeds germinate before winter, overwintering as frost-hardy rosettes that bloom in April.

In colder northern climates (zones 3-6), there is also dormant sowing. This is where seeds are sown directly into garden beds once the ground is cold enough to prevent immediate germination. Soil temperatures consistently below 45°F (7°C) allow seeds to sit dormant until early spring. For native perennial flowers or regions with erratic thaws, the best approach is winter sowing. This means sowing in outdoor containers and placing in a protected area, like an unheated cold frame, to shield seeds from rodents and heavy downpours while still providing natural chilling.

Before sowing, ground preparation is vital. Check soil temperatures before you start sowing with a good soil probe. Budget-friendly Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter, available from Amazon gives a reliable read on current moisture and temperature levels. Then clear away thick, suffocating leaves, remove weeds, and lightly rake the top inch (2.5cm) of soil into a fine, crumbly tilth. Pay attention to seed packet instructions regarding sowing depth, as this can have a big effect on germination. Some larger seeds may require burying an inch deep, while fine wildflower seeds need light to germinate and need to be surface-sown with just a whisper of sand or light compost.

Water the seedbed gently with a fine mist to settle the soil without dislodging the seeds, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Mark each row clearly with durable weatherproof tags, and cover vulnerable beds with breathable floating row covers, mesh, or clean straw to deter birds. Whether sowing directly in the soil or indoors, these gorgeous flowering picks are all good to go this month…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Sweet peas (Lathyrus odoratus) are the quintessential cottage border bloomers. They are celebrated for their intoxicating scents and ruffled hues, which can cascade across trellises from late spring through early summer. These vintage darlings thrive in cool weather. Sowing sweet peas in November allows the seeds to develop deep roots while temperatures are low. This leads to more prolific flowering displays, with longer, sturdier stems. If you fancy a floriferous blend of lavender, violet and maroon blooms, buy Sweet Pea Burgundy Mix Sweet Peas from Eden Brothers.

In milder climates (zones 7-10), you can direct-sow sweet peas along sunny, well-draining trellises. In colder zones (3–6), sow seeds indoors in deep root-trainer tubes or biodegradable pots, and keep in an unheated greenhouse, sheltered porch, or cold frame. Sweet pea seeds have hard shells, so nick these with a nail file (or soak in room-temperature water for 12 hours prior to planting) to speed up moisture absorption. Plant seeds an inch (2.5cm) deep in rich, organic-rich soil, and pinch the central tips once seedlings develop 3 sets of true leaves for bushier plants.

With their luminous, silky petals, California poppies (Eschscholzia californica) bring effortless cheer to borders, gravel gardens, and sunny slopes. These tough-as-nails wildflowers thrive in sandy or rocky soils, making them ideal for challenging areas where other ornamentals struggle. However, because they have brittle taproots that resent disturbance, they should be direct-sown where they are intended to bloom. Buy Marde Ross & Co California Dreaming California Poppy Seed Mix from Amazon for a near-neon flush of tangerine, melon and magenta blooms.

You can sow seeds now in regions with milder winters (zones 7-10). In these areas, fall rains will trigger late-fall germination, establishing fern-like foliage that bursts into bloom by April. To sow California poppies, scatter them over the soil in an area that drains well and has full sun. Lightly rake the seeds into the soil so they are barely covered, as poppy seeds require light to germinate. If you have colder or very wet winters, it’s best to wait until spring to sow these seeds.

Offering the vertical grandeur of delphiniums without the fussy growing requirements, annual larkspur (Consolida ajacis) produces epic flowering spires in shades of royal purple, lavender, rose, and white. This cottage garden classic is a cool-season annual that is ideal for November sowing. In fact, waiting until spring often results in poor, erratic germination, as seeds need a period of stratification to break dormancy. For a shock of saturated purple-blue spires, buy QIS Dark Blue Larkspur Seeds from Eden Brothers.

Direct-sow in a rich, sunny, well-drained bed. Cover very lightly with an eighth of an inch of fine compost or sand. Winter rain and freezing nights should satisfy the seed's chilling requirements, triggering early emergence in spring. Fall-sown larkspur often blooms up to a month earlier than spring-sown seeds, beating the summer heatwaves that can cause these cool-season annuals to fade. If your winters are very cold, try winter sowing in containers.

Also known as cornflowers, bachelor’s buttons (Centaurea cyanus) are cherished vintage annuals. Their blue ruffled blooms erupt in late spring and summer to create a dazzling contrast with cottage perennials and ornamental grasses (though you can get varieties in shades of pink, purple and white). Also cold tolerant, they are naturally adapted to late-season sowing. Sowing in November helps it to grow strong roots that can withstand hotter summer days far longer than spring-started plants.

Sow in a bright, sunny border with average to poor, well-draining garden soil. Sow at roughly a quarter-inch (0.6cm) deep, firming the soil gently. For the best results, ensure the area with seeds doesn’t erode or get waterlogged over winter. In mild winter regions, seeds will sprout within a few weeks; in northern climates, they will sleep until early March, flowering from late spring all the way to July. Buy SVI Store’s Bachelor Button Mix Seeds from Amazon for a lively mixture of floral heirloom tones.

Black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia hirta) are prairie icons that light up borders from early summer well into fall. With their sunny yellow petals and chocolate-brown cones, these pollinator-friendly perennials and biennials are often bought as transplants. Hardy in zones 3-9, they are super tough. However, their seeds possess dormancy inhibitors that can lead to patchy germination in spring soil. November sowing solves this problem naturally. By scattering now, you allow the rhythm of winter rains, snow cover, and sub-freezing nights to break dormancy smoothly.

Clear away heavy mulch and scatter seeds thinly over the surface. They require light to germinate, so press them into the soil without burying them. While fall-sown plants spend their first spring developing roots and crowns, many will reward you with late-summer blooms in the first year. Buy Harris Seeds’ Rudbeckia Goldilocks Seeds from Walmart for a ruffled twist on the dazzling classic. Just keep in mind that many varieties benefit from cold exposure, but not all, so know your type before you sow.

With their delicate, two-toned blooms and graceful spurs, columbines (Aquilegia spp.) bring woodland romance and grace to borders, cottage beds, and rockeries. Native across North America and Europe, Aquilegia species are hardy down to zone 3. Seeds require 4-6 weeks of cold, damp stratification, making November sowing the easiest, most reliable way to propagate them. Buy Blue Star Columbine Seeds from Eden Brothers for a vivid bounty of iconic violet-blue and white blooms.

Select a site that receives gentle morning sun and dappled afternoon shade with rich, well-draining soil. Some varieties require sunlight to trigger germination, so check the seed packet. Scatter seeds onto the soil surface and press lightly into the earth, but don’t cover with soil. If you live in an area with winter gales or heavy rains, you can winter-sow columbines into ventilated plastic jugs in a shaded outdoor spot. Seedlings will emerge in spring, providing pretty nectar for returning hummingbirds.

Purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) is a perennial staple in the sustainable, pollinator-friendly yard. Featuring daisy-like blooms and spiky cones, echinacea feeds native bees and butterflies in summer, while offering seed cones for goldfinches in fall. Seeds have evolved to weather harsh winters before germinating, making November a great time for sowing. Buy Purple Coneflower Heirloom Seeds by the Kviter Store from Amazon for a generous supply of purple drifts.

Broadcast seeds in a sunny spot with well-drained, average soil. Echinacea seeds need minimal light filtering through to sprout, so rake them into the earth no more than an eighth of an inch deep, firming the soil. Winter's freeze-thaw cycles settle the seeds, softening their husks so that strong roots push down early in spring. While coneflowers focus heavily on root establishment in the first year, November-sown echinacea tend to bloom reliably by the second season.

Your gardening season doesn’t have to be over in November. Taking a little time this month to start off some pretty cottage garden and pollinator favorites is such a rewarding investment in future backyard bloomers. By partnering with winter’s cold cycles rather than fighting them, you give these key annuals and perennials a real head start on early spring beauty. Using seeds is also a cost-effective way to get more flowers. If some don’t germinate or establish, you haven’t lost a lot of money. So grab a few seed packets, prep your beds, and get planting. It’s time to start looking forward to an effortless run of blooms well ahead of the neighbors.

Youâve probably heard by now that feeding wet food to your cat is better than feeding dry food. This has a lot to do with hydration and moisture levels. As it turns out, most cats donât drink enough water, and a diet of dry food compounds the issue by further dehydrating them.

Feeding canned or wet food is a great solution to this issue. Unless, of course, you travel, work long hours, or otherwise donât have the bandwidth to open can after can for your hungry feline.

This is where the Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder comes in. This isnât another automatic wet cat food feeder that requires constant refilling and cleaning. Oh no, this is something completely new.

But does this high-tech contraption live up to the hype? I had the opportunity to test this space-age automatic cat feeder with the help of my hungry-hippo kitty, Makoa. Keep reading to see what we liked about it and if itâs worth the purchase in my full Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder review.

Domestic cats are descended from African desert wild cats. These wild felines got most of their hydration from their prey. Their kidneys became ultra-efficient at retaining moisture, and their drive to find fresh water sources nearly disappeared completely.

Our house cats retain this same physiology and lack of interest in hunting down fresh water. The problem? They arenât typically chowing down on juicy rodents a dozen times a day. Which means they often donât get the moisture they need to keep those specialized kidneys healthy.

This is why 40% of cats over 10 years old and 80% of cats over 15 years old develop chronic kidney disease. After a lifetime of chronic dehydration, their kidneys simply canât keep up.

One solution is to increase the amount of water cats consume through their food by offering wet food or adding water to their dry food. This is doable if you are home during meal times every day. But if you work long hours, have a million other things to juggle, or occasionally (or often) travel, feeding moist meals consistently becomes more of a challenge.

Some turn to automatic wet food feeders that keep pre-prepared portions of wet food cool, automatically opening each portion on a set schedule. While these work in the short term, they hold only a limited amount of food (generally between three and six meals) and require a lot of cleanup and constant restocking.

For those who travel or already struggle to get everything done in a day, this is far from being a convenient or effective solution.

The Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder combines the health benefits of a wet-food diet with the convenience and high-capacity of a dry-food automatic feeder.

Unlike traditional automatic wet food feeders that can only store a handful of meals, the Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder can hold weeks of food at a time and dispense meals up to every hour, keeping kitties with even the most specialized dietary needs happy and hydrated throughout the day.

Rather than canned or wet packaged food, the Riko works with freeze-dried cat food. This shelf-stable food is ground up into portions, mixed with water, and allowed to rehydrate before serving.

No refrigeration or constant refilling needed. Just fill the hopper with a bag of freeze-dried food of your choice, add filtered water to the reservoir, set the amounts and feeding schedule on the app, and take a well-deserved break from fretting over your catâs meals and hydration status.

Neakasa is a smart-home and pet-care brand operated by Genhigh, a technology company headquartered in Shenzhen, China. Founded in 2017 as Neabot, the company specializes in automated solutions designed to make everyday home and pet care easier, including robotic cleaning and smart pet products. The Riko is manufactured in China, where the company is based.

Given the price point of this product, I wouldnât recommend it to cat owners simply hoping to unload some of their kitty chores to automation. There are less expensive automatic feeders for that. But for cat owners who normally feed wet food but are taking a long trip or frequently travel and want a feeder that can provide meals more often than their cat sitter can, the Riko Wet Meal Feeder is a worthwhile investment.

It is also a great option for cats who require small portions frequently throughout the day or who already eat freeze-dried food and can benefit from a more consistent schedule and more moisture in their diet.

Because this feeder allows for highly customized feeding routines and portions, it works well for kittens, adults, and seniors. But do be aware that the meal sizes cap out at 15g of dried food, which means larger cats may require multiple feedings throughout the day rather than the typical two meals they might be used to, something the app makes easy.

The Neakasa Riko takes the guesswork out of serving moistened meals. Simply fill the food hopper with compatible freeze-dried food, fill the water tank, and use the app to create a feeding schedule.

At mealtime, Riko automatically grinds the food, adds your selected amount of water, and allows the mixture to soak while the bowl is hidden out of reach. Once the food is ready, the bowl swings out so your cat can enjoy their fresh meal.

You can adjust the water-to-food ratio to create a consistency your cat prefers, from thicker to more soupy. Riko can schedule multiple meals throughout the day, add water to keep uneaten food fresh, and track food consumption through the app.

Beyond preparing moistened meals, the Riko packs several thoughtful features into the feeder itself:

Large capacity: The 3-liter food hopper and 2.4-liter water tank can hold enough for 10+ days of feeding.

Freshness-focused design: An airtight food compartment, desiccant system, and sealed grinder help protect freeze-dried food from moisture.

Precise portions: Riko weighs each serving for approximately Â±1-gram portioning.

Easy cleaning: The removable stainless-steel bowl is dishwasher-safe, while other components can be removed for cleaning. Each order comes with two bowls, so you can pop one in the dishwasher while the other is in use.

The Neakasa app gives you control over Riko from your phone, whether youâre home or away. You can create feeding schedules, adjust portion sizes and water-to-food ratios, and trigger extra meals remotely.

The app also records your catâs food and water intake, making it easier to spotchanges in eating habits over time. Youâll receive alerts for low food and water storage and potential feeding problems, while adjustable settings let you configure features such as freshness detection, child lock, and desiccant replacement reminders.

Through the app, you have control over the amount of ground food in each meal, the ratio of water added, how long it sits to rehydrate, and how often water is added if food is left over. You can even program âwater onlyâ meals to encourage even more moisture intake.

Riko can be customized with a few optional accessories. The rechargeable battery pack provides up to seven days of cordless operation and backup power during outages, while the Multi-Cat Access Module uses microchip recognition to restrict feeding to each designated cat in multi-cat households.

Neakasa also sells replacement silicone desiccant packs with a color-changing indicator that lets you know when the pack needs replacing.

Number of meals per fill: about 10 daysâ worth

Compatible with: most types of freeze-dried food

Number of meals per fill: 3 daysâ worth

Compatible with: all types of canned food

If youâve read any of my reviews before, then you know that my cat, Makoa, is a BIG fan of food. So any device that makes meal times less of a hassle for me and more accessible for him is worth trying out. And, since our family also travels fairly frequently, I thought this high-tech contraption might be helpful in multiple ways.

When the Riko arrived, I immediately felt like I was unboxing some kind of fancy kitty espresso maker! Itâs about the same size as one, and the grinder really does look very similar to a coffee grinder.

Getting the Riko set up was fairly painless. I followed the Quick Start Instructions to assemble the few parts that had been stored internally during shipping, then downloaded the app and connected the device to my Wi-Fi.

From there, things got a touch trickier. Because the Riko works using weight, not volume, it can be a little difficult to set the proportions for each meal. For example, I typically feed Makoa Â¼ cup twice per day. How many grams of ground freeze-dried food plus water is that? No idea.

Luckily, the app does have a very helpful Smart Feeding Plan setup that allows you to use your catâs weight and select the type of food you feed to automatically create a feeding schedule based on the food brand's recommended intake.

The downside here is that it defaults to 10 meals per day. Which probably isnât a bad thing since cats did evolve to eat multiple small meals throughout the day (and this also guarantees better hydration). But if your cat is used to a couple of big meals at the same time each day, this can make for a tough transition.

I ended up manually adding up the dry food total it recommended, then manually adding meals that were more aligned with his typical schedule.

The other hangup I ran into is that the feeder (in the US, at least) maxes out at 15g of ground food per meal. For comparison, my 12-pound cat needs about 60g of ground food per day. In other words, I had to schedule at least four meals per day for him to get all the food he needs.

These smaller meal sizes are intentional. Not only does it help avoid food being wasted (or left out for too long without being eaten), but it also ensures your cat is continually taking in food-based moisture throughout the dayâthe way they evolved to.

So I wouldnât say this is a bad thing or design flaw, but it is something you and your cat may need to adjust to.

Beyond the tricky parts of portioning and scheduling, I really do love this feeder! It is so easy to fill and, once the schedule is set, you really can just forget it. It starts preparing each meal ahead of time so that the food is ready at the scheduled mealtime.

It makes a recognizable beep when food is ready, so your cat can learn to come as soon as dinner is served. (Makoa learned to recognize the low buzz of the grinder almost instantly, and now waits for his meals twenty minutes before they are served.)

Not only has this gadget taken the stress off me (now Makoa has something else to obsess over when itâs dinner time), but it has made it so much easier to ensure consistent, moist meals throughout the day. And I know it will be a lifesaver for those weekend trips and long vacations our family likes to go on.

I highly recommend this feeder to anyone who is looking for a way to automate their catâs meals without having to rely on dry kibble. The rehydrated freeze-dried food isnât the same as canned food, but the texture is similar, and most cats love this type of food, especially when it is mixed with water. Even better, freeze-dried food tends to be healthier and more nutrient-dense than even the best canned food options.

No. Riko is designed to grind and rehydrate freeze-dried food, not conventional wet food. Do not put canned, pouch, or other wet food, or kibble, dehydrated, or air-dried food into the hopper.

Riko's smart features and remote app controls require a Wi-Fi connection, but once programmed, the feeder can still perform its feeding schedule if the internet connection is interrupted. It supports 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi networks.

Because Riko adds water to the food before serving, the resulting meal should be treated like wet food. Neakasa recommends that your cat consume it within about three to four hours.

Riko's freshness settings can detect leftover food and pause the next scheduled feeding when the amount remaining exceeds your chosen threshold. The feeder can also retract the bowl after food has remained uneaten for an extended period.

If hydration is a concern for your cat and providing consistent moist food is a challenge for you, then the Neakasa Riko is worth looking into.

This high-tech automatic feeder can store 10 days' worth of freeze-dried food at a time and provide up to 20 freshly rehydrated meals per day. Each meal can be scheduled and proportioned to meet your catâs needs while ensuring their moisture intake is optimal to avoid future health issues. It's perfect for busy cat parents, extended periods away, and cats who require frequent, moistened meals.

#8033. "Covert Contracts" Might Be Wrecking Your Relationship

If you’ve ever thought “after everything I do,” therapists say you might have one.

You did bedtime solo every single night this week. You did the baths, with all the splishing and the splashing and the bubble anarchy. You fielded the lightning round of existential questions at 8:47 p.m. (“Mommy, what happens to doggies when they die?”). You tucked everyone in and then did your regular closing-time routine to get the rest of the house buttoned up for bed.

So when Saturday morning rolls around, you’re planning to sleep in. You fully expect your partner to wake up and handle the kids, the breakfast, the early morning dog walking duties. The whole shebang. Tit for tat.

Then your kids are in your face before you can even pry your eyes open, wondering where their soccer cleats are or if you can get more juice. Cue the rage, right? OK, so here comes the uncomfortable gut-check… did you communicate your expectations to your partner? Or did you just sort of assume it was a done deal?

This scenario has been dubbed a "covert contract," and therapists say it can lead to a whole lot of resentment building up in a relationship over time. Here’s what experts want you to know about where this behavior comes from, how to spot it in your own actions, and how it differs from the imbalance of the invisible load.

“A covert contract is a deal only one person signed,” says Kristyn Carmichael, Esq., a family mediator, certified divorce financial analyst, and founder of Couples Solutions Center. “It sounds like ‘If I do X, you’ll do Y,’ but the other partner never saw the terms, never agreed to them, and usually doesn’t know the contract exists.”

And she often has a front-row seat to what happens when those deals go unaddressed for a prolonged period of time. “In mediation, I see the end stage of these: one spouse arrives with years of unpaid ‘invoices,’ and the other is honestly confused about what they owe.”

Cheryl Groskopf, an anxiety, trauma, and attachment therapist who authored The Somatic Healing Workbook, likens it to writing a big ol' agreement and assigning your partner an equally big role in it. Somehow, your partner is the only person unaware of said agreement.

But your partner being unaware doesn’t change the way you feel. The hurt is just as real as if they’d actually broken a promise. “In your brain, they did,” Groskopf explains.

Um, yes. One hundred percent. This was something every expert agreed on! However, the need itself isn’t the issue here; it’s the delivery method.

“The need underneath is reasonable, but if it’s not articulated overtly, then it’s unreasonable to think your partner would be a mind reader,” says Dr. Jenni Skyler, Adam & Eve’s resident sex and relationship therapist.

Already, as a busy working mom who happens to be the default parent, I instinctively start to feel myself bristle at this idea. No one tells me these things or what needs to be done — I just notice and do it because someone has to. The experts say that sort of thinking is a fast path to frustration.

“‘I want my partner to make an effort on my birthday’ is a totally reasonable desire,” Groskopf says. “‘I shouldn’t have to tell them what I want because if they really loved me, they’d already know’ is when it becomes problematic.”

Now, the experts were also abundantly clear that none of this means moms should just silently accept an unfair split.

“One person also shouldn’t have to become a household manager simply because they are more organized, quicker to notice what needs to be done, or less comfortable leaving things unfinished,” says Ilona Phillips, a psychotherapist and founder of Lotus Counseling in Ann Arbor, Michigan. “Expecting shared responsibility is reasonable. Expecting a partner to recognize an unspoken sacrifice and reciprocate exactly one-for-one can get partners in trouble.”

“If I ask for a break and you say no, that’s a direct rejection,” Carmichael says. “If I never ask, I’m protected from that, and I keep the moral high ground.” And, yes, there’s also that belief so many of us carry that “if I have to ask, it doesn’t count,” she adds, “as if a gesture only proves love when it’s unprompted.”

That belief tends to run deep, too (ask me how I know). Says Groskopf, “If you grew up learning that your needs were inconvenient, asking can feel incredibly vulnerable.” Instead of just asking, we end up creating these little litmus tests our partners don’t even know they’re taking.

She uses flowers as an example. If you ask for them, you know they showed up because you asked. But if your partner brings them on their own, "There’s this feeling that you were appreciated, that they noticed you, that you MATTER. And for someone who grew up feeling overlooked or emotionally neglected, that distinction can feel huge.”

Oof. The catch here is that this strategy often just backfires.

“There is a fear that if we directly communicate what we need, and that need is not met, we will be hurt,” explains Dr. Paulette Didia, a licensed clinical psychologist in New York City. “However, if we do not communicate what we need, our partner will not know, our partner will not do it, and we will be hurt anyway. We think hurting in our own mind ‘hurts less,’ and that is not true.”

Admittedly, the lines are a bit blurry. When you’re doing the lion’s share of invisible work in your home and family, it’s hard not to “keep score” or have a running tally in your head of what your partner did versus what you did.

Unfortunately, that scoreboard warps how both partners see each other.

“Once you develop a narrative that your partner isn’t doing enough, it becomes very easy to fill that bucket with examples of how they’re falling short. Meanwhile, your spouse feels like they’re always in the doghouse and starts to wonder if it’s even worth trying. One person is thinking, ‘Don’t you see how hard I’m working?’ while the other is thinking, ‘What did I do wrong now?’” says Mary McLaughlin, LCSW, a couples therapist and discernment counselor.

So while it’s fair to feel frustrated by an invisible (or visible) load imbalance, a little communication can go a long way. That’s true on both sides of the line. “Even if the score is unequal, if all parties know the score and acknowledge it and offer gratitude, this can offset resentment,” says Skyler.

Well, obviously this is tricky since you probably don’t know you’re making them. However, there are a few tells you can look for, according to the experts:

First and foremost, resist the urge to try settling years of “back pay.” You can’t Uno Reverse this one. Instead, focus on rewriting the terms and making sure you and your partner are, in fact, on the same page. Here are a few practical pointers from our pros on how to pull that off.

Didia asks couples to fill out a simple weekly worksheet together that includes tasks along with who does them and when. She has couples do this at the same time each week so that it doesn’t become one more thing Mom has to track, and they post the list where both can see it so no one becomes the default reminder.

If you want to follow suit, start by listing every task (big and small). Next, let each partner choose what they’ll take, and split the ones nobody wants. Very important info: The person who owns a task decides how and when it gets done. “Maybe you think this should be done by Monday, but your partner indicates it will be done by Wednesday,” Didia says. “Since it is their task, they get to decide and, by Tuesday, you will not already be annoyed.”

Phillips encourages a weekly check-in where partners take turns asking: What’s been working well between us? Is anything feeling off? Extra difficult? Frustrating as hell? Unacknowledged? And, finally, how can I be a better partner to you this week?

You may be tempted to stop doing certain things, like washing the dishes, hoping that someone will notice. That’s just a covert contract in a different outfit, says Phillips. And even if your partner does pick up the task, resentment can still linger. You might then think, Why did I have to stop before they noticed?

“Relationships change. What worked when you were first dating, before kids, 10 years ago may not work anymore,” reminds McLaughlin. “Couples need to renegotiate instead of assuming the old arrangement still works.”

When you realize you’re locked in a pattern that won’t budge, it’s probably time to see a couples therapist. Carmichael’s advice is to get help sooner rather than later. By the time couples land in her office, she says the covert contracts show up even in how they divorce, i.e., “I gave up my career, so I deserve more.”

At the end of the day, adds McLaughlin, “Resentment paired with avoidance is a particularly risky combination for couples.” And that means the fix, both annoyingly simple and incredibly hard, is saying what you need out loud… and holding each other accountable to those needs in a way that feels fair and equitable to you both.

Adopting can be one of the most rewarding ways to welcome a new pet into your life. But for many would-be adopters, the biggest hurdle isnât necessarily that they don't want to adopt; it's feeling confident that theyâre making an informed and responsible decision.

Whether you have concerns about a pet's medical and behavior history, or understanding what to feed them, there are lots of questions to consider before welcoming a new dog into your home.

Mars is #ClearingThePath to pet adoption by giving prospective and new dog owners access to practical, expert-backed support throughout the journey.

Responsible adoption is about more than picking the right dog; it's about making sure you can realistically meet their needs. Before adopting, think about your living space, daily routine, work arrangements, and how much time you can dedicate to helping your new dog settle in and meeting their exercise, enrichment, and training needs.

Surprising for some, living in an apartment, for example, does not automatically mean you cannot adopt a dog. The right match depends less on the size of your home and more on whether you can meet that individual dogâs physical, mental, and social needs.

Always mention if you have existing pets or children at the beginning of the adoption process too. Shelter staff can help identify pets whose personality, energy level, and other needs may be a good fit for family life.

The more you speak honestly and openly with the shelter about your home, family, and daily routine, the more they can help you understand which dog will be the right match.

Moving from a shelter into a home is a huge change for your new best friend, and youâd be amazed by how many dogs are returned to shelters within their first few days, before theyâve even had a chance to decompress, let alone adjust to their new situation.

A useful way to think about the transition is the â3-3-3â guideline: the first three days, three weeks, and three months.

During the first three days, your dog may feel overwhelmed. Dogs may hide, sleep more than usual, show less interest in food, or simply seem unsure of their surroundings. Some dogs may even show signs of fear or defensiveness, and itâs important to understand that this is not necessarily their true personality.

Keep things calm and predictable, and let your dog set the pace.

Once they become more comfortable, you may start seeing more of their personality from around three weeks, and this can be a good time to introduce gentle routines, socialization, and basic training. By around three months, many dogs may feel much more at home, although every pet is different, so donât worry if your dog seems to need longer. Just be patient and give them the time and space they need to feel safe.

Mars research found that 71% of adopters change their petâs diet immediately after adoption. However, switching your new dogâs food right away may not be the best option, even if their previous diet wasnât the best quality. Ask the shelter what your dog currently eats, how much they are fed, and how often. Keeping their existing food and routine initially can help reduce unnecessary disruption.

If you want to change their food, wait a week or so to allow them to adjust, then do so gradually by adding a small proportion of the new diet to the dogâs regular diet. On the first day, their old food should make up around three-quarters of the meal, with the new food making up the rest.

Puppies in particular need age-appropriate nutrition to support growth and should not be switched onto adult food too early.

A dogâs diet should be complete and balanced for their age, size, activity level, body condition and health needs, and plenty of fresh water should always be available.

Consistency can help your dog understand their new environment and build trust.

Establish regular times for meals, walks, rest, and play. As your dog becomes more comfortable, you can begin introducing basic training using positive reinforcement. Keep sessions short, fun, and rewarding.

Itâs normal for there to be some bumps along the way as your dog adjusts to a new home and routine. Behaviors they had previously learned â toilet training, for example â may temporarily change while they settle in, so patience and consistency are important.

If you notice any sudden, persistent, or concerning changes in behavior, speak to your veterinarian or a qualified behavior professional for advice.

Adopting and bringing a new dog home is just the beginning, and itâs completely normal for questions to come up as they settle into a new routine. If you need extra guidance regarding their behavior, health, nutrition, or day-to-day care, donât be afraid to reach out. Trying to make compost from fallen leaves takes forever, right? Not if you know this gardeners’ trick to get it ready to use in your yard in time for spring.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Making free compost from fall leaves is such an easy win, and with these smart hacks you’ll have a nutritious mix ready to enrich your garden soil by spring. While creating traditional leaf mold compost can take up to two years, this quick and easy method speeds up decomposition to bring garden-ready compost in 4-5 months. What’s more, it’s mess-free!

Want to know the secret? Any compost pile relies on tiny organisms, way too small for us to see without a microscope, to break plant matter down. These microbes are responsible for around 80-90% of the chemical decomposition process when making compost, and this method simply creates the ideal conditions for the speediest members of this recycling workforce to flourish.

It’s cheap, too, as you’re going to make compost in a black trash bag. Heavy-duty contractor bags such as Brute Super Tuff Bags, available from Walmart, are best as they’re much stronger than those designed for residential use. Your reward will be a rich and crumbly, well-structured compost that will feed plants as well as help soil hold moisture. Spread it as a mulch onto perennial borders and around shrubs to lock moisture in and deliver nutrients to roots. Dig it into veggie beds to fuel healthy crops, or mix with coco coir to make your own potting mix. You can even steep a scoop in a bucket of water for a couple of days to make a compost tea that’ll help protect your plants from disease.

Ready? Part of the Weekend Wins series, making a quick compost from fall leaves is one of those easy garden jobs that brings a big reward. Here's what to do.

Not all leaves break down at the same speed, and many species have evolved strong defences against microbes. Oak, beech, sycamore, horse chestnut, holly, laurel and magnolia leaves are all high in a compound called lignin that acts as a protective armor against microbes. They’re also rich in tannins, a compound that effectively halts the digestive action of microbes, so they're slow to decompose.

Instead, use foliage that’s thin, flexible and soft to make compost from autumn leaves. Maple, ash, elderberry, willow and fruit tree foliage are all far lower in lignin and tannin so they’ll break down in a fraction of the time. It doesn't matter if a few high-lignin, high-tannin leaves get mixed in, but keep them to a minimum. And don't worry if you're not sure about tree identification: just avoid using thick, leathery or glossy leaves.

Cutting the leaves up into smaller sections also speeds up the process by increasing the surface area and exposing the less protected innards of the foliage for the microbial feasting. Shredding leaves before composting is the equivalent of chopping a log into kindling: you give the microbes plenty of vulnerable material that quickly gets the process going.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The chopped-up material won’t mat together like whole leaves do, and it'll absorb water rather than repelling it, both also speeding decomposition.

Shredding leaves is easy to do, even if you don’t have a leaf shredder. Simply run your lawnmower over the leaves multiple times or tip the foliage into an old trash can and shred with a string trimmer or weed whacker.

In any compost pile you need to mix carbon – the ‘browns’ – with nitrogen – the ‘greens’ – for microbes to work efficiently. And this applies when you make compost from fall leaves, too. Leaves are very high in carbon so, to get a good balance of browns and greens to keep those microbes happy, you need to add some nitrogen.

Grass clippings are super-high in nitrogen: use a lawnmower to shred leaves on your lawn and the job’s done for you. Coffee grounds are also nitrogen-rich so toss those in, and if you have access to free chicken manure, that works a treat, too. Aim for one part greens to three parts brown.

To kickstart the decomposition process, toss a shovelful or two of garden soil – or homemade compost if you have it – into the mix. This will be packed full of microbes that will immediately get to work.

Microbes work best in damp conditions so pour water over the leaf mix, unless of course it's recently rained and the leaves are already wet. Aim for moist not wet, as you don’t want the leaves sitting in water.

Making compost this way requires oxygen so when you tie the sack closed (using a zip tie is easiest) don’t squash all the air out of the sack first. So this air can be replaced, delivering a fresh supply of oxygen, use a sharp knife to punch air holes into the sack. Around 15 holes in a regular contractor sack is about right, and try to distribute them well around the sides and base of the sack.

Those microbes are going to generate plenty of heat as they get to work, and you can help retain that warmth by storing the bag in a sunny, sheltered spot so the black plastic absorbs lots of solar heat. Tucking the bag against a south-facing wall or shed-side is ideal as here it'll enjoy plenty of sunshine and be shielded from cold northerly winds.

When you make traditional leaf mold compost, you rely on the battalion of slow-working fungi among the microbial army to do the hard work. But in this accelerated composting method, you want to encourage the fast-working bacteria contingent to head up the recycling force. To do this, you need to regularly aerate the compost and add fresh oxygen, and the easiest way to do this is to give the bag a shake, flip it over or simply kick it along the ground every few days.

Do all these steps and your homemade compost will be ready to use in 4-5 months, right on time for when your garden wakes up in spring. You’ll know when it’s ready, even without opening the bag. While the microbes are busy breaking down the leaf mix, the contents will feel warmer to the touch; once they’re done, the temperature of the bag with match the ambient air temperature.

When you do open the bag, the compost should smell earthy, like a fresh forest floor. If you notice a slightly sour note, simply leave the sack open for a week or so to allow the compost to air.

Then you’re all ready to use your free compost to give your garden plants a nutritious boost for healthy growth, abundant blooms and bumper crops. Making a quick compost is one of the best ways to use fallen leaves in your garden so put this easy task on your list of garden jobs to do in fall.

This feature is part of the Weekend Wins series, packed with quick and easy gardening tasks that bring a big reward.

Waterlogged soil is the prime reason potted plants fail in fall and winter, and this speedy solution couldn't be simpler.

This great-value gardening tool transforms lawns in fall, fast, if you want lush grass next year for next-to-no effort.

Imagine going from daily sifting and scooping to just ditching a bag of used kitty litter one or twice a week â It is bliss.

There were only a couple of things I was a bit bummed about with the AutoScooper 12. Not having an alternative litter guard option to allow the use of long-fiber cat litters like tofu is a shame, particularly as these more eco-friendly materials are becoming more popular.

Another slight design flaw is that litter and debris accumulate around the top of the tray where the liner meets the unit, and need to be dislodged with a brush.

Overall, I think the AutoScooper 12 from PetPivot is a really nice little unit, particularly for the price. It could be a tad small if youâve got a big Maine Coon or similarly large breed of cat, but for everyone else, the compact size means you wonât struggle to find space to accommodate it.

If youâre on the fence about getting a self-cleaning litter box, but arenât sure if your budget can stretch to such luxuries, itâs time to check out the AutoScooper 12 from PetPivot. Your cats deserve it, and so do you. And at this price, an automatic litter box isnât just wishful thinking; it belongs on next weekâs shopping list.

PetPivot recommends only clay, mineral, or bentonite clumping cat litter. Crystal litter, non-clumping litter, or materials with long pieces like tofu litter are not suitable.

PetPivot advises that the unit is only suitable for cats over 6 months and weighing over 3 lbs. However, you can switch the unit to manual mode or keep it turned off to allow younger kittens to get used to it.

Yes! Although the litter tray sits at around 10 inches tall, the removable 6-inch step makes entry and exit easier for older cats.

The AutoScooper 12 comes with a 30-day return policy (unused units only) and a 12-month limited warranty. You can also purchase up to 3 years of accident protection when you buy from the PetPivot website.

The AutoScooper 12 is manufactured in China. PetPivot is a US-owned and operated company.

Every cat should have access to a clean litter box, and one of the most important parts of being a responsible cat parent is making sure that happens. Itâs also one of the most tedious parts, which is why weâre all very grateful to an engineer named Brad Baxter, inventor of the automatic litter box. For most of us, however, these technological wonders have long been seen as luxury items that only the super-rich could afford.

The compact & stylish AutoScooper 12 proves that those days are well and truly over.

This self-cleaning litter box from PetPivot is quiet, easy to use, and is more than a match for units that cost five or six times its price. So unless you love the daily drudgery of scooping out the litter box, go out and treat yourself to an AutoScooper 12 â you wonât regret it.

#8028. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Orphaned Kittens Are Suckling Each Other! (October 19, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

Our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their important social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are currently targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.
