A few thoughtful changes will keep your garden landscape looking effortlessly stylish through the cooler seasons.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While you might be thinking that the gardening season is drawing to a close this month, there's plenty to look forward to, especially if make a few simple switches to help your yard transition from fall into winter. As the year segues into the cooler months, it's time to enjoy colorful stems, textural bark, sculptural seedheads and shrubs bejewelled with bright berries, and relish the quiet beauty of this season.

Check through our landscape designer tricks to take a fall yard into winter, and add one or two to your outside space now. An injection of structural evergreens, naturalistic ornamental grasses, a tree with fiery foliage or colorful autumn bulbs can make a huge difference at this time of year now the late-season flower show is coming to an end.

Consider, too, how to make your fall garden user-friendly so you feel inspired to spend plenty of time outside still, perhaps by including a cosy gathering area around a fire pit. Which of these easy tricks landscape designers use to carry a garden from fall into winter are right for your yard?

Adding a mix of ornamental grasses is a fundamental element of fall garden design and these low-maintenance plants will continue to look good all through winter. While many annual and perennial flowering plants will happily grow through airy grasses in summer, the blades will keep borders looking full once they've finish blooming.

Choose varieties that offer bold autumn color such as Panicum virgatum ‘Shenandoah’, available from Nature Hills. Also known as switch grass, this well-behaved clump-forming grass develops stunning red and damson tones in fall, topped by wiry stems of flowers. Reaching 3 feet high, it looks fabulous planted among taller shrubs as well as with perennial blooms.

Another option favored by landscape designers is blue-green-leaved Festuca glauca 'Elijah Blue', also available from Nature Hills. Growing to just a foot high, it's perfect for border edges and winter containers.

Landscape designers often choose trees with fiery foliage to create a stunning focal point with brilliant shades of scarlet, russet, gold or burgundy. Even if space is limited, there are plenty of smaller trees that will squeeze into a compact garden.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some of most spectacular fall color is typically associated with Acer (maple) trees, but to carry the interest on into winter, choose a type with textural bark, too. Acer griseum, the paperbark maple and available from Plant Addicts, has peeling, papery warm-brown bark. Caught in the light of a low winter sun, its peeling curls of bark are nothing short of spectacular. The coral bark Japanese maple, available from trees.com, has bark in an intense red tone that's equally eye-catching.

Another option if you're wondering what to plant in fall is a multi-trunked tree that, once the bright foliage has fallen, brings architectural interest to your garden, like the Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry tree, available from trees.com.

Attractively planted container gardens are a landscape designer's best friend during the cooler months of the year. These portable pots of color and texture can be positioned wherever you want, adding a welcoming touch to an entrance or a bright splash to a patio table.

There are all sorts of vibrant plants that love life in a patio pot and last from fall into winter for a wonderful cool-season display. The go-to formula is to combine a thriller (height), filler (body) and spiller (edging) to create a full, textured look. Good choices for fall and winter include compact evergreens or ornamental grasses to add the height element, pansies to fill out the body of the planter, and ivy to tumble over the edges. For a modern look, squeezing a container full of a single variety is an even easier option.

Dwarf pine trees are enjoying a surge in popularity with landscape designers, and no wonder. While in spring, summer and fall they provide a green, textural foil to colorful flowers and leaves, once winter arrives they emerge as standout sculptural shapes. The beauty of slow-growing dwarf pines is that they naturally stay compact and well-shaped, so need very little looking after.

Dwarf Mugo pine (Pinus mugo var. pumilo) is a particular favorite thanks to its dense, dark needles. While it eventually grows to 3-5 feet high, its easily kept pruned into a neat mound. Dwarf Mugo pine, available from trees.com, keeps its seed cones all through winter, adding to the display. Adding one, or an odd number dotted through your outside space, is a great way to ensure your garden has character throughout the year, and helps avoid that sensation of sparseness that often happens in winter when many plants are dormant.

When summer perennials and annuals fade you will need something else to take their place. Autumn-flowering bulbs will pop up reliably year after year to add color and, if you choose the right sunny spot, will naturalise, gently spreading to reflect how comfortable they are in your landscape. This repetition will strengthen the planting design, as well as adding continuity.

Nerine bowdenii (also known as as Bowden lily) brings an explosion of color to rejuvenate tired fall borders. These beautiful bright blooms on sturdy stems grow to 24 inches, and can be added to pots as well as planted in drifts through a flowerbed. In addition to the standard pink petals, there are varieties from white through to a deep ruby red, and Dutch Grown stocks a good nerine selection. While it's too late to plant the bulbs this year, you can pre-order ready for planting in spring for floral fireworks next fall.

Another favorite is hardy cyclamen, which you'll likely find potted at your local garden center in fall. Plant a mix of the hardy ivy-leaved cyclamen (Cyclamen hederifolium), which flowers in fall and has pretty foliage that lasts through winter, and winter-flowering cyclamen (Cyclamen coum) which blooms winter into spring, for a long season of interest.

Even during the cooler months of the year, your outdoor space should be an inviting spot where you want to linger. A fire pit creates an ambient spot to gather around at dusk offers the opportunity for year-round entertaining, and is a go-to for landscape designers interested in creating an outdoor space with year-round usability.

Whether you want the crackle of real wood burning or the convenience of starting a fire with the click of a button, a fire pit will add visual as well as physical warmth to your fall and winter garden. Opt for a design that complements your overall aesthetic and add layers of textured cushions and throws in a palette of warm, earthy tones to garden furniture to build on the cozy vibe.

This fire pit is perfect for patio evenings, bringing friends and family together around a warm, inviting flame. Though it burns real wood, an airflow system facilitates efficient combustion to reduce smoke levels.

Fuelled by wood or wood pellets, this 7-inch diameter stainless steel mini fire pit brings the s'mores experience to a patio table. Efficient burning means it's smokeless and a removable ash pan makes clean-up easy.

Fuelled by propane gas, this stylish fire pit has an adjustable flame and can deliver plenty of warmth to keep your outdoor gatherings cozy. A lid lets it double as a coffee table and it's also available in black and stone-look.

Landscape designers often use a mix of materials to maximize texture and interest in garden design. These are automatically thrown into the spotlight during the cooler months of the year when plants die back and leave the hardscaping exposed. Gravel offers a softer alternative to bare paving slabs, and buff-toned pea gravel in mixed sizes and shapes like this landscaping pea gravel from Lowe's creates a particularly natural look.

Softening the edges of hard landscaping with plants is another landscape-designer trick that comes into its own as a garden moves from fall into winter. Use evergreen creeping thyme to blend the edges of a curving pathway and a functional garden element becomes an attractive winter feature. You can also use gravel as a mulch to avoid areas of bare border soil in winter, an option that's also easy on the budget.

Another way to maximise texture and help your garden transition from fall into winter without missing a beat is to add warm lighting from a low angle. In fall, a ground-stake spotlight will highlight foliage but then is easily moved to throw a glow through ornamental grass blades. Even a wash of light across a gravel path creates a play of shadows that shows off texture to the full, and allows you to appreciate your garden from indoors on dark evenings.

The easiest way to create individual pools of low light is with solar spotlights, although you'll need to shop smart when buying outdoor solar lights that will generate enough power in fall and winter. For a start, choose lights with adjustable solar panels so they can be angled to match the sun's lower position in the sky. Look for a high conversion rate and a large capacity battery of at least 1500 mAh, too, and opt for warm-toned LEDS that will create more ambiance than bright white lights. These Solar Spot Lights from Wayfair tick all three boxes.

Lifestyle journalist Sarah Wilson writes about garden design and landscaping trends. She has studied introductory garden and landscape design, and also has an RHS Level 2 qualification in the Principles of Plant Growth and Development. She is a regular contributor to Homes & Gardens and Livingetc. She has also written for Country Living, Country Homes & Interiors, and Modern Gardens magazines.

#7969. ‘Fireworks’ Goldenrod: A Pollinator Favorite with Bold Yellow Blooms

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Learn more about ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod, one of Melissa Starkey’s favorite underappreciated native plants.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

We’re moving into fall for this next pick. Goldenrods are amazing plants in general, even though they get a bad rap. People sometimes associate them with allergies, but they are confusing goldenrod with ragweed (Ambrosia spp.). Not all goldenrods are too aggressive. They are host plants for over 120 different moth and butterfly caterpillars, and the seeds feed birds and other animals.

If I had to pick just one to highlight, ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod would be my gateway plant to goldenrods. Anyone can use it in their garden, including in formal settings and in containers. ‘Fireworks’ is an appropriate name for this cultivar, as spires of bright yellow flowers explode in early to mid-autumn. It has a compact, clumping habit. This goldenrod can spread a little bit in moist soil, but it is not difficult to control, and it will stay put if you site it in a drier area. It likes full sun, but I have it in partial shade and it still looks lovely.

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.

Goldenrod photo courtesy of Deborah Gruca.

#7968. 10-Year "Harassment"/"Stalking" Sentence for Repeatedly Criticizing Police Detective Violated First Amendment, Amicus Brief Argues

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I was delighted to sign on to this brief in State v. McMenamy (Mo. Ct. App.) just filed by the ACLU of Missouri Foundation and the Wash. U (St. Louis) First Amendment Clinic, on behalf the ACLU of Missouri and Profs. Jane Bambauer and Lyrissa Lidsky and me. The Introduction:

The First Amendment and article I, § 8 of the Missouri Constitution broadly protect the right to speak to the public about other people. This is true even when the speech "is intended to trouble or annoy, or to make another timid or fearful." United States v. Sryniawski, 48 F.4th 583, 587 (8th Cir. 2022). And it is true even when speech uses "social pressure and the 'threat' of social ostracism … to embarrass others or coerce them into action." NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co., 458 U.S. 886, 910 (1982). While individuals who are the subjects of unwanted speech may be able to limit some speech directed to them, they cannot limit offensive speech about them directed to others. Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe, 402 U.S. 415, 419 (1971).

Contrary to this established law, Matthew McMenamy was convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison for openly and vigorously criticizing a local police detective he believed had engaged in misconduct. Mr. McMenamy used his public social media accounts and publicly distributed flyers to attempt to draw the community's attention to the detective's actions. He expressed his hope that his revelations would result in the officer's removal.

While Mr. McMenamy's speech was certainly concerning to the detective, the circuit court did not make any finding that either the flyers or any one of the dozens of social media posts submitted as evidence fell within any category of unprotected speech, such as true threats. Nor could the circuit court have done so, as none of Mr. McMenamy's speech was outside the bounds of the First Amendment's protection. His convictions for harassment and stalking violate the First Amendment and should be reversed.

The opening paragraph of the section on the facts (for the full discussion of the facts, read the brief):

In August 2023, Matthew McMenamy began posting on social media about what he viewed as misconduct and racism by a local police detective, who years before had been involved in Mr. McMenamy's involuntary commitment. See State's Exs. 60A–M. Mr. McMenamy sought to publicize one of the detective's public Facebook posts, where the detective wrote: "If black lives matter then why are they shooting and killing each other at an alarming rate." State's Ex. 60B ("Let's make this racist post go viral … #BLM #RacistCop ….); State's Ex. 60A ("The people want answers. Is [detective] a racist? Does he feel that people of color do not matter because of an idea that they murder each other at an alarming rate?"). Many of Mr. McMenamy's posts were aimed at sharing with the public his concerns about the detective's fitness for his position. For example, Mr. McMenamy posted he was "in talks with a billboard company to put [detective's] racist quotes up next to a picture of him in uniform" because "[s]omeone like that shouldn't be a detective, an election [sic] official, or let alone anything near public service." Tr. 736:10–21, State's Ex. 60K. Mr. McMenamy's posts also described his feelings about his prior involuntary commitment and thoughts about hurting his parents before getting help. See State's Ex. 60E (Mr. McMenamy's post that he "had a bad day last Sunday … I still need time to heal but … I am going to counseling and I will be looking for support groups").

And the opening material in the legal argument (again, read the brief for much more):

All of Mr. McMenamy's social media posts and his distribution of flyers were protected by the First Amendment. Harassment and stalking laws may, in some circumstances, be constitutionally applied to protect unwilling listeners from unwanted, one-to-one speech directed to that listener. The government's power to protect an unwilling listener from speech about them directed to the public, on the other hand, is sharply limited, even when that speech is annoying, offensive, or alarming. Unless such speech falls within one of the narrow, historically recognized categories of speech that the U.S. Supreme Court has held may be regulated without violating the First Amendment, such as "true threats," it is presumptively protected.

Here, Mr. McMenamy spoke to the public, and his speech did not fall within any unprotected category. This Court should reverse Mr. McMenamy's convictions. Even if this Court does not find that all Mr. McMenamy's speech is protected from criminal prosecution by the First Amendment, he is at least entitled to a new trial. The circuit court allowed the State to present evidence of more than four months' worth of social media posts to the jury and then instructed the jury it could find Mr. McMenamy guilty based on unidentified "alarming content" in these posts. This means a juror could have convicted Mr. McMenamy based on speech protected by the First Amendment.

[I.] The State's prosecution of Mr. McMenamy for harassment and stalking based on unwanted speech about individuals directed to the public violates the First Amendment.

Speech directed to the public at large is presumptively protected unless it falls into one of the narrow, historic exceptions to the First Amendment. This is because even if some listeners are likely to be offended, others may be willing listeners who find the speech valuable. For this reason, while harassment and stalking statutes may, in some instances, be constitutionally applied to repeated unwanted communications to an individual, they cannot be constitutionally applied to communications to the public about an individual.

[A.] Stalking and harassment statutes were originally intended to limit unwanted communications directed to a specific person.

For decades, laws have "restricted certain kinds of unwanted speech said to a particular person." For example, state and federal criminal harassment statutes were enacted to prohibit unwanted telephone calls to a particular person. Similarly, the federal government and some states have banned certain unwanted mailings into the home. These laws reflect an intention to protect individuals from repeated, unwanted communications to them, particularly in the home.

More recently, states enacted stalking laws to proscribe behaviors such as physically following, surveilling, or engaging in repeated unwanted personal contacts with a particular person. Courts have relied on stalking laws or restraining order laws to ban repeated or annoying letters, phone calls, or personal contact from a particular person. While some of these laws have been struck down in some states, "they have generally been upheld by lower courts; and the U.S. Supreme Court has upheld the federal ban on repeated unwanted mailings."

These laws share something in common: In the vast majority of their applications, they restrict unwanted speech to a person, not unwanted speech about a person. It is in this context—where the laws are being applied to "one-to-one speech"—that they "have generally been upheld against First Amendment challenge." Id.

As the internet has made it easier for communications to reach the public, maintaining this distinction between constitutionally permissible punishment of certain one-to-one speech and constitutionally impermissible punishment of one-to-many speech is critical. Social media is "the modern public square." However, the increased exposure for "upsetting" or "frightening" online speech can bring with it an increased risk of overcriminalization. Online communication "lack[s] many normal contextual clues," including tone of voice and expression. "The ubiquity of this speech raises the possibility of highly discretionary enforcement." Thus, in the context of online speech, courts must exercise particular caution to ensure the state's application of harassment and stalking laws does not exceed the laws' original intention or permissible constitutional boundaries.

[B.] The First Amendment grants broad protection to speech directed to the public at large, even when the subjects of that speech may be alarmed or offended.

The U.S. Supreme Court has consistently recognized a distinction between speech directed to the public at large and interpersonal speech for First Amendment purposes. Even when the content of the speech is subjectively offensive or alarming, the U.S. Supreme Court has typically protected public statements about a person—absent a showing of a narrow and well-established First Amendment exception, such as true threats, fighting words, or defamation.

As now-Justice Alito stated: "There is no categorical 'harassment exception' to the First Amendment's free speech clause." Saxe v. State Coll. Area Sch. Dist. (3d Cir. 2001); [citing other cases]. Many courts have endorsed this very point, quoting Saxe, in the context of criminal harassment laws and the closely related harassment restraining order laws. [Citing still more cases].

Unlike prohibitions on speech said to a particular unwilling listener, restrictions on speech to the public deprive a speaker of the opportunity to communicate with willing listeners. Denying access to potentially interested audiences undermines the use of speech to influence opinion and conduct and, as a result, hinders the robustness of public debate—particularly when the restricted speech concerns a matter of political, social, or other concern to the community. One's interest in being free from public criticism is insufficient to overcome protection for speech….

Accordingly, public statements about a person that coerce, annoy, alarm, offend, or embarrass are generally protected by the First Amendment. {The State may have some power to restrict narrowly defined categories of speech that reveals private information about a person that is "almost never relevant to any discussion on either public or private topics" (e.g., nude photos, Social Security numbers). No such speech is at issue here.} In Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), a local civil rights organization believed a local real estate broker's practices were improper. After the broker refused to sign an agreement not to solicit property in the organization's community, the organization distributed leaflets critical of the broker's supposedly racist real estate practices at a local shopping center, on the doors of his neighbors, and to people going to and from his church. Some leaflets accused him of being a "panic peddler" that employed tactics to scare white homeowners into selling their properties; others encouraged recipients to call his home phone number to express their disapproval. The U.S. Supreme Court concluded that the organization's "inten[t] to exercise a coercive impact … does not remove [speech] from the reach of the First Amendment. Petitioners plainly intended to influence respondent's conduct by their activities; this is not fundamentally different from the function of a newspaper." The U.S. Supreme Court explained, "so long as the means are peaceful, the communication need not meet standards of acceptability," particularly where the target of the speech "is not attempting to stop the flow of information into his own household, but to the public."

While speech that is intended to solicit violence against particular people may be punishable, speech to the public that harshly criticizes its target or that attempts to persuade through social pressure does not lose its protection even if some listeners may react with threats or violence. In NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co. (1982), organizers of a boycott of stores owned by white merchants read aloud and published the names of Black residents who weren't following the boycott to place pressure on them. As in Keefe, the U.S. Supreme Court held the disclosures constitutionally protected, noting the First Amendment extended beyond abstract discussions to protect "offensive" and "coercive" speech intended to influence action. This was true even though some of the people who chose not to comply with the boycott were beaten, had their property damaged, or had shots fired into their homes. The U.S. Supreme Court explained that speech designed to persuade "through social pressure and the 'threat' of social ostracism … does not lose its protected character … simply because it may embarrass others or coerce them into action." …

For a couple of articles of mine on the subject, see One-to-One Speech, One-to-Many Speech, Criminal Harassment Laws, and "Cyberstalking" and Overbroad Injunctions Against Speech (Especially in Libel and Harassment Cases.

The brief was signed by Kristin M. Mulvey, Jonathan D. Schmid, Gillian R. Wilcox, Jason A. Orr (ACLU Missouri) and Lisa S. Hoppenjans, Benjamin J. Wilson, and students Lindsey Bennett. Megan McConnell (Wash. U. First Amendment Clinic).

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: October 30, 1735

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7967. Susan’s Minnesota Garden, Part 2: Spring and Summer

Hi GPODers! We’re back in St. Paul, Minnesota (Zone 5a), for Part 2 of Susan Warde’s garden tour! Earlier this week, Susan shared a look at her garden from late July through October. Today we’re heading back to spring to see what was growing earlier in the season. Let’s take a look!

Here are some photos from late May through July.

The back garden. Wild cranesbill (Geranium maculatum, Zones 3–8) in the upper left corner is the only plant in flower at this time (late May), but the foliage is pretty, I think. The dominant hosta is ‘Blue Ivory’ (Hosta ‘Blue Ivory’, Zones 3–9).

Front garden (late May). I think the azalea is ‘Rosy Lights’ (Rhododendron ‘Rosy Lights’, Zones 3–7) from the Northern Lights azalea series.

Tall bearded iris (Iris ‘Cherished’, Zones 3–9), late May.

Tall bearded iris ‘Sultry Mood’, late May.

A Siberian iris (Iris sibirica cvs., Zones 3–9); I don’t know the cultivar name (late May).

My earliest clematis (Clematis ‘Acropolis’, Zones 4–9), with ‘Kansas’ peony (Paeonia lactiflora ‘Kansas’, Zones 3–8) in the background (early June).

This Asiatic lily (Lilium ‘Stracciatella Event’, Zones 3–8) was labeled ‘Stracciatella Event’, but it doesn’t look like the photos of that cultivar. Within a couple of days of this photo, taken July 6, the lily was demolished by scarlet lily beetles, which ultimately made mincemeat of all my lilies. The foliage looked so terrible that I had to cut them all down.

‘Lavender Moonchild’ daylily (Hemerocallis ‘Lavender Moonchild’, Zones 3–9), mid-July. Deer are a very rare occurrence in the city. I hadn’t seen one for years, but this summer two young bucks roamed the neighborhood, and every night they snacked on daylily buds and blossoms. They were not deterred by either of the sprays I tried.

This daylily is ‘Marquee Moon’. Set farther back in the garden, it was spared by the deer (mid-July).

A view of the side yard (July 25). Daylilies, garden phlox (Phlox paniculata cvs., Zones 4–8), coneflowers (Echinacea cvs., Zones 3–9), black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia cvs., Zones 3–9), and blazing stars (Liatris cvs., Zones 3–9) are all in bloom.

Thank you for sharing another look at your garden, Susan! I especially enjoyed seeing your collection of irises and daylilies, although I’m sorry the deer and lily beetles caused so much trouble this year.

If you missed Part 1, you can see Susan’s garden from late summer through fall.

#7966. Justice Department Announces Coordinated Actions to Combat North Korean Remote IT Worker Schemes Affecting More Than 70 U.S. Companies

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through remote information technology (IT) work for U.S. companies. These actions include an indictment, two arrests, searches of multiple known or suspected “laptop farms” in Texas pursuant to “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” and the seizure of approximately 187 computer devices used by DPRK IT workers.

“North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These schemes threaten the security of the IT systems and data of the deceived U.S. employers and leave countless victims of identity theft. NSD, along with our law enforcement partners, will use every available tool to track down anyone assisting the DPRK and to protect our national security.”

“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability. Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

“North Korea continues to deploy remote IT workers using stolen identities to infiltrate American companies and generate revenue for the regime and its weapons programs,” said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division. “Today, the FBI and DOJ announced a series of coordinated actions against this threat, securing charges against 14 individuals, conducting two arrests, seizing nearly 190 devices, and executing operations at more than 40 suspected ‘laptop farms’ across Texas. Close coordination between the private sector and federal law enforcement was central to this operation. To further combat the threat, the FBI has issued a Public Service Announcement with detailed mitigation guidance for U.S. companies.”

Sun Sheng Ming, et al. Indictment and Arrests – Northern District of Ohio

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio announced the arrests of U.S. nationals Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas pursuant to a four-count wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft indictment. The indictment describes a multi-year fraud scheme by Bostelle, Pena, and their co-conspirators to obtain remote IT work with U.S. companies that generated more than $3 million in revenue. The indictment also charges China-based Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang, Jin Long for their roles in the scheme. The identities of two additional defendants remain under seal.

According to the indictment, from 2019 to in or around July 2025, DPRK IT workers applied for and obtained remote positions by using stolen or fabricated identity documents, virtual private networks and proxy infrastructure to appear as though they were U.S. persons working from within the United States. They also relied on U.S.-based facilitators who received and hosted multiple laptop computers — issued by victim U.S. companies — at their residences in the United States (“laptop farms”), housed and configured those devices, installed remote-access software and transferred earnings to DPRK‑controlled accounts.

In total, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers. The revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by the DPRK. Victim employers included companies in the health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio, sixteen additional states, and the District of Columbia.

The FBI Cleveland Field Office is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Duncan T. Brown for the Northern District of Ohio and Trial Attorney Neeraj Gupta of the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section are prosecuting the case.

Operation Lonestar Roundup Disrupts Multiple Known or Suspected Laptop Farms in Texas

Between Sept. 21 and Sept. 25, the FBI conducted searches and other law enforcement action at over 40 residences in Texas known to be, or suspected of operating as, laptop farms for DPRK IT workers. Over the course of the entire operation (Operation Lonestar Roundup), the FBI seized approximately 187 laptops and KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) devices that DPRK IT workers and their U.S.-based facilitators used to commit fraud, obtain remote employment, and generate revenue for the North Korean regime’s sanctioned weapons programs. U.S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has identified this group of DPRK IT workers and their helpers as “Famous Chollima.”

Investigators discovered that the DPRK operatives allegedly used a network of fraudulent email accounts to facilitate their criminal activity. The following accounts were among those identified as being used in these schemes:

Employers are encouraged to add these accounts to the list of indicators they use to identify and disrupt DPRK IT worker employment.

Today, the FBI published a public service announcement describing the evolving DPRK IT worker threat, including tips on how to detect the threat. Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. Additionally, CrowdStrike today published a blog post describing its efforts at monitoring customer networks for DPRK IT worker activity and its successful collaboration with the FBI to disrupt this threat.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, the FBI’s Dallas Field Office, and the FBI’s Cyber Division coordinated Operation Lonestar Roundup. Valuable assistance was provided by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio.

Today’s announcements represent the Department’s latest actions to combat North Korean IT worker schemes as part of a joint NSD and FBI Cyber and Counterintelligence Divisions effort, the DPRK RevGen: Domestic Enabler Initiative. This effort prioritizes targeting and disrupting the DPRK’s illicit revenue generation schemes and its U.S.-based enablers. The Department previously announced other actions pursuant to the initiative, including in June 2025, November 2025, April 2026, and May 2026.

As described in Public Service Announcements published in May 2024, January 2025, July 2025, and today, North Korean remote IT workers posing as legitimate remote IT workers have committed data extortion and exfiltrated the proprietary and sensitive data from U.S. companies. DPRK IT worker schemes typically involve the use of stolen identities, alias emails, social media, online cross-border payment platforms, and online job site accounts, as well as false websites, proxy computers, and witting and unwitting third parties located in the U.S. and elsewhere. North Korean IT workers leverage these third parties, which include U.S.-based individuals, to gain fraudulent employment and access to U.S. company networks to generate this revenue.

Other public advisories about the threats, red flag indicators, and potential mitigation measures for these schemes include a May 2022 advisory released by the FBI, Department of the Treasury, and Department of State; a July 2023 advisory from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and guidance issued in October 2023 by the United States and the Republic of Korea (South Korea). As described the May 2022 advisory, North Korean IT workers have been known individually to earn up to $300,000 annually, generating hundreds of millions of dollars collectively each year, on behalf of designated entities, such as the North Korean Ministry of Defense and others directly involved in the DPRK’s weapons programs.

The U.S. Department of State has offered potential rewards for up to $5 million in support of international efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s illicit financial activities, including for cybercrimes, money laundering, and sanctions evasion.

The details in the above-described court documents are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7965. Halloween in the Garden: 3 Spooky and Creative Displays

Happy Friday, GPOD! Halloween is tomorrow, so for our last post of the week, I couldn’t resist digging through past GPODs for a little spooky-season garden inspiration. Over the years, contributors have shown us that Halloween decor doesn’t have to stop at the front door. A foggy morning can turn a familiar garden wonderfully eerie, homegrown pumpkins can become an entire cast of characters, and flowers and foliage from the garden can transform simple gourds into works of art. Today we’re revisiting three very different Halloween displays that all have their own charm and appeal.

We’ll start in Hebron, Kentucky, with Keri Shinault’s perfectly spooky garden. Keri and her husband, Brandon, began hosting an annual Halloween masquerade after their October 2005 wedding, eventually decorating their home and garden with creepy critters, ghouls, headstones, and plenty of other spooky surprises.

A beautiful sitting area surrounded by lush plants becomes instantly more mysterious when fog blurs the garden beyond.

Sometimes Mother Nature provides the best Halloween special effects.

Sit a while! Take a load off those tired bones.

Stepping stones set into lush ground covers guide you around massive oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia, Zones 5–9) shrubs.

Next up are Tom and Jeannie Tremont’s delightfully ridiculous pumpkin people. Rather than simply lining the porch with gourds, Tom and Jeannie turned their pumpkins into an entire cast of characters with their own poses, props, and personalities.

Why settle for a jack-o’-lantern when your pumpkins can go for a bike ride? Tom and Jeannie turned their fall harvest into a whole cast of characters, complete with wheels.

Tom and Jeannie Tremont clearly weren’t interested in ordinary jack-o’-lanterns. This pumpkin person looks like they got caught with their pants down while a family bikes by in the background. It’s ridiculous in the best possible way.

The mama-and-baby pumpkin pair might be the sweetest of the bunch. Even commenters on the original GPOD singled this little duo out as a favorite.

We’ll end with something completely different from Cherry Ong in Richmond, British Columbia. For her dazzling pumpkin display, Cherry repurposed the pallet-wood auricula theaters she and her husband had built for spring into a stage for decorated pumpkins and squash.

Auricula theaters traditionally protect auriculas (Primula auricula, Zones 3–8) from harsh rain and wind, but Cherry discovered they make a pretty spectacular fall display too.

Cherry and her husband built these pallet-wood auricula theaters a couple of years earlier—he constructed and hung the boxes, while Cherry designed and stained them. In fall, the shelves get a totally new look when pumpkins and gourds take the place of spring flowers.

Cherry had a little fun displaying the smaller pumpkins before giving them away, using old mini terra-cotta pots to add height and variation. Some pumpkins were decorated with seasonal flowers and foliage from the garden, turning the whole theater into one big botanical arrangement.

A small white pumpkin topped with clusters of Chinese tea rosebuds shows just how detailed Cherry gets with these creations. Elsewhere in the display, she also incorporated dried dahlias and other flowers and foliage from the garden.

I love how each of these gardeners found a unique way to bring Halloween into their outdoor spaces. That might be my favorite thing about Halloween in the garden: there really aren’t many rules. You can go creepy, silly, beautiful, botanical—or somehow all four at once. I hope everyone has a happy Halloween tomorrow! If you’re decorating your garden, porch, containers, or homegrown pumpkins this weekend, I’d love to see what you come up with.

#7964. Discovery Sanctions Recommended in "Are You a Jew? … Are You a Zionist?" Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The factual allegations, from a Sept. 2025 decision in the case by Judge Susan Illston (N.D. Cal.) (the case is Radice v. Jerusalem Boxing Club, LLC consolidated with the federal government's U.S. v. Harara):

The Jerusalem Coffee House [which Harara owns] is a business establishment open to the general public. The coffee house is located on the premises of the East Bay Community Space, "which regularly hosts events that are open to the general public for exhibition or entertainment …."

According to the complaint, on June 10, 2024, Michael Radice—who is Jewish—went to the East Bay Community Space "for the purpose of viewing the establishment for a fundraising event for his organization." Radice was wearing a dark blue baseball cap with a light blue Star of David and white Hebrew lettering. As he approached the community space from the side where the coffee house is located, a man sitting at a table in front of the coffee house asked, "Are you a Jew?" Radice answered in the affirmative. The man then asked, "Are you a Zionist?" Radice declined to respond.

The complaint alleges that "[t]he man then began shouting numerous accusations at Mr. Radice, including that he was complicit in Israel's military actions in the Gaza Strip following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks and guilty of 'killing children.'" As Radice began to walk away, the man stood up and asked, "Where are you going?" The complaint alleges, "Mr. Radice saw another man, whom he later learned was Harara, walk out of the coffee house and speak to the man, and the two went inside." …

And now from Judge Thomas Hixson's Report and Recommendation yesterday:

There is no dispute that Defendant Abdulrahim Harara violated at least six discovery orders. Motion at 4-7 ("Harara has flouted at least six discovery orders," and enumerating the violations); Opp. at 7 ("But the question on this motion is not whether any order was violated; it is whether the record as a whole shows the kind of deliberate, deceptive obstruction that makes a fair trial impossible and justifies ending the case without one.")….

The real issue is what remedy the Court should impose for the serial violations of its discovery orders. The impact of Harara's conduct basically falls into three buckets: documents were produced late that should have been produced earlier; some document productions are incomplete; and there has been a wholesale failure to produce email. But having reviewed the voluminous evidence submitted in support of Radice's motion for sanctions, the Court thinks truth is available to the parties, and they should go ahead and have a trial on the existing record.

Harara's biggest failure in discovery is the nonproduction of email, and he does not have a good excuse. In many cases the total failure to produce email would justify terminating sanctions or at least adverse inference instructions.

But the Court is skeptical that this is such a case. The relevant events are alleged in-person refusals to serve Radice and another individual because they are Jewish. In other words, the relevant events did not occur by email. Before email existed, public accommodation discrimination claims like this were tried the old fashioned way: The participants in the alleged events testified, and the trier of fact decided who to believe. That option is still available here.

Email is still relevant, of course, because it could contain statements about what happened, or have evidence of the defendant's allegedly prejudicial intent. But here a lot of that type of evidence was produced in the form of Harara's text messages and social media feeds and other electronic records. These include a statement that seems to be by Harara that seems to say he throws pennies on the ground when Jews walk by; the coffee shop menu and outdoor signage with inverted red triangles, which Radice alleges is a symbol used by Hamas to mark Israeli targets in propaganda videos; the apparent introduction on the one year anniversary of the October 7 attack of a juice item named for a mastermind of the attack; a video of Harara telling a Jewish customer to leave because he had "a violent hat," referring to the Star of David on the hat; and a repost by Harara to his X account bearing the "Bay Area" screen name of a November 2, 2024 post calling that same Jewish customer "a genocidal, bottom dwelling Zionist scum" who "should be kicked out of every public establishment not just Palestinian owned ones!" There are also text messages that replicate the kind of thing a plaintiff would dream of finding in a defendant's emails—and certainly at trial Radice and the United States will argue these texts are strong evidence of liability.

Radice is certainly of the view that he has uncovered good evidence, even if it was produced later than it should have been, and even though it does not include email. See Motion at 15 ("The 6134 Bates-labeled pages and 2474 native files that Harara produced on or after August 7 include inflammatory documents that Harara willfully withheld until after discovery closed."); id. ("For example, a January 3, 2025 JCH Instagram post shows JCH advertising for sale a t-shirt featuring the Jerusalem Coffee House name ringed by flags with the emblem of Hamas, a designated terrorist organization dedicated to violence against Jews and Israelis."); id. ("His Instagram direct-messages contain both antisemitic tropes and antisemitic slurs.").

With all this evidence, can it really be said that Harara's failings in discovery have prejudiced Plaintiffs to such an extent that a meaningful and fair trial is no longer possible? That adverse inferences are needed because there is not enough evidence for the trier of fact to reliably draw conclusions about what happened?

No. These cases are about whether a coffee shop committed discrimination, and Harara has produced enough documents that Radice and the United States have what they need to go to trial. Even with the nonproduction of email, it is not true that discovery failed or that truth cannot be ascertained. The public policy in favor of deciding cases on the merits applies here.

Accordingly, the Court RECOMMENDS that the district judge DENY the request for terminating sanctions because there's just no need or basis for it. The Court DENIES the request for adverse inferences because it is essentially a request for a directed verdict. Each side should put on their case at trial, and truth should be determined in the normal way. There is no reason for the Court to stack the deck.

But that doesn't mean Harara escapes sanctions. He needs to pay for what he did. His serial violations of Court orders significantly drove up Radice's cost of litigating [the case]. Radice requests $166,500.50 against all Defendants. The entity Defendants have been in default during the period of time when Harara violated the Court orders, so are not the cause of Radice's increased legal expenses, and therefore will not be sanctioned.

Plaintiff's counsel's rates are reasonable. However, both the Benesch and ADL attorneys seek fees for work that preceded the violations of the Court orders, a problem that requires deducting about a third of the Benesch time and about a fifth of the ADL's time. That brings the total down to $118,000. In addition, even though Harara violated multiple discovery orders, it is also true that Plaintiff's counsel litigated [the case] with excessive ferocity. At times it seemed they were not just litigating a discrimination case but were out to destroy Harara. As a result their fees were excessive. The Court estimates that about half of the fees Radice incurred during the time when Harara was violating the discovery orders was due to the violations and the other half was for work that would have needed to be done anyway or that should not have been done at all because it was excessive. Accordingly, the Court SANCTIONS Harara in the amount of $59,000 and ORDERS him to pay that amount to Radice within 30 days.

In his opposition, Harara proposes some remedial measures. However, the Court will not adopt any of them. The proposal to remedy the lack of email production presupposes that Harara will have a lawyer to represent him. Opp. at 16 ("The full inbox Mr. Harara exported on September 3, 2026 will be reviewed by counsel, consistent with the Court's ruling that counsel rather than Mr. Harara conduct that review. That counsel will be either counsel Mr. Harara retains or volunteer limited-scope counsel appointed through the Court's Federal Pro Bono Project under General Order 25, to which Mr. Harara respectfully requests referral. Since his counsel withdrew, Mr. Harara has contacted lawyers and legal organizations and has not found a lawyer who will take his case."). However, Harara's inability to work cooperatively with two sets of counsel means this is an unrealistic proposal. And if no lawyer represents him, Harara's proposal contains no particular deadline by which emails would be produced. Opp. at 16 ("If counsel has not been retained or appointed within 30 days of the Court's order, Mr. Harara will file a status report every 14 days thereafter. In all events, the production under this paragraph will be complete within 90 days of the Court's order; if it is not, Mr. Harara will show cause why not, and the Court may then impose such further measures as it finds appropriate after notice and an opportunity to be heard.").

Harara's proposal to serve further interrogatory responses is highly unlikely to achieve anything. And there is no need for a further deposition of him; Plaintiffs' counsel can cross-examine him at trial….

NEXT: 10-Year "Harassment"/"Stalking" Sentence for Repeatedly Criticizing Police Detective Violated First Amendment, Amicus Brief Argues

#7961. Amicus Brief in OneTaste Criminal Prosecution

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Matt Kezhaya (Kezhaya Law PLC) wrote an amicus brief on my behalf in this case (U.S. v. Cherwitz & Daedone) a few weeks ago—many thanks to him for all his work on it!—and I thought I'd pass it along:

Under the Government's theory of spiritual coercion, people who at one point believed that volunteering for a religious organization is the path to enlightenment or salvation, but who later become disillusioned with their former beliefs, can be found to have been retroactively "coerced" into providing that labor. The same logic could apply to nuns who had felt religious pressure to do the educational or nursing work that their order was known for, or to monks who had felt religious pressure to do agricultural work that supports the monastery. Any religious organization that runs a monastery, convent, or any other institution where adherents are expected to work as part of their religious vocation could likewise face felony prosecutions.

Such a theory of criminal liability violates the Free Exercise Clause because it is not "neutral." Governments depart from neutrality not just when legislators pass laws designed to suppress religion, but also when courts enforce otherwise-neutral laws in ways that suppress religion precisely because of spiritual or religious qualities. Liability in this case turned precisely on the religious nature of the allegedly coercive conduct, and was imposed in the absence of any secular coercion such as violence or the threat of violence.

The sexual subject matter and conduct inherent within OneTaste's beliefs and practices is beside the point. The forced labor statute is not limited to sexual labor. 18 U.S.C. § 1589. Rather, it generally prohibits any "labor" obtained through "threats of serious harm." 18 U.S.C. § 1589(a)(3). Indeed, the "labor" subject of this charge was ordinary, non-sexual administrative work entailed in running a religious organization that features events and communal living.

To be sure, laws that restrict sexual labor will usually be neutral and generally applicable, precisely because they do not turn on any claims of religious or spiritual coercion. If any business, religious or not, offers its employees' sexual services in exchange for money, that might well violate generally applicable bans on prostitution or pandering. Likewise, if any business, religious or not, conditions employment on the employee's performing sexual services, that will usually constitute civilly actionable quid pro quo sexual harassment. And enforcing such laws would not jeopardize ordinary religious labor, precisely because they are focused on a narrow range of secularly-defined behavior that is seen as harmful (the exchange of sex for money or employment) rather than on a theory of spiritual coercion that can apply to a wide range of labor.

But such laws were not used in this case. The essence of this charge was punishing a particular religious group. The Court should vacate the convictions, or at least reverse and remand for a new trial with proper limiting instructions.

[I.] A theory of "spiritual coercion" violates the Free Exercise Clause.

The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment prohibits governments from targeting specific religious beliefs or practices as such. Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993). That prohibition bars more than just legislative enactments expressly targeting religion; it extends to criminal prosecutions that apply facially neutral laws in ways that target disfavored religious beliefs. Fowler v. State of R.I., 345 U.S. 67 (1953).

Of course, as Part III will discuss, "neutral" and "generally applicable" criminal statutes may be applied to religious behavior precisely the same way they are applied to secular behavior; otherwise, each of us would "become a law unto himself." Emp. Div., Dep't of Hum. Res. of Oregon v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872, 885 (1990); see also Reynolds v. United States, 98 U.S. 145, 167 (1878). But this power cannot be used to target religious actions because of their religious or spiritual character.

The threshold inquiry is whether the ideas are, within OneTaste's scheme of things, "religious." See Patrick v. LeFevre, 745 F.2d 153, 158-59 (2d Cir. 1984). Indisputably, Defendants, OneTaste, and adherents of OneTaste (including the so-called victims) all considered the doctrines subject of this criminal trial to be "religious." See A-977 ("We believed that … your path to God was through your orgasm") (emphasis added); see also A-1053 (adherents of OneTaste seek "something more" beyond ordinary existence believe "Our most potent biological drive, Orgasm, is the key to unlocking this power.").

OneTaste's doctrines addressed distinctions between the physical and spiritual realms in a dichotomy between the "third dimension" and the "fourth dimension." See A-694. They addressed issues of worldly suffering and promised both enlightenment and transcendence through ceremonial rites. A-1114 (orgasm "was more about energy," borrowing from "Buddhist principles like the concept of qi"); see also A-1446 ("OneTaste teachings integrate the principles of mindfulness with the practice of orgasm"); A-1089 (OneTaste teachings included sex "as a ritual practice" and "Magic School … where we had sort of like priests and priestesses of orgasm"); see also A-1426-1427 (PowerPoint presentation outlining "Alchemize shadow into power through orgasm" and "Orgasm Magic: Bringing out the elements of magic [and] Put the principles of OM into practice in creating what you want … [including] Rituals and ceremonies"). Specific ceremonies described in the record include a marriage ceremony at A-891, a foot soaking ritual at A-1085, and a shower ritual at A-1152. The central ritual tenet of OneTaste was ritualistic sexual activity is, OMing, or "Orgasmic Meditation," which adherents of OneTaste regard as a mindfulness practice, a "meditation on sensation without a goal," A-577, A-785.

The Government made much of the sexual nature of those beliefs and practices. E.g., A-1229. But it is no business of the government, including the courts, to "prescribe what shall be orthodox in … religion." W. Virginia State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624, 642 (1943). Because OneTaste and its adherents considered these beliefs and practices to be "religious" within their scheme of things, the Free Exercise Clause protects their beliefs and practices from governmental targeting.

And the Government did not seriously contest OneTaste's religiosity; instead, it acknowledged, and even stressed, the spiritual and religious nature of OneTaste's activities. According to the Government's closing arguments, the essence of the charge was that "the defendants indoctrinated the victims to believe that Nicole Daedone was a guru and that her teachings were the path to enlightenment and spiritual growth." A-1222. Prosecutors took issue that "Nicole Daedone taught that orgasm was God." A-1232. And "[n]early all of them [victims] lived in OneTaste housing and were subjected to these teachings incessantly." A-1234. The complained-of "indoctrination" and "teachings" is the very essence of religion: leading adherents to accept doctrines as spiritual truths. That these supposed victims ordered their lives in accordance with OneTaste's beliefs and practices is evidence of spiritual and religious belief, not of criminally punishable coercion.

Had there been evidence these "victims" were physically coerced into accepting OneTaste's religious doctrines, such physical coercion would certainly have been illegal. But that was not the Government's theory. Each of these so-called victims freely admitted that they voluntarily joined the organization. A-267-268; A-872-873; A-939; A-1152-1153. And they freely admitted that they voluntarily left it. A-882; A-939; A-1107. The "indoctrination" and "teachings" for which Defendants stood trial only describes proselytization, the very essence of religion, which cannot be criminally punished.

Likewise, the prosecution argued that Defendants "disrupted victims' personal relationships and isolated them from their friends and family." A-1222; see also A-1235 (victims "felt like OneTaste was all they had"). More particularly, Defendants did so by encouraging some of their adherents, including these "victims," to live in a commune with other like-minded believers. A-262, 359-60, 775, 893-894, 1004-06. But this disruption likewise stemmed not from physical coercion or threats of violence, of deportation, or of other secular harm. Rather, it stemmed from the adherents' sense of the spiritual value of participating in a particular religious and spiritual community. A-872; A-1008-1009 (Ms. Kandell, particularly, described her time at the commune as "one of the greatest experiences of my life," partly because of "the sense of community" and "the focus of the communal living"); A-1138-1139.

This is a commonplace practice among many religious orders. By definition, any follower of any monastic tradition could be described as having their personal relationships "disrupted" or becoming "isolated" from their less committed friends and family. Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1190. Nor does it say anything that a religion discourages association with non-adherents, as many religious groups do. E.g., Paul v. Watchtower Bible & Tract Soc'y of N.Y., Inc., 819 F.2d 875, 883 (9th Cir. 1987) ("The harms suffered by Paul as a result of her shunning by the Jehovah's Witnesses are clearly not of the type that would justify the imposition of tort liability for religious conduct. No physical assault or battery occurred.").

The Government also invited the jury to convict because Defendants "financially harmed victims by driving them into debt and not paying them for their labor." A-1222. More specifically, the Government stressed that Defendants accepted, and even encouraged, these "victims" to volunteer their services to their chosen religious organization. A‑908‑910; A‑1028‑1030; A‑1095-1103. But these "victims" were not coerced or defrauded into performing these volunteer services; they knew full well that their services would be unpaid, and they still chose to volunteer their efforts. A-947-48; A-1152-53; A872-76. This too is commonplace among religions: Under our constitutional tradition, it is a defining feature of religion that it relies on charitable contributions of money, goods, and services from its adherents. See generally James Madison et al., Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments (reproduced in full at Everson v. Bd. of Ed. of Ewing Twp., 330 U.S. 1, 63–72 (1947)). Indeed, many religions call for participants to tithe 10% of all their secular income. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1180 n. 5. But for First Amendment protections, a hostile jury could punish that practice as extortion because of religious pressure constituting "the threat of social ostracism or eternal damnation, or from the promise of community or of eternal." Id., at 1180.

The crux of the Government's charge was that the Defendants "forced" the purported victims to perform voluntary services through religious indoctrination and, more generally, made them feel reliant on OneTaste. See A-1236 (victims "felt like their whole world was OneTaste. It was their community, their friends, where they worked, and where they lived. And the defendants did all of this by design"). But such feelings of deliberately induced reliance on a religious community are entirely unremarkable in the religious context. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1183 (observing that a common technique among many religions is to "slowly lur[e] people into a community and a belief system that they may eventually find emotionally hard to leave, even if they feel some desire to leave").

Many Christians preach eternal damnation without Christ. Buddhists preach eternal suffering without dharma. Latter-day Saints encourage extensive participation in church callings, missionary service, and a tightly integrated congregational life. Countless religious traditions promise spiritual fulfillment, enlightenment, or eternal happiness through faithful adherence to their beliefs and practices. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1180, 1190. Many religions cause each of us to act and believe in ways non-adherents of our chosen path would find to be irrational or even "rank heresy." See United States v. Ballard, 322 U.S. 78, 86 (1944).

It is no answer for the Government to charge that these so-called victims felt "compelled" to perform the subject services because that compulsion was the product of religious conviction. If each of us are to be entrusted with the right to enter and exit our chosen religions at will, then each of us must also accept the risk that our chosen religions may cause us to donate time, money, or goods. The Court should find that the Free Exercise Clause prohibits this conviction.

[II.] The trial itself was not religiously "neutral."

Government's enforcement action, even under a facially religion-neutral generally applicable statute, violates the Free Exercise Clause when the enforcement of the statute is itself not "neutral," See Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado C.R. Comm'n, 584 U.S. 617, 634 (2018). In Masterpiece Cakeshop, the government sought to enforce Colorado's public accommodations statute in part because of the religious motivations of a baker. Commissioners departed from neutrality by describing the baker's religious beliefs as "despicable" and characterized them as merely rhetorical. Id., at 635. Even "subtle departures from neutrality" on matters of religion are prohibited, not just when a legislative branch enacts a law but also when the executive branch enforces it. See id., at 638.

Just as in Masterpiece Cakeshop, the record in this case is replete with denigration of this particular religion. Ms. Gupta invited the jury to scrutinize OneTaste's vocabulary and the specific doctrines as evidence of wrongdoing. A-1232. She emphasized the specialized use of words or phrases "TurnON" (which seemed [synonymous] with the yoga phrase "state of flow"), "muggles" (meaning non-adherents of OneTaste), "matrix" (referring to "my fake reality of problems"), and "tumescence" (in the specialized spiritual sense of "bad energy that you were holding onto"), and the dichotomy between the "third dimension" (the "concrete world") and the "fourth dimension" ("the higher plane"), and asserted these words or phrases were being used to "indoctrinate the victims." A-1232, A-1235. This argument directly invited the jury to judge unfamiliar or strange religious concepts as proof of religious illegitimacy, which neither prosecutors nor jurors may do. See Masterpiece Cakeshop, 584 U.S. at 639; Fowler, 345 U.S. at 70.

Religions routinely use specialized phrasing like "saved," "possessed," "called," or "enlightened," which may appear unacceptable or incomprehensible to outsiders. That strangeness does not deprive OneTaste of First Amendment protections and certainly cannot underlie a felony criminal conviction, especially when the phrasing refers to spiritual or transcendental concepts. See Thomas v. Rev. Bd. of Indiana Emp. Sec. Div., 450 U.S. 707, 714 (1981). Quite the opposite: Our natural aversion to other religions is why we have tolerance protections enshrined in the First Amendment to begin with. See Ballard, 322 U.S. at 87; see also Marsh v. Chambers, 468 U.S. 783, 792 (1983).

The prosecutor also described OneTaste as a "sex cult." A-1223, A-1264. That label was inherently pejorative. See United States v. Helbrans, No. S219CR497NSR0102, 2021 WL 4778525, *17 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 12, 2021) (prohibiting the Government from referring to defendants as being part of a "cult," prohibiting insinuations that "leaders brainwash or force members of the community to behave in or observe their religion in a certain way," and prohibiting "incendiary and irrelevant references" to the religious organization). The prosecutor was using this label as a rhetorical device to persuade jurors that OneTaste's teaching should be regarded with suspicion because they were unconventional. Just like in Masterpiece Cakeshop, this label was employed with the impermissible goal of suggesting the illegitimacy of a particular set of religious beliefs and practices. See 584 U.S. at 635.

The prosecutor argued, "that's not because OMing  was actually spiritual. They connected OMing to spirituality for legal protection, and so people would follow Nicole Daedone's teachings." A-1233; see also A-1381 ("They [Defendants] whittled them [victims] down by … indoctrinating them with so-called spiritual teachings and practices."). But what forms of meditation are "actually" spiritual and what are just "so-called" spiritual is not for secular courts to decide. It is no business of our secular government to "prescribe what shall be orthodox in … religion." Barnette, 319 U.S. at 642. The Government simply cannot put the legitimacy of religious or spiritual ideas on trial. Ballard, 322 U.S. at 86-88. Yet the Government did exactly that by arguing:

It is not okay to teach your employees that their spiritual purpose is to fuck the war out of men and that if they stray from the [path] set by OneTaste and by Nicole Daedone, they will be spiritually ruined.

And while there is a narrow zone in which a properly instructed jury can determine whether people's religious beliefs are sincerely held, United States v. Seeger, 380 U.S. 163, 165 (1965), no such instruction was given to the jury in this case. Quite the contrary, the District Court declined to provide jury instructions that any "alleged threats were covered by the First Amendment." A-1211. The District Court even warned defense counsel against referencing Defendants' First Amendment rights: "I'm not going to let you instruct the jury or even come close to instructing the jury on the First Amendment." A-1212. And the District Court refused to order a mistrial despite that the Government "ask[ed] the jury to hold their spiritual beliefs against them." A-1315-1316 (argument); A-1318 (denial).

The Government's rhetorical devices are a far cry from the neutrality required by Masterpiece Cakeshop. The Government was overtly hostile to Defendants' religion in itself and openly invited the jury to judge the legitimacy of OneTaste's religious doctrines and practices. It is no answer that the jury accepted the Government's invitation because the highest law of the land removes that power from legislator, judge, juror, and prosecutor alike. "If one could be sent to jail because a jury in a hostile environment found those teachings to be false, little indeed would be left of religious freedom." Ballard, 322 U.S. at 87.

[III.] Defendants were not charged with commercial sexual practices.

To be sure, nothing in this argument precludes the application of genuinely neutral laws to regulate commercial sexual behavior. For instance, an organization that sells members' or employees' sexual services for money can still be subject, under Employment Division v. Smith, to neutral and generally applicable bans on prostitution. Such laws can be applied without resorting to arguments about spiritual coercion, or claims that the defendant supposedly "indoctrinat[ed people] to believe that [she] was a guru and that her teachings were the path to enlightenment and spiritual growth." A-1222. It would not matter whether the  defendant "taught that orgasm was God." A-977. Commercial sale of certain services that lead to orgasm would be the crime, with no need to address the spiritual significance of the orgasm itself.

Likewise, if an employee claims that an employer required sexual services as a condition of employment, the employee could sue for quid pro quo sexual harassment, again a matter that is entirely religion-neutral. Indeed, the government could even criminalize such quid pro quo sexual harassment. See Tex. Penal Code Ann. § 39.03 (criminalizing sexual harassment under color of public office).

Unlike with the Government's expansive reading of the coerced labor statute, none of this would threaten religions that have a tradition of monasticism, or of religious labor as a calling. None of this would treat religious or spiritual teachings as "coercion." And none of this would treat such teachings as crimes when they lead people to feel moved, or even spiritually or religiously obligated, to perform certain tasks that are given to them by a spiritual or religious community.

Of course, in this case the Government chose not to prosecute under statutes banning commercial sale of sexual services—perhaps because there was no evidence that money was being exchanged in return for sexual activity. But these laws exist, and deal with genuine commercialization of sex. Likewise, laws banning rape and sexual assault exist, and deal with genuine physical coercion of sexual acts. There is no reason for a concern about possible commercialization of sex to be used to justify an overbroad reading of coerced labor statutes, which would apply far more broadly than just to sex.

Because the Government's theory of coercion rested in part on "indoctrination" into religious and spiritual beliefs and threats of excommunication from a religious and spiritual community, these criminal convictions cannot withstand Free Exercise Clause scrutiny….

#7960. Kathy’s Fall Garden

Happy Monday, GPOD! Halloween may be behind us, but fall still has plenty to offer in Kathy’s Zone 6a garden. I love how she keeps the seasonal decorating simple and lets what’s already happening in the landscape do most of the work. A few pumpkins, a refreshed container, and plants still hanging onto their color are enough to make the whole front garden feel ready for November.

Keeping it sweet and simple this fall! It has been a beautiful fall in Michigan so far. Although I’ve been gardening for more than 40 years, this is my eighth year gardening at our current home in Macomb.

I love these Japanese forest grasses (Hakonechloa macra cvs., Zones 5–9).

I replaced this summer container display earlier than usual, and these plants have been hanging tough since the first week of September.

Just sweet! There has been a multitude of fancy pumpkins for sale this year, more than usual, and I think they are so pretty!

Boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), Fire Chief arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis ‘Congabe’, Zones 5–8), ‘Orange Rocket’ Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii ‘Orange Rocket’, Zones 4–9), and Little Lime® panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘Jane’, Zones 3–8) grow in front of our home.

Already, I’m looking forward to spring when I can plant this new garden arch! I’m thinking clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9).

Here is Belleza Dark Pink gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri ‘KLEAU04263’, Zones 6–9) and yellow ‘Lady Stratheden’ avens (Geum ‘Lady Stratheden’, Zones 5–9). They are hanging tough so far!

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Kathy! I really like the little bed by the driveway. The purple tones of the ajuga carpeting the ground against that bright orange mum and the pumpkins make for such an effortlessly beautiful fall display. #7959. A November Garden Walk in Downtown Milwaukee

November is definitely settling in here in downtown Milwaukee, Wisconsin (Zone 6a). Most of the summer flowers are gone, leaves are piling up, and plenty of perennials are heading into dormancy. But there’s still so much to appreciate. Today we’re staying close to home for a walk around my neighborhood. I walk these streets with my dog all the time, and there are a handful of gardens I always slow down to admire.

Starting off strong with this one! This prairie-inspired garden is always buzzing with pollinators in summer, and it’s one of my favorites to walk by. In fall, the large sweeps of switchgrass (Panicum virgatum, Zones 4–9) and little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, Zones 3–9) really come forward. And wow, those fluffy switchgrass plumes make a statement when planted en masse.

From the other side, the pinkish-copper tones of little bluestem become much more prominent. The planting even carries across the sidewalk into the curb strip, making this small garden pretty hard to miss.

A few houses down is another garden that inspires me. The whole yard is planted so elegantly, with interest no matter the season. Bare spaces are usually filled with annuals. But even in November, we still get to see roses in bloom and hydrangeas giving it their all to remain relevant. The urn in the background with the pumpkin is a lovely seasonal touch.

This garden might look messy to some, but this is the kind of fall mess I truly enjoy. The hostas (Hosta cvs., Zones 3–9) spilling over the stairs, surrounded and covered by fallen red maple leaves… I love it!

This deep burgundy shrub covered in bright red berries certainly caught my eye. Unfortunately, it’s Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii, Zones 4–8), an invasive shrub here in Wisconsin. If you like the look, consider one of these native alternatives to Japanese barberry, including chokeberry, fothergilla, Virginia sweetspire, summersweet, and inkberry.

This Siberian crab apple (Malus baccata, Zones 2–7) is absolutely covered in clusters of warm orange fruit. Once so many summer flowers have disappeared, fruiting trees like this become some of the strongest color in the landscape.

It’s nice to see another garden extend beyond the front yard and into the curb strip. These often-overlooked spaces have so much potential. They can become a small garden, pollinator planting, or even a bee lawn.

And, of course, who can resist a strip of marigolds (Tagetes cvs., annual)? Especially when they’re still looking this good!

And one final reminder to leave the leaves this fall! Fallen leaves provide important overwintering habitat for pollinators and other beneficial insects, so leaving some in garden beds gives them a place to shelter until spring.

Thanks for coming along on my afternoon walk! While I wish this were a fall update from my little concrete jungle of a backyard, it’s all packed up now… because I’m moving to Georgia in just a few short weeks! I’ll definitely miss these neighborhood gardens, but I’m excited to see what new gardens and plants catch my eye down South.
