#7958. New Brennan Center Report on Curbing Executive Power

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Many of their recommendations are well-taken.

The NYU Brennan Center for Justice recently published a valuable report entitled "Seven Solutions to Rein In Abuses of Executive Power." The Brennan Center is well to the left of me. But I agree with the vast majority of their recommendations here. We do indeed have an overgrown executive, and it needs to be pared back. I particularly agree with the excellent section on constraining emergency powers:

With just a signature, presidents can declare a national emergency and unlock special powers contained in more than 130 statutory provisions. These run the gamut from the seemingly trivial to the near-dictatorial, including powers to shut down or take over communications infrastructure, freeze Americans' bank accounts, and control domestic transportation. They are intended for sudden, fast-moving crises that Congress can't address quickly or flexibly enough. But presidents of both parties have stretched the meaning of "emergency" far beyond reason, enabling them to draw from a growing stockpile of statutory authorities with few real safeguards.

There are currently 51 active states of emergency, and the longest-running has lasted 47 years.10 Any emergency that persists for generations is, by definition, not an emergency; it's a problem that can be addressed through ordinary lawmaking. Yet presidents have used emergency powers to bypass Congress and unilaterally advance their policy goals.11

The National Emergencies Act once allowed Congress to terminate emergencies with a simple majority vote and without the president's signature. But the Supreme Court struck down that procedure, known as a legislative veto, in 1983. Today, ending an emergency effectively requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto.

Congress should amend the National Emergencies Act to constrain executive overreach.12 Emergency declarations should expire automatically after 30 days unless Congress approves a one-year extension, renewable annually with Congress's assent. And presidents should be required to share detailed reports on their uses of emergency powers. Proposals along these lines have received widespread bipartisan support, with versions of these reforms overwhelmingly passing out of the relevant House and Senate committees in 2024.13

Additionally, Congress should amend specific emergency statutes whose extensive delegations of power and inadequate safeguards make them susceptible to misuse. Of particular concern is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the most frequently invoked presidential emergency authority.14 Sanctions imposed under this law can equate to a "financial death sentence" lasting years or decades.15 Although the Supreme Court blocked Trump's effort to use the law to set global tariffs, the potential for other abuses remains.

I completely agree, and have previously advocated similar reforms, myself. Brennan is right that IEEPA should be tightened up. While the Supreme Court did rule (in a case I helped litigate) that IEEPA cannot be used to impose tariffs, it still includes a lot of other dangerous powers.

I would add, as I did in this article, that invocations of emergency powers should be subject to  nondeferential judicial review, to ensure that they are used only in the event of genuine emergencies, not bogus ones. Congress would do well to amend relevant emergency statutes to make clear that such nondeferential judicial review is available.

I also strongly endorse Brennan's recommendations on constraining laws governing the domestic use of the military. The Supreme Court did strike down Trump's attempts to use bogus pretexts for federalizing the National Guard; the Ninth Circuit recently reinforced that ruling by rejecting the administration's broad definition of what qualifies as a "rebellion" justifying federalization. But, as the Brennan report indicates, there is still a lot of potential for abuse, especially when it comes to the Insurrection Act.

I also agree with the Brennan report's advocacy of constitutional amendments eliminating presidential immunity from criminal liability for acts undertaken in office, and barring him from pardoning crimes committed by" members of their inner circle, including immediate family members and senior administration officials" and those "convicted of crimes ordered by the president or committed on the president's behalf."

I doubt that these amendments have much chance of being enacted, given the extreme difficulty of passing any constitutional amendment. On the other hand, the reforms to emergency powers and domestic use of the military can be adopted through ordinary legislation. In some cases, they can also be bolstered by stronger judicial review under existing laws and provisions of the Constitution.

I do have a few disagreements with the report. For example, it is not clear to me that the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter goes as far as the authors suggest. The decision's scope remains uncertain. Among other things, it's not clear how wide a range of federal agencies it applies to and how to reconcile it with Trump v. Cook, decided on the same day. I also think they may overestimate Slaughter's impact, since most federal agencies are already not independent in the sense that there are legal constraints on the presidents' power to fire their heads.

I would also have liked to see more recognition that curbing excessive executive power requires curbing the scope of federal power generally. It is virtually impossible to have a federal government that regulates almost every aspect of human activity without simultaneously delegating vast - and often dangerous - discretion to the executive.

That said, the vast majority of the Brennan report's recommendations are well-taken. I hope future Democratic administrations and members of Congress act on them.

For those keeping score, it's worth noting that Brennan Center emergency powers expert Elizabeth Goitein, one of the authors of the report, is a long-time critic of abuses of emergency powers under Democratic administrations, as well as Republican ones. For example, she condemned President Biden's attempt to use emergency powers to effectuate massive student loan forgiveness. And so did I.

NEXT: Amicus Brief in OneTaste Criminal Prosecution

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7957. Winter Container Inspiration From New Jersey

Hi GPOD! Today we’re returning to New Jersey to see more from Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick. After sharing their beautiful fall containers with us, Ellen is back with some winter inspiration using colorful branches, evergreens, berries, pinecones, and more.

This beautiful antique lead planter in Ridgewood, New Jersey, always calls for a generous amount of greenery and nice height. We try to change what we do from year to year. This time we used curly willow, artificial white berry picks, magnolia leaves, red winterberry (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9), and frosted pinecones. Silver bell eucalyptus, silver brunia stems, noble fir (Abies procera, Zones 5–6), and incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens, Zones 5–8) fill out the arrangement.

This is the same antique planter and house as in the previous photo, but from another winter. That year we used a combination of yellow twig dogwood (Cornus sericea ‘Flaviramea’, Zones 3–7) and red twig dogwood (Cornus sericea cvs., Zones 2–7) for lots of winter color. We also used artificial berry picks in pink and white and natural brown pine cones.

We like to use real berries, but sometimes the birds eat them before the season ends. Artificial berries give the client guaranteed color for longer. For greenery, we used desert juniper (Juniperus osteosperma, Zones 3–9), balsam fir (Abies balsamea, Zones 3–6), and incense cedar.

This slim planter sits on a small sliver of a step at an entry in Ho-Ho-Kus, New Jersey. It is simple but one of my favorites, with stunning red twig dogwood stems. We buy these from a farm that also grows and sells the more common darker-red stems.

Beneath the red is a froth of desert juniper. Dried lotus pods (Nelumbo cvs., Zones 4–10) and clusters of silver brunia punctuate the greenery. The finishing touch is a frilly skirt of bright chartreuse incense cedar.

This one sounds like an outfit, doesn’t it?

One of a pair of pots on the front porch of a Mission-style house in Teaneck, New Jersey, these had plenty of space for tall branches. We liked the combination of golden curly willow (Salix matsudana ‘Tortuosa’, Zones 4–8) and redtwig dogwood against the creamy tan stucco.

We tucked in shiny magnolia leaves with taller silver bell eucalyptus, then added natural brown pinecones and small clumps of silver brunia. A generous, draping swath of incense cedar finishes the bottom of the arrangement.

This is a window box in Englewood, New Jersey. A classic house calls for a classic planting. We used red winterberries, magnolia leaves, frosted pinecones, and silver brunia clusters. Some noble fir and our favorite evergreen, incense cedar, finish the arrangement.

This is a close-up detail of a planter in Franklin Lakes, New Jersey. Dark red twig dogwood stems are mixed with curly willow and branches of multiflora rose hips. We love using the rose hips, but they are sometimes hard to find.

This pot also had artificial white berry picks and Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus, Zones 3–8). Silver brunia on longer stems, noble fir, and incense cedar complete the arrangement.

Thank you for sharing more of your beautiful container designs with us, Ellen and Tracy! I love seeing how many different looks can come from a relatively small palette of winter materials. Changing the color and shape of the branches, berries, cones, and evergreens gives each container its own personality.

We have even more of Ellen and Tracy’s winter containers to share, so we’ll be back tomorrow with another round of inspiration!

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Flying saucers, voodoo dolls, and ancient plagues.

Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit, a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.

New on the Short Circuit podcast: It's our biannual election law special! Anonymous speech! The Founders and pamphlets! Motor voter! Purcell! Prefilling ballots! Vote early! Vote often!

New on the Beyond the Brief podcast: Automated license plate readers are a lot of things, but one thing they definitely are is great tool for stalking. Hoo boy!

New cases! Last year, in two separate airport seizures, DEA and CBP agents seized a total of nearly $1.4 mil in cash from IJ client Steven Bailey and his small currency wholesaling business, which, among other things, buys U.S. dollars in Mexico and brings them back to the states—all above board and in compliance with numerous federal rules and reporting requirements. What's not above board is each agency's failure to say what they think Steven did wrong, denying him a chance to meaningfully contest the deprivation of his property. That violates due process, and, in CBP's case, the agency's own rules. Click here to learn more.

#7955. Court Blocks W. Va. AG's Subpoena to Environmentalist Nonprofits

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Part of the AG's argument was that the nonprofits relied on a climate change scenario, RCP8.5, that has been recently "retired."

From yesterday's decision by Judge Joseph Goodwin (S.D. W. Va.) in W. Va. Rivers Coalition, Inc. v. McCuskey:

The Attorney General of West Virginia has used the State's power to compel two citizen organizations to open ten years of their files: their drafts and internal arguments, the groups they have funded, the people who serve on their boards, the coalitions they have joined, and what they have told the agencies they petition. Neither organization markets goods nor services relevant to the subpoenas. The Attorney General identifies no consumer who was cheated, no sale, and no purchase made in reliance on anything either group said.

What these organizations do is argue in public about what coal, oil, and gas do to West Virginia's waters and climate. The State's chief legal officer, who has publicly condemned that advocacy, now demands to know how they reached their views and who stood with them.

The First Amendment forbids a State from using its investigative power that way, and I will not allow it while this case is pending.

The country was founded on the premise that a citizen owes the government no account of his opinions or of the people he holds them with. The Attorney General has demanded that two citizen organizations hand the State their working lives.

The State wants a decade of what they published, down to a note sent to a single person outside the organization, along with the unreleased drafts and the internal arguments over what to say. He demanded the names of the organizations that fund them and what each gave, and he has now withdrawn that demand. He still wants the groups they paid, the board members they share, the coalitions they joined, and the comments they filed with the agencies they were petitioning. Because the demand period runs to the date of compliance, the subpoenas reach new communications written while they remain outstanding. No demand identifies a consumer, a sale, or a statement anyone relied on. The subpoenas go into how these citizens arrived at their positions on public questions and who helped them get there.

The Plaintiffs in this case, West Virginia Rivers Coalition, Inc. ("WVRC") and 350.org, promote clean waters, reduced carbon emissions, and healthier lives for the people of West Virginia and beyond. They do not sell any service. They do not advertise a certain product of their own. Instead, they promote ideas. Some of that advocacy and some of those ideas are based, in part, on one model. For that, they have been subpoenaed and asked to turn over ten years' worth of information far beyond any use of that one model.

AG McCuskey's actions violate the protections afforded by the United States Constitution. The Plaintiffs, on this record, have only engaged in protected advocacy speech, not commercial speech. The subpoenas issued on the Plaintiffs trespass on their freedom of association, chill their exercise of the First Amendment, and deter others from engaging in similar conduct.

Because Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their claim that the subpoenas violate their First Amendment freedom of association, and because the remaining injunction factors also favor Plaintiffs, their Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order, is GRANTED.

Attorney General McCuskey is enjoined from enforcing these investigative subpoenas for the next fourteen days as set out in the Conclusion of this Memorandum Opinion and Order….

Plaintiff WVRC is a river advocacy nonprofit corporation organized under the laws of West Virginia, and its "mission is to promote clean and healthy West Virginia waters for all." The nonprofit is committed to "clean water and healthy rivers through research, public education, policy advocacy, citizen water-quality monitoring, and engagement with state and federal agencies." It has a modest staff of 15 and an annual budget of approximately $2 million primarily funded by foundations and other organizations. WVRC regularly submits comments on proposed legislation, permits, and rules concerning water quality. And as this court is familiar, WVRC is a party litigant in multiple cases across the Fourth Circuit that challenge permits and approvals for infrastructure projects, pipeline projects, injection wells, and toxic discharges. Because of its litigation efforts, WVRC coordinates "with other organizations through shared counsel" about litigation strategy.

WVRC also engages in public education and information campaigns, including "statements about the effects of climate change in West Virginia's waters and communities, and about the environmental effects of fossil-fuel extraction, transport, and combustion." It is a member of multiple different coalitions committed to similar goals. To fund ts work, WVRC "solicits charitable contributions from the public through its website, mailings, emails, and events," but it does not publish the identities of its funders.

Plaintiff 350.org is a nonprofit corporation, and its "mission is to build a grassroots movement to end the use of fossil fuels and to accelerate the transition to renewable energy." The organization publishes information about climate change, organizes public demonstrations, and coordinates with other organizations with similar goals. 350.org also "solicits charitable contributions from the public through grant applications and through its website, mailings, emails, and events." Those grants and contributions are subject to opt-in confidentiality in some cases and agreed upon confidentiality in other cases.

And an excerpt from the court's First Amendment analysis (for more on RCP8.5, see this N.Y. Times article):

[T]he Court applies "exacting scrutiny" to compelled disclosures of protected First Amendment speech and association. To be a permissible intrusion on the First Amendment, "there must be 'a substantial relation between the disclosure requirement and a sufficiently important governmental interest.'" …

The subpoenas … "… concern[ ] an investigation into alleged unfair or deceptive acts or practices and other possible violations of the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act ('WVCCPA')." State code authorizes the Attorney General, if he "has probable cause," to "subpoena witnesses, compel their attendance, adduce evidence, and require the production of any matter which is relevant to the investigation."

Under West Virginia law, "[u]nfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are … unlawful." Trade or commerce "means the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any goods or services and shall include any trade or commerce, directly or indirectly, affecting the people of this state." "Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices" includes 16 different definitions including "[e]ngaging in any other conduct which similarly creates a likelihood of confusion or of misunderstanding."

Deploying these broad definitions, AG McCuskey's theory is that the Plaintiffs, environmental advocacy groups, published information, made comments, and advocated based on a study, the RCP8.5, that has been determined "implausible." According to AG McCuskey, this reliance, and subsequent advocacy, is a deceptive act or practice that affects the energy marketplace of West Virginia.

Begin with common sense—in what way could WVRC and 350.org violate the WVCCPA? They are not financial institutions, lenders, or creditors. They are not businesses seeking to make a profit by engaging with consumers. In fact, both are 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations. They do not sell services of any kind. As explained, Plaintiffs are advocacy organizations committed to climate issues. Their missions are public education, dissemination of information, advocacy in support of their ideals, and public support of those who align with their beliefs. What little items they sell are merchandise bearing their names and logos. Surely these minimal sales from advocacy organizations are not the transactions the West Virginia legislature sought to protect consumers from….

Plaintiffs do not engage in commercial speech. By virtue of their missions as nonprofit environmental advocacy groups, their interests are not economic. Their interests include public education, funding environmental projects, modeling and projecting the effects of climate change, and contributing to a society that values clean air, clean water, and healthier lives. The fact that their advocacy touches on the economy is insufficient to be commercial speech. Therefore, Plaintiffs' protected speech and advocacy alleged in this case cannot be regulated under the WVCCPA.

Accordingly, I find that the WVCCPA cannot supply a "sufficiently important governmental interest" under the "exacting scrutiny" applied to freedom of association claims. I next turn to the severity of the "disclosure requirement" under the "exacting scrutiny" analysis….

As discussed, the subpoenas broadly assert that a violation of the WVCCPA might have occurred. And in his response, AG McCuskey admits that there may not be any WVCCPA violation. He does, however, have authority to issue subpoenas to investigate "whether a violation … has, in fact, occurred."

That violation, AG McCuskey argues, arises from only a few instances of Plaintiffs using a certain climate projection model, RCP8.5. Any publication born from that model, he asserts, is potentially unfair or deceptive. So to assess the breadth of the subpoenas and the compelled disclosure Plaintiffs are subjected to, the court turns to the subpoenas' demands. It is reasonable to assume that the demands would roughly track the RCP8.5-related violations and the allegations of unfair or deceptive trade practices.

Not so. The subpoenas ask for much more. The 16 categories of demands include every statement Plaintiffs have ever published about a West Virginia energy business with a "Climate Claim." But that demand is not limited to climate-related statements supported by the RCP8.5 model. It includes every climate-related statement that names a West Virginia energy business which is published and supported or informed, at least in part, by any model, study, project, plan, projection, or paper. Demand No. 4 is similarly broad: the subpoena demands every published projection concerning West Virginia and all documents related to those projections, without narrowing it down to those supported by the RCP8.5.

The rest of the demands do not even try to mask their broad and sweeping intentions. Donation requests, payments to third parties, and licensing and funding documents of all projects concerning West Virginia are demanded. Every document projecting costs and damages is demanded, as well as every report, study, model, or paper that the Plaintiffs directly or indirectly supported. Documents pertaining to internal considerations are demanded wholesale. So, too, are all documents pertaining to third-party communication and coordination in any fashion. And even with AG McCuskey's last-minute withdrawal of certain demands for donor information, Plaintiffs will still be obligated to disclose "board affiliation, coalition partners, grantees, agency submissions, internal deliberations and drafts, solicitation totals and targeting."

Plaintiffs call this a fishing expedition. In part, I agree. The subpoenas demand a large share of documents in Plaintiffs' control for the last ten years. But even on a fishing expedition, hoping to just get one bite in the vast and quiet water, a person brings a fishing pole. And in other cases, perhaps, a net. Here, AG McCuskey has abandoned both the fishing pole and the net. Instead, he has brought dynamite to the lake. Tossing a couple in, he hopes to catch something.

As stated, compelled disclosure that invades First Amendment protections can only stand if there is a substantial relation between what must be disclosed and a "sufficiently important governmental interest." Here, I find neither a sufficiently important government interest nor do I find a substantial relationship between the compelled disclosure and the government interest….

And the court also briefly notes plaintiffs' retaliation claim, without resolving it:

Plaintiffs have alleged substantial evidence to support their [retaliation] claim. AG McCuskey has publicly disparaged pro-environmental groups and has called for the DOJ to investigate similar groups. He has joined contentious litigation against environmental advocacy organizations. And the chasm between the subpoenas' demands and the purported basis for investigation suggests a retaliatory motive.

This phenomenon of state and federal investigation into the affairs of advocacy non-profits has begun to permeate our culture. The courts have enjoined civil investigative demands on comparable records. [Citations omitted. -EV]

However, because retaliation concerns the Attorney General's motive, I will reserve judgment on Count One until he can present evidence at a hearing for a preliminary injunction. Having already determined that an injunction is warranted on the basis of Count Two (freedom of association), the court declines to address the remaining counts….

Derek Teaney and Amanda Demmerle (Appalachian Mountain Advocates, Inc.) represent plaintiffs.

#7949. A Libertarian Perspective on the 2026 Election

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Why we should vote "Democrat by Default" for federal offices - with a few rare exceptions. I build on a post by political philosopher Dan Shapiro.

I was going to write a post about why, in this election, the right thing for libertarians to do is vote for Democrats for all federal offices, unless either 1) the Dem candidate is DSA, or 2) the GOP candidate is one of those very rare Republicans who oppose all or most of Trump's awful policies. But libertarian political philosopher Dan Shapiro beat me to it, in an excellent post at the Bleeding Heart Libertarian substack. I agree with the vast bulk of what he says. But I have a few additions and caveats that I will append after quoting a few key passages from Dan's post. Before getting into detail, I will note that I generally believe in voting for the lesser evil among those candidates with a realistic chance to win. Thus, unlike Dan, I don't usually vote for third party candidates, even in more normal times. If you're opposed to "lesser evil" voting on principle, we have a disagreement that goes  far beyond the present election. But I would urge you to check out my defense of that practice, where I explain why you should even vote for the evil Queen Cersei over the even more evil Sauron, if those are the only available choices.

I don't expect this post or Dan's will change the outcome of the election. They almost certainly won't. But they might still be helpful in thinking through big issues we face in the current political moment.

Most of my voting life I voted for the Libertarian Party when they advocated classical liberal/libertarian policies. Now those who care about and prioritize liberty and a free society—however they label themselves—should vote Democratic unless the candidate is a Democratic Socialist….

There's been so much criminality and misdeeds in the Trump administration that it's exhausting to cover it all, but keeping "the land of the free and the home of the brave" means remembering the essentials. I provide links when the points I make are not common knowledge and/or might be controversial.

January 6: Trump is the only presidential candidate in the US who refused to concede that he lost. He told a crowd to "fight like hell," and the mob then stormed the Capitol to try to overturn the results. The House impeached him for "incitement of insurrection," and 57 senators, including seven Republicans, voted to convict—short of the two-thirds required. After his campaign of lies and deception and pressuring election officials to falsify the results failed to overturn the election, he later pardoned all the perpetrators of the violence.

ICE: masked secret police who kidnap people and send them to hellholes in El Salvador, where they were subject to constant beatings, sexual abuse, and torture; to the Central African Republic, in the midst of a brutal civil war with severe human rights abuses; to Florida's "Alligator Alcatraz," where large numbers of detainees were held in cages the size of phone booths; and to Fort Bliss, Texas, where guards grabbed detainees' testicles while beating them. There've been zero consequences for this; indeed, Trump says they are "immune."

Not only were the deportations done without any notification to families or lawyers, but ICE has disappeared from databases those they seized so lawyers and families can't find them.

ICE and CBP have rammed people in their cars, dragged the occupants out, and rammed into houses without warrants. They have murdered, wounded, and assaulted protestors and ICE monitors—Alex Pretti and Renee Good, during the ICE occupation of Minneapolis, being the most publicized—but there have been many others.

There is now "expedited removal" for anyone undocumented, which means no hearing before a judge. (And this is even though immigration judges are—wrongly—a part of, and not independent of, the executive branch.) Indeed, Trump fired any immigration judge who disagreed with him or whom he perceived as not being deportation-friendly enough, and replaced the Board of Immigration Appeals, which has denied appeals for almost all deportation orders.

The administration removed TPS (temporary protected status) for immigrants fleeing violence and is deporting them to the very countries the State Department has declared unsafe—e.g., Haiti.

ICE apprehended immigrant parents after they dropped their kids off at school (see here, here, and here), as well as apprehending children and toddlers and using them as bait (the Liam Conejo Ramos incident)….

Trump sent Marines to LA, and National Guard troops to Chicago and DC. This violates a basic norm since the Founding and violates Posse Comitatus, a statute banning the military from policing.

Trump and FCC chairman Carr threatened talk shows and networks for dissenting political opinions.

As mentioned, ICE murdered, assaulted, and wounded protestors and ICE monitors.

The administration targeted people for their political views and for writing op-eds. Rochester resident David Streever sent a critical email to the director of ICE, and five months later, federal officers tracked his movements and staked out his New York City hotel as he returned from an overseas trip….

There is much more, including explanations of why the Democrats (with the notable exception of DSA types) are far less bad than this, despite their considerable flaws. I myself have written about the evils of the DSA here, explaining why they are comparable to MAGA nationalist Republicans.  In addition to the harm individual DSA members might cause if elected to office, it is important to reduce their numbers as much as possible, so as to minimize the chances that socialists could take over the Democratic Party, as MAGA nationalists have done with the GOP.

I have a few additions to Dan's arguments.

First, it is essential to consider the enormous scale of Trump's harmful and unjust immigration and trade policies. When it comes to setting issue priorities, scale matters a great deal. Even under normal administrations, immigration restrictions threaten the economic and civil liberties of American citizens (to say nothing of those of immigrants themselves) more than any other federal policy. Trump's vast expansion of exclusion and mass deportation has made things a lot worse. The liberty and well-being of millions of people are at stake.

Trump's trade policies seek to impose the highest tariff levels since those that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression, and also are a grave menace to the rule of law. Here too, we're talking about massive effects on the liberty and welfare of millions. Judicial review can and has helped curb these abuses (more on the tariff front than immigration). But there is much Congress can do to help, including curbing funding to ICE and other agencies complicit in wrongdoing. Congressional Democrats also plan to cut back executive tariff authority. That may not succeed while Trump remains in office, but can help set the stage for later progress.

Dan raises the issue of whether non-DSA Democrats might be worse than the Trump-era GOP on economic liberty issues. This becomes an easy issue if you recognize that immigration restrictions and tariffs are also violations of economic liberty. Due to their massive scale, Trump's actions in this area easily outweigh the very real economic policy flaws of non-DSA Dems. And then we have such things as his acquisition of federal government stakes in numerous private firms, something that even the most left-wing recent Democratic presidents didn't attempt. It's a dramatic example of how MAGA nationalists have dangerous economic policies similar to those of socialists.

It is also important to remember that a Democratic Senate could block Trump's horrible executive and judicial nominees. I don't want to see any more Pete Hegseths and RFK, Jrs. In Trump's first term, he had some good judicial nominees. In the second, he has mostly  bad ones (Emil Bove is a particularly egregious example). From a libertarian perspective, I'd rather have a standard liberal nominee fill the next Supreme Court vacancy (despite all the flaws such jurists have) than the type of right-winger Trump II is all too likely to nominate. Such a person would probably be selected for his willingness to turn a blind eye to executive abuses of power, trample civil liberties, and bulldoze constitutional obstacles to MAGA nationalist policies, such as federalism and separation of powers. There may well not be any Supreme Court vacancies, of course. But lower court nominations will arise, and they matter too.

Finally, I'm more hawkish than the average libertarian, and I think it's important to counter Trump's policies of undermining the Western alliance, and coddling mass-murdering dictators like Vladimir Putin and (to a lesser extent) Xi Jinping. We should care about defending liberty worldwide, not just in one country, especially since the two are interconnected. The Democrats (except for a few far-leftists) oppose this awfulness and could use control of Congress to help curb it.

In these and other areas, a Democratic-controlled Congress could not fully stop Trump's abuses. The executive has accumulated too much power for that, often in constitutionally dubious ways. But congressional control of nominations and purse strings can do much to constrain the executive at the margin. And electoral repudiation of Trump's abuses can reduce the risk that future presidents will imitate them.

I do have a few caveats to attach to Dan's otherwise compelling points:

First, Dan doesn't differentiate between elections for federal offices and those for state and local ones. I do. Beating the GOP in federal races is vital for countering Trump's awful agenda. At the state and local level, other issues are dominant, and Republicans are often better than Dems on the crucial issues of housing, state-level taxation, and state and local economic regulation. Which party is better on these and other state and local issues will vary from state to state. For example, red state Republicans are much better on the crucial issue of housing deregulation than blue state ones (who often back exclusionary zoning against Democratic reform efforts). Thus, it might make sense to vote for Republican candidates in some state and local races, but not others, depending on the issues involved.

Second, when it comes to the DSA problem, there can be difficult questions about what to do with Dem candidates who are not actual DSA members, but seem closely adjacent to them. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a notable example. He says he's not a socialist, but also is closely aligned with socialists like Bernie Sanders, and "influencer" Hasan Piker, the guy who - among other things - praises communist mass murderers like Mao Zedong.

In this post, I'm not going to try to adjudicate each individual candidate and race. I will merely say that if you're trying to figure out whether a non-DSA member is actually a socialist, two noteworthy indicators are 1) whether he or she supports government control of all or most of the economy and 2) whether they praise socialist despots abroad, such as Mao, Fidel Castro, and others. If the answers to one or both questions are "yes," that's a strong indication they might be socialists, and therefore not worth voting for, except perhaps against the very worst Republicans.

There is a similar calculation in identifying the few Republicans who have opposed Trump's worst policies. Here, key indicators are whether they have opposed his tariffs, his mass deportations, his kowtowing to Vladimir Putin, and his attacks on civil liberties. Sadly, Republican candidates with consistent strong records on all or most of these issues, are few and far between, though Republican criticism of the tariffs and policies towards Russia have picked up in recent weeks.

Finally, as Dan would agree, voting for Democratic candidates does not imply supporting everything the Democratic Party does, or abstaining from criticizing Democrats on the many occasions when they do bad things.

Elsewhere, I have argued that libertarians, in the current political moment, should seek an alliance with "abundance liberals." But alliance is not the same thing as total agreement. And the Democratic Party obviously includes various factions who are much worse than the abundance types. We should keep that in mind, even as we recognize that right now the Republicans are much worse.

#7940. 14 Space Heater Safety Mistakes That Could Burn Down Your House

By Michelle Ullman, Updated by Amy Anderson

Updated Oct 26, 2026 10:36 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Nearly half of all home heating fires take place between December and February, according to the National Fire Protection Association. Surprisingly, fireplaces are not causing the heaviest losses. Between 2018 and 2022, space heaters and heating stoves caused 46 percent of the fires but 76 percent of deaths related to home heating.

Since space heaters can be an integral part of an efficient home heating plan, space heater safety is a vital priority this winter to mitigate these fire risks. So how do you avoid a house fire? Know the most common and costly mistakes people make with portable heaters, and don’t repeat them in your own home.

Give your space heater a wide berth, particularly around textiles. Space heaters and fabrics of any type are a deadly combo. “Keep your space heater at least 3 to 5 feet away from any fabric items such as furniture, bedding, curtains, rugs or anything flammable,” says Todd Tripp, general contractor and home improvement expert with JustAnswer. In fact, space heater fires are most commonly caused by some sort of fabric, including clothing, upholstered furniture, or even mattresses, that comes in contact with or sits too close to the heater.

Don’t set your space heater on top of a dresser, table, or other piece of furniture. An accidental bump or a curious cat could knock the heater to the floor, leading to a burn injury or a fire hazard. “Space heaters should not be placed on furniture or countertops, even if your countertop is a flat surface. That placement could pose a variety of risks to your home,” says Mollie Treloar, heating expert at Tractor Supply. The furniture or countertop could also be damaged, especially if the surface is not heat-resistant. “Additionally, elevated surfaces like furniture or countertops often offer more restricted airflow than the floor does, which may lead to overheating,” Treloar adds.

“If you don’t have any hard surface flooring, [place] your heater on a stable, non-flammable surface… [such as] ceramic tiles or a heat resistant mat.”

Not only must your space heater sit on the floor, but it’s safe only when the floor is a hard surface. Never place a space heater on top of an area rug or carpeting. They tend to trap heat and could ignite if they get warm enough. “Having carpeted floors can make using a space heater tricky, but that doesn’t mean it’s not possible,” Treloar says. “If you don’t have any hard surface flooring, then placing your heater on a stable, non-flammable surface is the best bet for safety. This could be ceramic tiles or a heat resistant mat. Just make sure the surface is bigger than the heater’s base, and set it on a level spot to prevent tipping.”

The Dreo Solaris space heater is lightweight, yet warms spaces up to 200

It’s a common scenario: You want the space heater close enough to chase away the chill, but the nearest electrical outlet is all the way across the room. You consider running the space heater’s cord underneath an area rug. Don’t do it! Running the cord under the rug introduces the much graver danger of fire. “The rug covering the cord can trap any heat generated by the cord during use and increase risk of overheating and fires,” Treloar says. “The rug fibers can also cause damage to the cord over time and lead to malfunction and spark risk. Also, the cord covered by the rug can pose a major trip hazard to your family and pets as they would not be able to see it while walking.”

As with any appliance or device that generates heat, never plug a space heater into an extension cord or a power strip. The high power demand of the space heater can cause the extension cord or power strip to short-circuit or overheat, potentially causing a fire. Instead, always plug your space heater directly into a wall outlet, and don’t plug anything else into the same outlet while the space heater is running.

The pleasant warmth of a space heater is like a magnet for cats, but a curious—or chilly—dog may also be attracted. Though they may want to hang out near the device, never leave pets unattended in any room with a running space heater. Turn the space heater off when you leave the room.

It might be tempting to use a space heater to warm up your bathroom while you shower, but resist the urge. “Because of a bathroom’s increased humidity and proximity to water, you have to take extra precautions with your space heater,” Treloar says. “Take care to use a model specifically designed for the bathroom, and make sure you place your heater far enough away from your sink, shower, or bathtub to eliminate the risk of water damage or splashing.”

Leaving your space heater running all night long while you sleep is a no-no. “Space heaters need to be respected as a highly flammable appliance,” Tripp says. If the unit overheats, tips over, or short-circuits overnight, a fire could break out while you’re fast asleep. Use the heater to warm up your room before bed, and then switch it off right before you slide between the sheets.

Before buying a space heater, check that it’s been certified. “Space heaters with a UL (Underwriters Laboratory), CSA (Canadian Standards Association), and ETL (Intertek) should only be used,” Tripp says. “Space heaters with one of these certifications have been tested and approved for safety electrically and fire hazards.” Normally, the certification will be indicated on the space heater’s packaging. These organizations perform rigorous tests to ensure that home electronics are as safe as possible.

“Any strange sounds, such as rattling or buzzing, or unusual smells, like burning or electrical odors, are immediate red flags. These could indicate internal damage or potential fire hazards.”

Found a space heater bargain at your local thrift store or neighborhood garage sale? Just walk away. While there are some electronic devices you can get secondhand and use with some safety precautions, space heaters should never be one of them. The certification sticker could be missing or never have existed. The wiring could be frayed, internal parts could be damaged, and it’s nearly impossible to determine how old a space heater is outside of the box. Using old or damaged space heaters is a recipe for disaster.

While just about all of today’s space heaters have multiple safety features, including an auto shut-off if the unit gets too hot, tips over, or runs for too long, that’s not true of space heaters made a decade or more ago. “If it’s over 10 years old, it may lack modern safety features and efficiency,” Treloar says. She says that signs the heating elements are wearing out include taking longer to heat up a room or not heating as effectively as the unit used to. Other reasons to look for a replacement: “Any strange sounds, such as rattling or buzzing, or unusual smells, like burning or electrical odors, are immediate red flags. These could indicate internal damage or potential fire hazards. Also, any signs of physical damage, such as cracks in the casing, frayed cords, or scorch marks. These are clear indicators that the heater is no longer safe to use and should be replaced,” she says.

Nothing should ever block the doorway of your bedroom or the route you would need to take from your bed to that doorway in an emergency, especially not something that gets scalding hot. To keep you safe from dangerous trips and tumbles, your space heater needs to be positioned at least a couple of feet to the side of any doorway, path, or high-traffic area of your home.

You might think the space heater is the perfect spot to dry those snowy mittens, but you’d be dangerously wrong. “Space heaters are designed to heat spaces, not to dry clothing, and using them for this purpose can pose significant safety risks,” Treloar says. “Clothing that is placed too close to a space heater can overheat and potentially catch fire, especially draping clothing over a space heater to dry it faster. Draping can block air vents and cause the heater to overheat, increasing the likelihood of a malfunction or fire.” The same is true for storing items on top of your heater. “Modern space heaters are built with overheating protection safety features, but these are not foolproof and should not be relied upon if the heater is being used inappropriately.”

Non-electric space heaters, such as propane space heaters, can release carbon monoxide when in use. To operate these heaters safely, place them in a well-ventilated area or outdoors on a patio. “You should also choose a model equipped with safety features like an oxygen depletion sensor (ODS), which shuts the heater off if oxygen levels fall too low,” Treloar adds. “Finally, when refueling, users should also take care to choose the correct fuel type for their heater and always let the space heater cool before refueling to minimize fire risk.

Winter drafts find every weak spot in your house, even if it’s a well-heated one. Warmth slips out through glass first, but small gaps around doors, a pull-down attic stairway, a garage door, and even the walls of a water heater tank can all let heat escape. Tracking down those weak spots is the first step toward keeping your home comfortable and using less electricity to do it.

The following list of proven solutions for sealing in the heat this winter includes everything from simple weatherstripping and draft stoppers to smart controls for managing your heating needs. It mixes affordable DIY supplies, decorating upgrades, and high-tech tools, and it includes several products the BobVila.com team has personally tested. There’s a fix here to suit nearly any space, and a few that would make a great gift for the handy homeowner on your list.

Runner-Up in our tests of the best window insulation kits, the Duck Brand Max Strength Window Kit uses thick, puncture-resistant shrink film to block winter drafts and keep warm air in, helping you save energy. Pull-down attic stairs are convenient, but the opening can break up an otherwise insulated attic floor. When you’ve already paid to heat the water in your water heater, it’s a real shame to have that warmth leak back out through the tank walls. Some home design features have been around for generations, such as grandfather clocks, wingback chairs, and wraparound porches. Often found in drafty homes and hung only in doorways, the portiere curtain is another example dating back to the Aesthetic Movement of the late 19th century. It is named for the French word meaning “porter” or “doorkeeper.” Portieres are heavy, functional door curtains designed to block drafts, divide spaces, or close off hallways without requiring permanent walls.

As portiere curtains make a comeback, explore how to incorporate this older feature into your home so you can enjoy the many benefits they provide.

To effectively insulate a room, portiere curtains are crafted from thick, substantial fabrics like rich velvet rather than sheer materials. Hang the portiere on a rod mounted directly above the door so it can be pushed neatly against the wall when not in use. You can also use rings inside the doorframe to ensure smooth opening and closing from both sides.

Because both sides remain visible, they are typically hung within the doorway frame so mounting looks the same from both sides. It’s also usually constructed with decorative fabrics on both faces or finished with deep hems to conceal any backing, ensuring a polished look from every angle.

Back before heating systems existed, portiere curtains were installed to help keep warmth in a room. Even today, they can still help reduce drafts by providing a physical barrier of fabric to limit the flow of air from one room into another or from entering a doorway due to its draughty condition, says Goorha. The heavier the fabric and/or more densely woven, the better the curtain will be at limiting airflow since there is less opportunity for air to move through.

“To maximize effectiveness, hang the curtain above the door opening so that sufficient fabric hangs down and covers the door opening without much space between the side edges and the floor edge,” she advises.

#7935. The Best Fire Starters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

By Glenda Taylor, Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tony Carrick, Donna Boyle Schwartz

Published Oct 27, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Fire starters make it easy for anyone to start a roaring fire. Rather than having to wrestle with damp wood or crumpled-up newspapers to get the first flames going, users can employ a fire starter to achieve this with a single match or the flick of a lighter. The catch is that these outdoor living aids aren’t all created equal.

Some fire starters stand out for their ability to help ignite a fire rapidly and effortlessly, while others are difficult to light or won’t stay lit long enough to ignite a wood fire. We wanted to know which ones were worth buying, so we tested them in our own fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, and fire pits, eventually choosing the Superior Trading Co. All-Natural Fire Starter as our favorite for its nontoxic ingredients and effective performance. Ahead, we’ll cover how the following products earned a place in our lineup of the best fire starters.

Bottom line: Discover the best fire starters of 2026, tested for performance, ease of use, and environmental impact, with options for every need and budget.

In total, we tested 15 different fire starters: 12 small accelerant products, and three ferro rods that could fit into a pocket on a camping or hiking trip. Our main goal was to determine which fire starters performed the best in their relative categories. We didn’t test matches or lighters, but we did use them to light the accelerant fire starters. Not every product we tested made the cut for this guide. Each of the products below earned a spot by being a top performer in our hands-on testing.

These Superior Trading Co. fire starters are safe, easy to use, and effective. We found that just one pod was typically all we needed to get a log fire lit and burning. Made from wood shavings and food-grade wax, the pods are odorless, nontoxic, and environmentally safe, making them ideal for everything from indoor fireplaces to camping bonfires.

It took about 4 seconds for the pod to catch fire when we lit it with a single match. It started burning slowly, but within 5 minutes, the flames were about 8 inches tall, and the pod continued burning for about 15 minutes, which was plenty of time for the logs to catch fire.

The manufacturer lists these fire starters as waterproof, so we dropped a couple in a glass of water before testing them. We couldn’t get them to light immediately, but that was understandable. Once they dried out, they lit quickly and burned well. We used them in a fireplace and a charcoal grill. We placed one Superior Trading Co. fire-starter pod under the charcoal basket in our grill and lit it. By the time the flame from the pod burned down, the charcoal was lit.

Get the Superior Trading Co. fire starters at Amazon or Superior Trading Co.

Forget about newspapers and kindling—we were able to get a real wood fire going using just one small Lightning Nugget. It took three matches to light the nugget, but once lit, it burned brightly with a hot flame about 6 inches high for a little more than 10 minutes.

The nuggets are made from a blended composition of all-natural, recycled, and nontoxic flammable materials, including pitchwood sawdust and paraffin wax. Pitchwood is a type of pine that contains natural resins that are flammable.

When burned, these nuggets give off a slight pinewood scent, making them suitable for fireplaces and campfires. We were hoping for more of an aroma, but it was pretty weak. Each box comes with 50 nuggets, and since it takes just one nugget to light most fires, one box goes a long way. They’re not suitable for use in grills, however, since they are scented.

Get the Lightning Nuggets fire starters at Amazon, Ace Hardware, or Tractor Supply Co.

Buyers don’t have to spend a lot to get quality fire starters. With 24 fire starter squares in a box, this option from Rutland is one of the more affordable fire-starting options.

We placed a couple of Rutland fire starter squares beneath logs in our fireplace. They lit quickly—within 1 or 2 seconds of touching them with a lit match. The flames rapidly engulfed the squares and continued burning for about 8 minutes, which was more than enough time to ignite the logs in the fireplace.

The fire starter squares are made from recycled wood chips, paper fiber, and wax. Although the manufacturer claims they’ll light when wet, we couldn’t get them to light after we dropped them in a glass of water and then took them out. After about 15 minutes, however, they were dry enough to light.

These are nontoxic fire starters, and we couldn’t detect any odor as they burned, making them suitable for starting charcoal fires for grilling food. It took two Rutland squares to get the charcoal in our grill started; the first one burned out before the charcoal caught, so we slipped a second one under the charcoal basket and lit it. The briquettes caught fire a few minutes after that.

Get the Rutland fire starters at Tractor Supply Co.

Nature offers excellent fire starters, but gathering traditional materials such as birch bark, tinder fungus, or cattail fluff is not always practical. One of the best natural fire starters, fatwood, comes from naturally resin-saturated pinewood. These fatwood fire starter sticks from Better Wood Products catch fire quickly, even when wet, and burn longer and hotter than factory-made fire starters. Our 10-pound bundle of fatwood contained 160 sticks, each measuring 8.25 inches long and about .5 inches in diameter.

After submerging two sticks in a bucket of water for 5 minutes, we pulled them out, shook off the water, and held a lit match against them. Within 5 seconds, both sticks were ablaze like giant matchsticks. They appeared to burn more intensely than typical wood shavings or compressed fiber and wax fire starters. Compared with those, these fatwood starters produced a larger flame with more heat—enough that we could feel it from 3 feet away. We were also impressed by the 14-minute burn time, but the downside was an excessive amount of smoke and pungent pine aroma.

Possibly the most intriguing quality of a fatwood fire starter is its versatility. The seller recommends lighting two sticks at a time with a match as an easy way to get a fire going with dry, seasoned firewood. We experimented with smaller amounts and managed to start one with just half a stick. Another time, we made a nest of fine fatwood shavings and lit it with sparks off of the ferro rod. However you light it, this stuff just works.

Get the Better Wood Products fire starters at Amazon.

Getting back to basics by creating a fire with friction no longer means using flint and steel; today’s outdoors enthusiasts trust ferrocerium alloy to supply the sparks. In skilled hands, a quality ferro rod and some dry tinder are all it takes to build up a roaring fire in no time. We preferred the Exotac FireRod XL over competing models, not least because of the massive shower of sparks it produced. We also appreciated its precision-machined aluminum handle with a watertight tinder chamber and the fact that the rod can be unthreaded from the body and replaced with a new one if needed. It did not come with a striker, but the spine of a fixed blade or lock-back folding knife served that role perfectly.

Before the ferro rod could make sparks, we had to scrape away some of the black surface coating. We then dropped it in the water bucket to find out if the tinder chamber was truly watertight. It was. Next, we dried our hands, opened the tinder chamber, and pulled out one of the three included cotton fiber tinder pieces. We loosened the fibers and placed the tinder in a bundle of dry pine needles shaped like a bird’s nest. The very first strike sparked into the tinder and ignited it, which then lit the pine needle nest. We built the fire up with kindling from there.

We’ve tried smaller ferro rods, such as spring-loaded UST BlastMatch, but the FireRod XL’s large rod and chunky handle made it easier to use with gloves, and it produced a larger spark shower to light the tinder. Three of the six fires we started with the FireRod XL only required a single strike. We also appreciated the built-in waterproof tinder chamber inside the handle, as this allowed it to serve as a complete fire-making kit at all times. On the downside, the precision-machined aluminum handle seems to be a costly addition, as the price was multiple times more than that of a similarly sized drilled ferro rod on a lanyard.

Get the Exotac fire starter at Amazon, Target, or Exotac.

These all-natural fire starters blend recycled pine “wood wool” (which is a fancy way of saying slivers of wood cut from logs) and stearin wax (a wax made from plant and animal materials) with no added chemicals. That makes GreenSpark’s fire starters a clean and eco-friendly way to get a fire going. We tested them to start a campfire and to create a traditional log fire in the fireplace.

To get the campfire going, we placed three GreenSpark fire starter squares on top of some small logs and lit them with a lighter. It took 3 or 4 seconds for the starters to catch. Once they were burning well, we added some small pieces of kindling and more logs. The GreenSpark squares sent up flames about 6 inches high and burned for around 8 to 9 minutes. That was plenty of time to ignite the larger logs we put on the fire.

The test in the fireplace had similar results, and we enjoyed a roaring fire there. These fire starters are billed as waterproof, so we dropped them in a glass of water and then retrieved them. We couldn’t light them immediately after we took them out of the water, but as soon as the moisture on the surface dissipated—which took about 10 minutes—we were able to light them again.

They contain all-natural ingredients, so the GreenSpark squares are also suitable for use in grills for cooking food.

Get the GreenSpark fire starters at Amazon.

Nothing lifts the mood in camp faster than a roaring campfire. Black Beard’s fire starter “ropes” are ideal for fire pits because they can be stored indefinitely, are completely weatherproof, and offer enough burn time to coax even wet firewood ablaze.

We tested a three-pack of “ropes” (which is how these come packaged) using several methods, and while a lighter and matches were the most straightforward approach, we also had success using the ferro rod. For our timed test, we cut a 1-inch section from one rope, lit an end, and stood it up like a little candle. It burned strong for 11 minutes.

Next, we cut another piece of the same size, dunked it in a bucket of water for a minute, shook it off, and lodged it beneath a mix of damp, seasoned kindling and greenwood logs that had recently been cut. Success. The residual water sizzled on the fire starter for a few moments as it began to burn. Within 5 minutes the kindling directly above the fire starter had dried and begun to catch fire. After 10 minutes, the kindling was well lit, the greenwood logs were beginning to char and smoke, and we had enough of a fire to build on.

The resulting fire was very smoky—not because of the Black Beard fire starter, but rather because of the uncured firewood. We performed this experiment to find out if the fire starter produced adequate heat long enough to actually dry out damp wood in the bottom of a damp fire pit, and it did.

Get the Black Beard fire starters at Amazon or Walmart.

When charcoal chimneys first became popular, newspapers were much more widely read—and sometimes, burned. Those who get their news online and don’t want to start the barbecue with a trash fire will be glad to learn about these quick-light fire starters from Kingsford. These simple bundles of wood shavings and paraffin wax light easily, burn for a long time, and won’t pollute food fires with questionable chemicals.

When it comes to grilling, Kingsford has been a household name for a long time, so we weren’t surprised that its hardwood fire starters ended up being one of the top performers. The average burn time with these was an impressive 13 minutes. Even after we dunked them in water, they lit within seconds and burned hot once ignited. We only needed one fire starter to get the fire going in our charcoal chimney, but some folks who are less patient may prefer to use two or three.

With an average cost of about $0.31 per fire starter ($9.99 for a pack of 32), this was one of the most affordable options. The only complaint we had was that the packaging fell apart in transit while the fire starters were being shipped to us, so we had to store them in our own plastic zipper bag.

Get the Kingsford fire starters at Amazon.

When it comes to fire starters for camping, ease of use, weather resistance, and burn time are critical factors. Compact packaging is also important. UCO’s Sweetfire fire starters combine the easy strike-starting of a match with the burn time of a waxed fiber fire starter. They come in boxes of 20.

Using this fire starter was just like using a match. We slid open the box, tore off one of the fire starters, and struck it on the side of the box. The “match head” was about four times the size of a conventional match, so it provided more than enough of a flame to get started. The individual fire starters measure 1 inch wide at the base, 2 inches from base to tip, and .5 inches thick—relatively small compared to the competition.

The burn time was pretty good at just under 10 minutes. That was more than enough time to start a fire under ideal conditions, and it worked fine in damp, drizzly conditions as well. It also performed well in our dunk test, starting on the first strike after a 5-second submersion. However, we suspect that the box with the built-in strikers could be a weak link if it absorbs too much moisture. This is a great choice for camp, but be sure to pack them in a zipper bag just in case.

Get the UCO fire starters at Amazon or Public Lands.

When the unexpected happens, a little preparation can make the difference between a rough day and an absolute disaster. Pull Start Fire was designed to start and burn for 30 minutes in all kinds of weather, and it can be lit without matches, lighters, or other devices. Just unwrap it, remove a tab, anchor it to a log, and pull a string. We’ve tried it, and it really was that simple.

This was by far the most expensive fire starter we tested on a per-fire basis. But it was also the easiest to operate in difficult conditions, such as one-handed, with hands in gloves, in high winds and rain, and so on. Each Pull Start Fire was sealed individually and, according to the manufacturer, has an indefinite shelf life. We held it underwater for 60 seconds and the cellophane wrapper didn’t leak. Then we opened the wrapper and followed the directions to start the fire.

This fire starter burns aggressively at first, like a roadside emergency flare, until the materials inside the inner packaging catch fire. In our test, it burned for 32 minutes with no additional fuel. On the second try, we placed it beneath a pile of moist but moderately cured 3-inch-thick firewood logs with no kindling. As the Pull Start Fire burned, it dried the wood directly above it. Within 10 minutes some of the damp logs began to burn, and after 20 minutes they were well engulfed. Bottom line, if we were the character in Jack London’s story To Build a Fire, we would rather have a couple of Pull Start Fires than a pack of matches.

Get the Pull Start Fire fire starters at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Lehman’s.

The fire starters that earned a spot in our lineup are all relatively inexpensive, and most are made from natural ingredients. For those who want something that not only ignites and burns reliably but looks good, too, consider making pine cone fire starters.

Making pine cone starters is fairly simple. It requires melting beeswax in the top of a double boiler and then dipping the cones two or three times until they have a nice wax layer. For fun, try rolling them in Epsom salt after the final dip while they’re still warm to lend them a frosty look. For scented pine cone fire starters, add natural essential oils to the melted wax, such as pine or cinnamon.

We considered a variety of factors when deciding which fire starters to test. We selected starters that would burn long enough to ignite wood or charcoal without needing to add other burnable materials, such as wadded-up paper or cardboard. A fire starter should also be easy to use, so we chose options that light easily with a match or lighter—with the exception of the ferro rods we tested, which function a bit differently.

During our testing, we followed the manufacturers’ instructions, placing one or two fire starters as suggested and using them to start the recommended fire types. For many of the tests, we used a traditional fireplace, but we also used a fire pit, a chiminea, and a wood-burning stove if the directions recommended using the fire starters with those appliances. We also tested a few fire starters to see how well they worked for lighting charcoal—but only if they were listed as safe to use for grilling food.

If a fire starter was advertised as waterproof, we dropped it in a glass of water and then attempted to light it. We determined that many waterproof fire starters aren’t genuinely waterproof but rather water-resistant. In other words, they needed a little time to dry out before lighting.

We timed how long it took for a fire starter to catch fire from a match or lighter, how tall its flames were, and how long it burned before extinguishing. We discovered a fire starter needed to remain lit for 5 to 9 minutes, at minimum, to fully ignite the rest of the wood and logs in a fireplace.

The only fire starter we tested differently was the ferro rod, which is intended to ignite finely textured, highly flammable tinder via sparks. We tested it on cotton-fiber tinder that was included with the rod, and then we built up the fire with progressively larger twigs and kindling.

During the testing phase, we awarded points based on how well each fire starter performed the tasks. After testing, we added and averaged the scores and compared packaging, prices, dimensions, and other factors to categorize the products for different applications.

Aside from considering the various types of fire starters, there are other features that shoppers will want to consider, such as ease of use and convenience. While any fire starter will make starting a fire easier than using tinder, not all fire starters are suitable for all types of fires.

In general, fire starters fall into two camps: flame/spark producers or accelerants. Shoppers already know about lighters and matches, but they might not be familiar with other types of flame/spark producers, such as ferro rods.

Accelerants are usually what buyers are usually looking for when shopping for fire starters, and these products are used in conjunction with typical fire-building materials, such as seasoned logs. An accelerant fire starter is placed beneath the other materials and then ignited with a match, lighter, ferro rod, or other flame/spark producers. Here’s the rundown on all of them.

A lighter consists of a metal or plastic container filled with a flammable liquid or compressed gas. A lighter lights by simultaneously creating a spark with the flint wheel while releasing a controlled amount of the fuel with a button. Unlike other methods, a lighter creates an actual flame, making it significantly easier to start a fire.

Matches are the tried-and-true method of starting a fire. Like a lighter, a match creates an actual flame rather than a spark, making it an easier way to start a fire. However, many matches are susceptible to water damage.

A ferro rod is a pencil-shaped piece of ferrocerium alloy. When a steel or carbide striker is scraped or struck against the rod, tiny shavings of ferrocerium oxidize and ignite as a result of the friction, burning at a high temperature of more than 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit.

Flint and steel consist of a steel striker and a piece of natural flint. When the two are struck together, they produce heated pieces of steel in the form of sparks that ignite a piece of cloth or tinder, starting the fire.

A magnesium fire starter typically consists of a small block of soft magnesium with a ferro rod embedded into one edge. The magnesium, which burns at an intense 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit, is an accelerant that works with the tinder to quickly build a fire. With a knife or the striker that came with the kit, scrape a quarter-size pile of magnesium into the tinder pile, then use the embedded ferro rod and striker to light the tinder. This will ignite the magnesium fragments, which will help set fire to twigs and kindling.

Accelerants are the most popular fire-starter products, and we tested a number of these. Nuggets and squares consisting of flammable oils, wax, and recycled paper and wood are the easiest to use; however, they require a flame ignition source, such as a match or a lighter. Once lit, these fire starters typically create tall, hot flames that light the materials above them.

As handy as fire starters may be, their usefulness is, to a degree, dependent on their convenience. Look for fire starters that are lightweight and compact, ranging from 1 to 6 inches in length. Typically sold in cases of 12 or 24, these pocket-size pouches, pods, or cubes can be stored in plain sight or easily tucked out of sight. Small, lightweight, neatly packed products are also more portable.

Most fire starters consist of wax, oil, and dense recycled wood, which holds up well in wet weather. Some fire starters are waterproof—drop a ferro rod in water, for example, and it won’t be affected. Just dry it off and it will still throw a spark that can ignite dry material. Fire starters also tend to burn at high temperatures of 800 degrees Fahrenheit or more, which allows them to better withstand windy and damp conditions.

Fire starters are meant to simplify the sometimes painstaking process of starting a fire by providing a persistent flame that can ignite nearby kindling. To do so, the fire starter must burn long enough to establish the fire. The longer the burn time, the more likely users can achieve a robust blaze. Our tests determined that most burn for an average of 3 to 15 minutes.

Earlier types of fire starters were typically infused with flammable compounds, which gave them a chemical smell. But the best fire starters in this day and age are nearly odorless. Many people appreciate the less noxious types of fire starters. However, fire starters that contain natural essential oils can lend a pleasing scent to the product that enhances the user’s experience without being toxic.

The best fire starters tend to be made of environmentally friendly materials, be it wood waste (sawdust or shavings), natural nontoxic wax, recycled paper, or waste textile fibers. Using fire starters typically results in faster and more complete ignition, which reduces airborne soot and smoke. Don’t miss our DIY fire-starter option above to find out how to make eco-friendly fire-starting accelerants from pine cones and beeswax.

A key to using a fire starter effectively is understanding how to arrange logs and kindling for the fire. Ahead, learn about how to build a fire correctly and use a fire starter to light it quickly.

To use a fire starter, begin by setting up your wood. If building a wood fire, you’ll need some kindling, which will ignite more quickly than full-size logs. Place the fire starter under the kindling or charcoal, leaving room so that you can reach the fire starter with a match or lighter. Light the fire starter and wait as it begins to burn and ignite the kindling.

To start a fire in a fire pit, gather wood, kindling, and a fire starter. Stack small pieces of kindling on top of one another, about four layers high, until you’ve formed a shape resembling a log cabin. Place the fire starter in the middle of your log cabin, pile kindling loosely in the middle, and then light the fire starter.

Begin by placing a layer of kindling and two or three small pieces of firewood on the fireplace grate, then place your fire starter in the space beneath the grate. Lighting the fire starter will ignite the kindling above it, which will, in turn, ignite the logs. Add larger logs as needed to keep the fire burning.

Fire starters are made up of materials that include recycled wood fibers, paper, oil, and wax that do not expire; hence, most fire starters do not have a shelf life. They may be attractive to insects, rodents, or other pests, so it is best to store them in airtight containers. Also, since heat may degrade the waxes and oils that are often used in these products, be sure to store them away from excessive heat.
