#7894. 40 Home Tasks to Tackle Before the First Frost

By Caitlin Castelaz, Michelle Ullman, Theresa Clement

Published Oct 30, 2026 10:16 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

When the dog days of summer give way to autumn’s cooler temperatures, it’s time to get your house in shape for the change of seasons. Fall is the ideal time of year to work outside because there’s just enough of a nip in the air to make being outdoors pleasant, but not so much that you need a heavy coat. Before Old Man Winter comes calling, take advantage of these temperate days to tackle this seasonal to-do list.

As the weather gets cooler, it’s time to put your garden to bed under a blanket of mulch. Protect annuals and perennials from the cold by covering them with a 2- to- 4-inch layer of organic material, such as shredded wood or wood chips, shredded leaves, or straw. For shrubs, trees, and rosebushes, wait to spread mulch until later in the season, when the soil is cool but not yet frozen.

Insects love nothing better than overwintering beneath dead flowers, leaves, and other plant material. Roll up the welcome mat by raking away fallen leaves, deadheading annuals, pruning perennials and roses, and clearing out your summer vegetables before the first frost.

Once nighttime temperatures sink below 50 degrees Fahrenheit, it’s time for your tender container plants to move indoors for the season. Before carrying them into your house or to a protected spot in the garage, first clip away any dead or damaged leaves and branches, and then check carefully for insects.

Nothing says spring is coming like colorful tulips, daffodils, crocuses, irises, and hyacinths, but if you want to enjoy these beauties in your spring garden, you need to plant bulbs in the fall. As a general rule, northern gardeners plant spring-blooming bulbs in late September through mid-October, while southern gardeners can wait until mid-October or early November.

Keep warm air in and cold air out, and reduce your heating bills at the same time, by sealing up leaky doors or windows now. Check for drafts by turning off fans or air conditioners, then holding a lit stick of incense near doors and windows. If the smoke wavers or is sucked outside, you know you have a problem. The solution is simple: Caulk any cracks or chips around windows, and install weatherstripping to ward off drafts around doors.

According to the National Fire Protection Association, three out of every five residential fire deaths occur in a home that either has no smoke detector at all, or a smoke detector with nonfunctioning batteries. Don’t let your family become a statistic. Check your smoke and carbon monoxide detectors at the very least twice a year, once in the fall and again in the spring.

The X-Sense detector has a photoelectric sensor to detect smoke particles and a display that indicates when CO is higher than 30ppm. Read the review.

It’s a good idea to have your home’s chimney inspected and swept before fireplace season gets underway. This job is best done by a pro—expect to pay around $150 to $200 for a professional chimney inspection—but if you’re comfortable on the roof, you can do some preliminary work yourself. First, clear out any fallen leaves, birds’ nests, or other debris from the chimney, and repair any small cracks in the masonry with refractory cement, which is formulated to withstand high heat. Ensure that the damper moves smoothly and isn’t cracked, rusted, or warped, and then clean away soot, creosote, and ash.

If you’ve been thinking that your entry door could use a refresh, a new coat of paint on the surrounding door trim can help. Entry doors and trim are hard workers in most homes, and they have the scuffs and smudges to show it. Just painting the trim and cleaning the door will give the entry a more polished look. Clean the trim, let it dry, and then apply exterior paint. Most homeowners choose gloss or semi-gloss when painting trim. Two coats should be enough to protect the trim and keep it looking fresh for a year or more, depending on the weather and how busy your household is.

Want your lawn to look its best come springtime? Then sow grass seed in early through mid-fall. Reseeding the lawn gives gardeners in cold-winter areas a head start on spring. As the weather warms up, the grass will germinate, crowd out weeds, and develop a strong root system before the high heat of summer. If you live in a warm-winter region and want to keep your grass green all season long, sow annual ryegrass in the early fall. This quick-sprouting grass will look great through the chilly months and then die down once higher temperatures return in the summer.

If you have an asphalt driveway, reseal it in the fall when temperatures are between 50 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit and no rain is in the forecast. For most areas, that means late September to early October. To start, sweep away dirt, leaves, and other debris from the asphalt, and then pour asphalt sealant over the driveway. Using an asphalt squeegee, evenly spread the sealant across the driveway’s entire surface. Let the sealant cure for at least 24 hours before parking on the driveway.

Winter can be hard on your roof, when rain, snow, freezing temperatures, and high winds all take their toll. That’s why fall is the best time to make sure to inspect your roof and complete any necessary roof repairs before cold weather sets in. You can hire a professional for this service or, if you’re up to the task, do it yourself.

Autumn means raking leaves, and raking leaves can mean back pain. Make the job easier on yourself by buying a good rake. The right one is long enough so you don’t need to bend over, has flexible yet durable tines to easily scoop up debris, and has a comfortable, ergonomically designed grip so your hands don’t feel the strain. Our researched guide to the best leaf rakes contains some terrific options, whatever your needs and budget.

In most regions, fall brings rain—and a parade of muddy shoes. Get your mudroom ready for the season by setting out a large mat to absorb water and a tray to hold wet, muddy boots and shoes. If you don’t already have one, add a bench where you can sit and pull on your boots, and consider including a coat rack or wall hooks to hold jackets, umbrellas, and scarves.

As they say, the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, and the second best time is now. If “now” happens to be autumn, you’re in luck: The cooler temperatures and moisture help the tree establish roots before the hot and stressful summer weather.

To ensure success, mulch your newly planted tree to keep the roots insulated. Water regularly if there’s not enough rain, but don’t fertilize until spring. Avoid heavy pruning, other than trimming away any broken branches. And if a severe cold snap is in the forecast, wrap a blanket or piece of burlap over the tree for a little extra protection while it gets established.

With summer fun in the rearview mirror, fall is the time for getting back to business. Creating an organization HQ for the whole family is a great way to help you stay on task. Put it in a central location like the kitchen, mudroom, or back entryway, where the whole family can see it.

Include a large wall calendar or weekly schedule, a dry erase board for appointment reminders or shopping lists, and a bulletin board for important announcements or incoming and outgoing school forms. If your family uses a chore chart or meal planning chart, this would be the place to put it. Set up caddies to collect keys and other daily necessities so they’ll be easy to find and won’t clutter up the rest of the house.

Drain your hot water heater to remove accumulations of lime and other minerals that naturally occur in your tap water. When left untreated, this buildup can keep your appliance from functioning its best and put your system at risk for leaks and other problems. It’s an easy enough job to do yourself, but if you’re not confident in your DIY abilities, call a pro to do it for you. Simple though it may seem, this one task can lengthen the life of your water heater and prevent the system from malfunctioning down the line.

As temperatures drop, mice and other pests will be looking for a warm place to bunk, which is all well and good unless they choose your home as their winter retreat. Stay pest-free by doing a walkabout around the exterior and through the interior of your house, plugging any potential points of entry with caulk or steel wool. Keep in mind that mice can enter your home through a dime-size hole, so pay attention to even the smallest cracks.

Fall leaves and winter snow can cause your patio furniture to fade, stain, and rust. Protect it with a tarp or patio furniture covers, or place it inside your shed, garage, or screened porch. Before you stow it for the season, give patio furniture a proper cleaning with mild soap and water to remove dust, pollen, and mold. Treat wicker with lemon oil to keep it moisturized over the dry winter months and protect it from mildew.

Core’s heavy-duty tarps have a smooth undercoating a good pick for outdoor furniture covers that won’t leave behind scuff marks. Read the review.

Soak and scour the grates, clean under the hood, remove any foil or food particles from the interior, and wipe down the exterior. When foul weather moves in for good, you can quickly cover the grill and store it for the season.

Keep mowing your lawn in the fall until the grass stops growing. Then, when it’s time to put it away for the season, make any necessary repairs the lawn mower to ensure that it will be in good working condition when you pull it out again in spring. Wipe away any grass or other debris that clings to the machine, and consider having the blades sharpened by a professional. If you have a gas lawn mower, use up the last of the gasoline in the tank or add fuel stabilizer to prevent damage (check the manufacturer’s instructions).

If your lawn receives a lot of foot traffic, it could be at risk for soil compaction, a condition that prevents the proper circulation of air and nutrients. To keep your turfgrass nourished, aerate cool-season grasses in fall by using a manual aerator, or a spike or plug aerator (available for purchase or rental at many home centers). Before you aerate the lawn, make sure the soil is moist but not soaking wet, because it can be difficult to aerate dry soil.

Cool-season grasses, like bluegrass and tall fescue, benefit from a fall application of fertilizer. Fertilize your lawn with a slow-release formula about 1 week before you mow for the last time in the season. High-nitrogen formulas that offer winter weather protection are helpful in colder climates.

That stunning fall foliage may look good on the trees in your front yard, but when those leaves drop they can make a mess of your gutters. More than unsightly, leaves and other debris can clog the gutters, posing a real hazard in winter when rain and snow thaw and freeze inside gutters and form dangerous ice dams.

Protect your home from damage by removing leaves, sticks, and other debris from gutters now, and consider installing a leaf guard to keep your rain gutters clean with very little effort on your part.

Button up the house and get ready for windy winter by swapping out your window screens for storm windows (if you have them). If you don’t have storm windows, particularly if you have vintage single-pane windows that you’re trying to save, consider installing them.

Storm windows offer an additional layer of insulation against cold weather and drafts, help keep your home more comfortable, and can help lower energy bills.

You don’t want to wait until snow is falling and frigid winds are howling to discover that your home’s heating system is on the fritz. Call a pro to come out and evaluate your heating system now. If the HVAC specialist detects any issues, have them fixed promptly to save yourself from a potentially chilly disaster later in the season.

It may seem counterproductive to turn on a ceiling fan during the coldest months of the year, but a ceiling fan helps maintain comfortable temperatures even in the winter. Starting in the fall, set your ceiling fan to rotate in a clockwise direction (opposite the operating ceiling fan direction in summer), and run it on low speed to create an updraft. This tactic draws the room air up and forces the warm air near the ceiling down and through the room.

Because water expands as it freezes, it’s important to disconnect and drain garden hoses before temperatures drop to prevent them from bursting or leaking. Be sure to disconnect hoses from the outdoor spigots to which they’re attached; store hoses in a covered area like the garage or a tool shed to protect them from harsh weather. Turn off and drain your sprinkler system and shut off your outdoor faucets before nighttime temperatures dip below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

It’s easier to identify dead limbs before your trees drop their leaves, so early fall is a good time to trim back dead branches. Trimming your trees now is more than an aesthetic choice, and doing so can protect your home from damage. In freezing conditions, dead limbs can become heavy with ice and break off, ending up on your roof or lawn, or posing a safety issue for family and passersby alike.

For as long as there have been air conditioning covers, people have debated whether they’re a good idea. Advocates love covers for the way they keep ice and debris out of the machinery, while detractors fear that covers can create ideal habitats for rodents and other pests that can nest within the wiring. Homeowners who live in colder regions may want to consider at least covering the top of their outside AC condenser unit with a tarp or sheet of plywood, even if they leave the rest of the unit exposed. Window air conditioning units, on the other hand, should be removed, cleaned, and stored in a safe place until they’re needed again in the summer.

Give your HVAC system a fresh start with a new furnace filter. Furnace filters help maintain cleaner indoor air and keep a home heating system in good working order. Continue to change the filter every few months until you turn off your heat for the season.

A clogged dryer vent can cause a perfectly good appliance to operate more slowly and less efficiently, but more importantly it poses a serious fire hazard. Clean out your dryer vent at least once a year to speed up laundry day, keep energy bills low, and protect your home from fires. You can do the job yourself with a vacuum cleaner and a long dowel or wire hanger (if you’re careful not to damage the vent), or hire a pro to do the job for you.

Mold counts are on the rise at this time of year, exacerbating indoor allergies. Mount an effective defense by giving your carpets a thorough cleaning. Rent a carpet cleaner or hire a professional service to deep clean your carpeting, paying special attention to the bedrooms and high-traffic areas. If you’ve been thinking about removing your carpeting in order to breathe more easily, now might be the time to do it. Who knows—you may even have pristine hardwood floors hiding under those old carpets!

Don’t wait until the first snowstorm of the season to stock up on snow removal supplies. Buy an emergency stash of ice melt, salt, and sand (or kitty litter, in a pinch) to give you traction in slippery situations. Some home centers start selling these supplies as early as September and October, but if your local shop doesn’t carry them, you can certainly buy them from online retailers.

Have you ever cranked up the heat in late fall and waited for your radiators to circulate warm air through your home, only to discover that one or more of your radiators remains cold to the touch? If one radiator isn’t working when the rest of your system is operating normally, it’s usually a sign that air is trapped inside. This problem can be avoided by bleeding the radiators at the beginning of the season. To do this, first turn off the heat, then engage the bleed valve with a radiator key. Wait for the hissing sound to stop and a stream of water to pour from the radiator before closing up the bleed valve.

Cracks happen, and it’s important to take care of them before winter freezes make them worse. To repair cracks in concrete walkways, patios, or driveways, first clear away any dirt or debris from the damaged area, and then fill in the crack with masonry crack filler or concrete patch. Once you’ve filled the crack, smooth the edges of the new material with a trowel, and let the repair cure overnight.

Be ready for the next big storm before it strikes with a “go bag” of emergency essentials, and give serious thought to buying a generator for the house if you don’t already have one. Generators are available in a variety of sizes and types, including portable generators and models that can be wired into a home’s electrical system. The larger the generator, the more power it provides. Before you make a purchase, be sure to determine which features and which fuel type best suit your household’s needs.

If you live in an area that sees a lot of snow and where a snow thrower or snow blower is a must-have, fall is the ideal time to make sure your equipment works. Have clean, stable gas at the ready, and then take the snow blower out for a quick test run. Fill the tank, start it up, and make sure all of the features work. Always be certain to have a spare spark plug on hand so you won’t be caught by surprise during a winter storm.

An easy way to get ready for cold, wet fall weather—and spruce up your entry while you’re at it—is to invest in a new doormat. With the return to school and a faster pace of life, fall is a time of year when many homes experience an uptick in foot traffic. A ragged, worn doormat may no longer do the trick, and it might not exude the welcoming vibe you desire. Because there are so many options in materials, sizes, designs, and styles, consider switching your doormats out seasonally so they won’t wear out as quickly.

In the colder months, as darkness begins to fall earlier in the day, having adequate light on a front porch or entryway becomes even more important. If you’ve had the same porch light bulbs for a long time and they aren’t LEDs, think about swapping them out for new ones. After all, an entry light fixture isn’t much help when it doesn’t turn on.

Landscape lighting elevates the look of a home’s facade and helps set a welcoming tone. With a range of available colors and options that include solar-powered landscape lighting, it’s easier than ever to line a walkway or driveway, or to spotlight trees and other landscaping or architectural features, creating a custom look for the exterior of your house.

#7892. Declutter Your Garage Space With These Smarter Solutions

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:12 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Upgrade your garage from a cluttered mess to a highly organized space you can use with the help of ATLAS Shelving’s next-generation heavy-duty industrial storage unit that features a clean, open, and adaptable design capable of holding up to 2,500 pounds per shelf and 10,000 pounds total, evenly distributed.

Decluttering the garage is a crucial step toward creating a safe, accessible, and high-functioning extension of your home. Because a garage serves as the main entryway for many households—as well as the storage hub for heavy tools, seasonal gear, sports equipment, lawn and garden supplies, and more—an unorganized space can quickly become an eyesore and safety hazard that makes daily routines frustrating and hard to maintain.

As professional organizer Abriana Sanford, founder of Sorted and Styled in Atlanta, Georgia, notes, “Garages tend to become the catch-all space for anything that doesn’t have a designated home. Over time, this can make it difficult to find what you need, but decluttering allows you to reassess what you’re storing, eliminate unnecessary items, and reclaim valuable square footage.” By turning a disorderly pile into a streamlined, easy-to-maintain setup using strategic organization solutions, you can eliminate everyday hassle, restore peace of mind, and ensure that every tool and bin serves a clear, functional purpose. Sanford shares her garage organization tips below so you can get the most out of your garage storage space.

The first step in any garage organization project is to assess what you have and to get rid of what you no longer need. “One of the most common mistakes homeowners make is purchasing storage products before evaluating what they actually need to store,” says Sanford. She recommends first sorting belongings into categories. Then eliminate duplicates and materials that you no longer need. Finally, take inventory of what’s remaining. “This allows you to create a system that works for your belongings, rather than trying to make your belongings fit a particular system.”

Once you narrow down what you have, spend some time grouping belongings by how they’re used, such as lawn care, sports equipment, tools, automotive supplies, beach and pool gear, and seasonal decorations. “Creating designated zones makes it easier to locate items and return them to their proper places,” says Sanford. She also recommends considering the frequency of use when determining placement. “Everyday essentials should be easily accessible, while seasonal belongings can occupy higher or less convenient storage areas.”

Garage floor space is valuable, especially when you park your vehicles inside, so choose a variety of storage solutions that use open areas on the walls and ceiling. “Wall-mounted shelving, pegboards, overhead racks, and vertical tool organizers allow homeowners to maximize storage without sacrificing usable floor space,” Sanford explains.

When choosing the right organizational tool, be sure to consider the weight capacity of shelving, wall-mounted systems, and overhead racks. “Heavier belongings are generally best stored on lower shelves, while lighter, less frequently used items can occupy higher storage areas,” notes Sanford. Always follow the manufacturer’s installation and load requirements.

It’s also important to consider how flexible and adaptable storage products are. “I encourage homeowners to think beyond their immediate storage needs. Adjustable shelving, movable racks, and modular systems provide flexibility as hobbies, equipment, and family needs change,” notes Sanford. As household needs evolve, the garage should be able to evolve with them. “For example, a family storing strollers and toddler toys today may need additional space for bicycles, sports equipment, or recreational gear in a few years.”

One of Sanford’s favorite approaches to garage organization is incorporating adjustable shelving and modular storage systems. The ATLAS 7304K builds on this idea with an open-frame design that allows convenient side access, including in tighter garage spaces. Its clean, streamlined structure also provides a modern appearance. Another idea is to make the most efficient use of drawer space by either buying or making dividers. You can also add labeled stackable bins to open shelves or closed cabinetry to maximize storage.

Convenience is a core component of organizing a garage. Storage placement should reflect how frequently an item is used, says Sanford. “Homeowners shouldn’t have to move multiple bins or climb a ladder every time they need something,” she explains. “The more convenient a system is, the more likely everyone in the household will maintain it.”

Here are some tips for organizing in a way that takes accessibility into account:

Plastic storage bins with tight-sealing lids are the best choice to protect items. “In humid climates, moisture can be particularly problematic,” notes Sanford. She recommends using appropriate moisture-resistant storage containers and keeping belongings elevated off the floor when possible. “Clear, durable bins with secure-fitting lids also help protect belongings from dust and debris, while allowing homeowners to identify contents quickly.”

Sanford suggests avoiding cardboard boxes for long-term garage storage, especially if pests are a concern. “Cardboard can absorb moisture and provide hiding places for pests, so durable plastic containers with secure lids are often a better alternative.”

Storage needs have changed, and storage products should evolve with them. By combining heavy-duty industrial strength with a clean, open, and adaptable design, the ATLAS 7304K is built not only for what homeowners need today, but for how those needs may change over time. Its next-generation design makes better use of the existing space while offering flexibility for the future. It’s built for heavy loads. Designed for changing needs.

#7889. How to Use a Shop Vac to Clean Up Wet Messes

By Tom Scalisi, Updated by Theresa Clement

Updated Oct 30, 2026 12:26 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

It’s not just dry messes that shop vacuums can handle. When unexpected wet messes happen, like a water main break, leak, or flood, a wet/dry shop vac is an indispensable tool that can quickly suck up the liquid into a canister for easy disposal. And, the variety of attachments that come with most shop vacs make them ready for flat surfaces, carpet, or even hard-to-reach crevices. The trick is knowing how to use a shop vac for water removal the right way. Here’s what you need to know.

Built for demanding cleanup jobs, DeWalt’s 9-gallon AC/DC et/dry vacuum combines heavy-duty suction power with the flexibility of corded or cordless operation. Whether you’re clearing water from a flooded basement or tackling a serious renovation mess, its large-capacity tank and dual-powered motor help reduce interruptions and keep projects moving.

Water and electricity don’t mix. Although modern shop vacs are typically double-insulated, it’s never a bad idea to plug yours into a GFCI outlet for extra assurance and if you use an extension cord, make sure it’s wet-rated.

Also, when using a shop vac for water, keep in mind that you will need to lift the shop vac’s canister to dump out the water when you are finished cleaning up a mess. It’s usually easier to dump out the water before it’s full.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

A shop vacuum can handle a ton of jobs like sawdust collection, carpet cleaning, and gutter cleaning. Here’s how to use a wet vac and how to suck up water with a shop vac.

If your model has a bag, remove it before using your shop vac for water. If you don’t, it will fill up with liquid and rip, making a nasty mess in the canister. These bags are typically very easy to remove and reinstall, so don’t throw yours out if it isn’t full.

Then remove the air filter. (If your shop vac has a wet filter, insert the model’s foam filter that’s designed for liquids.) If the air filter is installed when sucking up water, it will clog quickly and reduce airflow. The motor will then work harder than normally necessary, which could shorten the lifespan of your shop vac.

It’s easier to remove water from a surface if the end of the vacuum is compatible with the surface. For flat floors, look for the wide, T-shaped attachment. This attachment does the best job of removing water from hard floors of all types. Some of these floor attachments even have rubber squeegees that you can insert to increase their effectiveness.

Consider using the crevice tool for vehicle floors, tight spaces, depressions, or other spaces where the floor attachment won’t fit. You can also shop for a handheld wet vac meant specifically for small spaces.

Place the shop vac near the spill, and then run the cord to the closest GFCI outlet to extra protect yourself from any possible shock during use. If the cord doesn’t reach a GFCI outlet, then run an extension cord that’s wet-rated. You’ll see a W on the cord’s jacket if it’s wet-rated.

Pushing the vacuum attachment back and forth across the floor rapidly will spread puddles and make them harder to clean up. Here’s how to start vacuuming water.

For carpets and areas that require the crevice tool, adopt the same approach but on a smaller scale. Work in small areas, and give the vacuum a few seconds at each location before moving it to a new space.

Your shop vac has a built-in safety device that stops the vacuum when it’s full. There is a ball or puck in the filter attachment that floats, and when the water reaches an unsafe height, this device blocks the suction. To keep vacuuming, you’ll have to empty the canister.

After you finish cleaning up the water, you will still need to clean and dry the shop vac to prevent mold and mildew.

Using a shop vac for something wet usually means it’s a surprise and an urgent situation. From plumbing emergencies to severe storms and accidental spills, a wet-rated vacuum is a handy tool that can help contain wet messes and speed-up the return to normal. Here are some situations when a wet vac is a smart tool that can help.

There are a variety of shop vacs that are designed to handle different types of messes. Since everyone’s situation is different, consider your needs so you can choose the best shop vac for you. Here are some popular types of shop vacs.

Watch BobVila.com’s tool tester vacuum up water on a concrete floor using a wet/dry shop vac:

If you have a surprise basement cleanup to tackle, it may make sense to rent a shop vac, since big box stores also rent shop vacs by the hour or day for less than the cost of a new one. However, it might make sense to purchase one if you expect that you’ll use it at least several times a year.

Experts suggest running a shop vac for 2 hours or less before giving the motor a break to cool down, which can help extend the life of the tool. It’s also important to keep in mind that tools have an expected lifetime. For example, Ridgid says their vacuums expect a life of about 500 to 700 hours.

Yes, a wet vac can suck up liquids beyond just water as long as the liquid is not toxic or hazardous.

A shop vac is a great first response tool, and it’s useful for smaller messes. However, for substantial flooding or when water’s been present for long enough to cause structural damage or mold and mildew issues, you might need to call in the experts.

#7887. Promise to Apologize Might Be Enforceable—but Court Can't Order Apology if None Was Finally Agreed to

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Mia Roberts Perez (E.D. Pa.) in Souderton Area for All v. Souderton Area School Dist., decided Sept. 28:

This case began as a case about Plaintiffs' exercise of their First Amendment rights by protesting at a Souderton Area School District ("District") school board meeting. It then became a case about keeping promises. Now, it is a case about which promises this Court can enforce.

When Plaintiffs protested the Souderton Area School Board outside a September 2024 meeting, the government officials for whom their message was intended were not the only ones affected. One school board member was accompanied by her teenage daughter as they exited the meeting. In the parking lot, Plaintiffs Christopher Spigel, Helen Spigel, and Patrick Kitt confronted them. Rather than constraining their critical expression to the adult members of the school board, the protesters directed their ire toward the child, who the District has consistently maintained was frightened by the adult Plaintiffs' conduct.

Here are plaintiffs' allegations as quoted in an earlier decision:

According to the Complaint, in August 2024, Plaintiffs and other District community members learned that then-member of the Board of School Directors of Souderton Area School District (the "Board") William Formica posted lewd comments on social media about Vice President Kamala Harris, disparaging teachers and non-English speakers, and deriding diversity programs. In response, Plaintiff Souderton Area For All ("SAFA") encouraged its members to attend District Board meetings to protest and demand Mr. Formica's resignation.

The August 29, 2024 Board meeting saw high attendance of community members opposed to Mr. Formica's remarks, as well as a rally organized by SAFA to protest. But the Board did not allow SAFA or its members to demonstrate on District property, requiring them to gather on a public sidewalk 80 feet away from where the meeting was held.

At the same time, the Board permitted supporters of Mr. Formica to gather and counter-protest directly outside the meeting's entrance on District property. Due to increased attendance, the Board began requiring meeting attendees to provide photo-ID so that they could prioritize seating for District residents. Several individual Plaintiffs were excluded from meetings as a result of this new rule.

On September 26, 2024, as Board members exited a Board meeting, Plaintiffs Patrick Kitt, Christopher Spigel, and Helen Spigel protested by making cricket noises and accusing the Board of being complicit in Mr. Formica's misconduct through its silence. One Board member was accompanied by her teenage daughter, who was upset and intimidated by the protesters directing questions and accusations to her.

Two weeks later, the District issued cease and desist letters to Plaintiffs Kitt, Spigel, and Spigel, informing them they could not be on school property for the remainder of the school year, including for public meetings. On November 20, 2024, Plaintiffs filed this lawsuit, alleging the District's actions violated their rights to free speech and due process. In addition to the Complaint, on November 20, 2024, Plaintiffs filed a Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order ("TRO"), seeking to enjoin the District from enforcing its ban on Plaintiffs from entering school property for the remainder of the 2024–25 school year and allowing Plaintiffs to enter school property to attend school board meetings and other events on the same terms as other members of the public….

[T]he Court enforces the settlement promises …: continued livestreaming and archiving of Board meetings; rescission of the cease-and-desist letters; completion and maintenance of the designated protest/gathering area consistent with applicable law; and payment of the attorneys' fees already authorized.

What exactly was allegedly said to the daughter? According to a letter from the school district's lawyer attached to the Complaint,

It is my understanding that you … began screaming erroneously believing that [Board member Kim Wheeler's] daughter was Bill Formica's daughter. You screamed: "Tell your father he's an asshole" and "Tell her dad he's a fascist and needs to resign."

We are also advised that Jim Wheeler admonished you not to speak to her daughter because she is just a child and Bill Formica was not her father. You once again began yelling at Kim Wheeler's daughter to: "Then tell your mother to stop saying silent and she's just as bad as Bill."

On the other hand, the plaintiffs' counsel describes matters differently (in response to an e-mail from me):

As to the plaintiffs' position regarding what was said at the September 26, 2024, school board meeting, Chris Spigel recalled asking "does the child know her dad is a fascist?" and Patrick Kitt recalled that he called Board Member Formica a "coward" and a "beta male" but did not say anything to Board Member Wheeler's daughter, who was 15 at the time.

The e-mail also disputes other claims in the letter from the school district's lawyer, related to how close some of the plaintiffs were to Formica and her daughter; it cites surveillance video at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Th8y29iZjY0 (though noting that the video has no sound).

And now back to the Sept. 28 decision on the apology:

After the District retaliated against Plaintiffs and Plaintiffs brought this lawsuit, the parties engaged in lengthy settlement negotiations. At all times, the settlement terms included a promise by Plaintiffs to issue an apology to the child who was personally, adversely affected by their conduct.

The settlement negotiations ultimately broke down, and this Court granted the District's motion to enforce the settlement agreement on promissory estoppel grounds. The Court found that Plaintiffs promised to dismiss the lawsuit and apologize to the child, that the District relied on those promises when it took definite and substantial action to fulfill its own obligations under the settlement agreement, and that it would be unjust to allow Plaintiffs to walk away after the District's actions in reliance.

Plaintiffs move for reconsideration of one part of the Court's order, which was sealed due to the confidential nature of the parties' agreement. The Sealed Supplemental Order required Plaintiffs to keep their promise to apologize to the board member's teenage daughter, an innocent bystander who no one disputed was caught in the crossfire of the protest and experienced emotional distress as a result.

As adults, as community members, and as parents, people recognize the importance of teaching children by example: showing them kindness and respect, and taking accountability for their choices so that their children may follow those examples in their treatment of others. It is not controversial to acknowledge that the ethical thing to do when an adult harms a child is to apologize to that child, even if the harm was inadvertent.

The First Amendment, however, limits the Court's ability to compel an apology. A party may waive First Amendment rights through an agreement, but courts presume against waiver of fundamental rights. Any waiver must be voluntary, knowing, and intelligent, and supported by clear and compelling evidence.

Here, the record does not establish such a waiver. The proposed apology changed throughout the negotiations—including who would issue it, what it would say, and how it would be delivered—and Kitt's willingness to apologize was conditioned on resolution of all other settlement issues, a condition that was not met. For these reasons, and those discussed more fully below, Plaintiffs' Motion for Reconsideration is granted….

Plaintiffs argue the Sealed Supplemental Order violates their First Amendment right against compelled speech. Defendants oppose, asserting that the Order at issue here merely enforces a promise Plaintiff Kitt made, through which he waived his First Amendment right….

[G]enerally applicable laws do not offend the First Amendment simply because they have incidental effects on speech. See Cohen v. Cowles Media (1992) (finding that allowing promissory estoppel action based on promise not to disclose confidential source's identity did not violate First Amendment despite incidental consequence of inhibiting truthful reporting because "the First Amendment does not confer on the press a constitutional right to disregard promises that would otherwise be enforced under state law"). "First Amendment rights can be limited via contract."

However, there must be "'clear' and 'compelling' evidence of waiver and that waiver is voluntary, knowing, and intelligent." "[C]ourts must indulge every reasonable presumption against waiver of fundamental constitutional rights." In the context of the First Amendment, a waiver must also be "freely given."

Typically, courts lack the power to order litigants to apologize. See Devonish v. Atl. Cnty. Justice Facility (D.N.J. 2010) (collecting cases and dismissing claim for injunctive relief directing an apology because "the remedy of 'apology' is not cognizable, either within the meaning of a Section 1983 action or as a general legal remedy that a court has the power to order, under any provision"); see also Woodruff v. Ohman (6th Cir. 2002) (finding district court exceeded its equitable power when ordering defendant to apologize for gender discrimination because "[t]he apology will not provide any remedy … for which the damages imposed have not already accounted," and there was no authority "that would permit a court to order a defendant to speak in a manner that may well contravene the beliefs the defendant holds"); Ali v. Barton (N.D. Fla. 2020) (noting that the Court lacks the power to order defendants to issue "an unconditional apology")….

Throughout the settlement negotiations, the parties themselves disagreed about the nature of the apology. The apology was first raised as a term of the settlement at the settlement conference on January 16, 2025. The parties initially agreed that Plaintiff Stephanie Barnett Jamison would deliver the apology to the minor. The minor thereafter expressed that she would not accept an apology from Jamison because Jamison was not directly involved in the actions that frightened her. As of February 5, 2025, the parties were still negotiating the specifics of the apology.

Plaintiffs eventually agreed that Kitt was willing to provide the apology "so long as all other issues in the case are resolved." The issues were not fully resolved. Between February and May 2025, the parties continued exchanging drafts of the settlement agreement and making changes to certain provisions, including whether the parties would issue a joint press release, individual press releases, or no press release at all. That term was never resolved because the District did not accept Plaintiff's final proposal that the agreement be silent as to a press release until the offer was terminated. The Court already found that term material to the agreement.

As this Court previously explained, each of the drafts the parties exchanged contained materially different terms. Each constituted an offer or counteroffer, such that there was no settlement agreement that the Court could enforce under traditional contract principles. The Court agrees with Plaintiffs that Kitt could not knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waive his First Amendment right to be free from government compelled speech when his promise was conditioned on the parties' resolution of all other issues—a condition that was not met….

I am looking into getting unsealed the sealed supplemental order and the briefing related to objections to that order.

Emily Morgan and Joy Ramsingh (Ramsingh Legal, PLLC), and Solomon Furious Worlds and Sara J. Rose (ACLU of Pennsylvania) represent plaintiffs.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. #7884. Snow Thrower vs. Snow Blower: What’s the Difference?

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

When a winter storm dumps a thick white blanket of the white stuff on your property, a snow blower or snow thrower can be your best friend. But which one do you need? Many often use the two terms interchangeably to describe snow removing power tools, but snow blowers and snow throwers are actually two distinct types of machines. While they serve the same purpose, they differ in size, power, snow removal ability, and price. Understanding the difference between the two is key to choosing a snow thrower vs snow blower to handle your winter snow clearing duties. Here’s what you need to know about.

Snow throwers and snow blowers clear snow in the same way: Both have a spinning auger that lifts the snow and launches it through a chute as you guide the tool along a driveway or walkway. But while snow throwers do this in a single step, or stage, a snow blower uses multiple stages to move the snow. There’s also a size difference: Snow throwers are smaller, more nimble machines that can handle moderate snowfall on smaller driveways, while snow blowers are larger and capable of clearing deeper snow from bigger driveways.

Snow throwers are ideal for removing small amounts of snow that are not extremely deep.They are single-stage machines that scoop up snow with an auger and launch snow out of a chute in a single action. Depending on the size of the snow thrower, they can clear a path that’s 18 to 24 inches wider and between 6 and 12 inches deep. Many can hurl it a distance of 15 to 20 feet, while some can send snow as far as 40 feet.

This Greenworks snow thrower weighs just 32 pounds and, in our tests, was powerful enough to clear snow up to 12 inches deep. Read the review.

Snow blowers are more powerful than snow throwers, making them a good choice for those who need to clear larger driveways or live in areas with harsher winters that receive higher snowfall totals. Like snow throwers, snow blowers have a rotating auger that scoops up snow, but they use two or three stages to clear snow. But instead of launching snow, it sends it to a separate impeller which blows the snow out through a chute and launches it 25 to 40 feet away. Some can even send snow as far as 50 feet away.

A three-stage model is even more powerful. This type of snow blower has an accelerator that breaks up the snow, allowing it to cut through compacted icy snow and large piles of snow more quickly than a two-stage model. Snow blowers can clear a path of snow ranging from 24 to 32 inches wide and 1 to 2 feet deep. With their two stage design in optimal conditions, some are capable of launching snow up to 60 feet.

Ryobi’s two-stage snow blower is easy to maneuver in tight spaces, has a powerful auger, and even works on gravel driveways. Read the review.

Choosing between a snow thrower and snow blower comes down to several factors, including snowfall totals, driveway type and size, ease of use, and price.

The average snowfall totals of the winter storms passing through your area are a big factor in determining whether to go with a snow thrower or snow blower. If snowstorms routinely drop snowfall of more than a foot of snow that’s wetter and more compacted, you’ll need a snow blower’s power and capacity to clear it. If your snowstorms are typically under a foot and consist of fluffy to moderately heavy snow, you can take on winter with a snow blower.

Keep in mind that the depth a snow blower or snow thrower can handle can vary from model to model, so make sure to check the manufacturer’s ratings. Some lighter-duty snow throwers max out at 6 inches, while there are compact snow blowers that might only be able to handle up to a foot of snow.

The type of driveway you’re clearing determines the type of snow removal machine you need. If you’re clearing a gravel driveway, don’t use a snow thrower. Since snow throwers have paddles that scrape across the ground, they can pick up and throw gravel, damage the auger, and send the gravel into your yard.

Snowblowers, in comparison, have skid shoes that prevent the auger housing from coming into contact with the ground, making them capable of clearing gravel driveways. But unlike snow throwers, which clear snow down to the pavement, snow blowers leave a thin layer of snow–about 1/8 of an inch–on smooth pavement.

The size of your driveway largely determines whether a single-stage snow thrower or multi-stage snow blower is the best choice. Snow throwers can cut a swath through snow that’s 18 to 24 inches wide, which makes them best suited for the typical two-car driveway.  Snow blowers have wider clearing widths of up to 32 inches, so they can cover significantly more ground than a snow thrower with each pass. They are a better choice for larger driveways.

Throwing distance is also an important factor when deciding between a snow blower and snow thrower. Most snow throwers can launch snow a distance of 15 to 25 feet away, though there are some single stage models that can throw snow up to 45 feet. A snow blower’s multi-stage design allows them to launch snow further, typically up to 50 feet, which is useful when clearing wider driveways or large patios.

With their ability to remove a wider swath of snow with each pass and launch it further, snow blowers are best suited for handling long winding driveways or larger driveways that hold three or more vehicles. While snow throwers have a narrower clearing width, their small size makes them easier to turn and maneuver, allowing you to clear 4 to 8 inches of snow over a smaller one- to two-car driveways.

However, these are recommendations. You can certainly use a snow thrower to tackle a larger driveway. Just plan on spending more time out in the cold to get the job done. Likewise, you can use a larger snow blower on a small driveway, but it may end up taking you longer. These larger machines require more room to turn and are more difficult to maneuver around smaller driveways.

Snow throwers are smaller and lighter, which generally makes them easier to maneuver, especially in tight areas. The controls on a snow thrower are also relatively simple, so there’s less of a learning curve when operating them.

Snow blowers are much heavier but are usually self-propelled and have power steering, so there’s less physical effort to operate them than a snow thrower. However, they are very difficult to move when the engine is off, which makes it more difficult to get in and out of storage.

A snow blower usually has more controls on the handlebars than a snow thrower, so expect a longer learning curve when learning how to use a snow blower.

Both snow throwers and snow blowers come in battery-powered and gas-powered versions. Cordless electric snow blowers are easier to maintain and start than gas models, operate with less vibration, and don’t produce exhaust. While gas-powered machines were once prevalent, today’s cordless electric models are comparable in clearing width, throwing distance, and snow capacity. That said, gas-powered machines still dominate when it comes to runtime. While it takes minutes to refill a gas tank, it can take hours to recharge a battery.

Snow throwers generally cost less than snow blowers. The transmission, large engines, and self-propelled system on these machines adds to their expense. Single-stage snow throwers are simpler machines, so they cost less. Snow throwers generally cost $500 to $1,000, while snow blowers can range between $800 and $2,000, with battery-powered snow blowers typically costing a couple hundred dollars more.

#7883. Why You Should Pay Attention to Diamond-Shaped Signs on Trucks

Those metal diamonds on the back of trucks serve a purpose. Learn how hazmat placard holders work and what an empty one actually means.

Drivers have a lot to pay attention to on the road. They watch their speed, check their mirrors, and keep an eye out for sudden stops. But one detail most drivers probably haven’t given much thought to is the diamond-shaped designs on the back of trucks, even after seeing them countless times.

No, they aren’t decorations. It’s a small detail that serves an important safety purpose, especially if there’s an accident involving dangerous cargo. Learn how the holders work, what the warning signs mean, and why some appear empty.

They’re called hazmat placard holders. These metal frames hold warning signs that identify certain hazardous materials a truck might be carrying. The bare diamond in the photo is simply a holder. Its lines and clips don’t send any special message to other drivers.

Truck operators leave the holders attached and change the signs depending on their cargo. Some hold removable placards, while others have several signs that drivers can flip between. Labelmaster, a company that makes flip-placard systems, explains that drivers can change the warning without replacing the holder.

The placards use colors, words, and symbols to identify different hazards. Red often indicates flammable materials, while a black-and-white sign marked “CORROSIVE” warns about chemicals that can cause damage. Other signs identify dangerous gases, explosives, or toxic substances.

“Placards serve as an easily identifiable, visual source of information used by millions of workers in the transportation, public safety, and hazmat industries,” according to the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA).

These warnings help emergency responders recognize potential hazards during an accident or spill. Some placards also display numbers that identify specific hazardous materials.

An empty holder may mean the truck doesn’t need to display a warning for its current shipment. Trucking companies leave the frames attached because their vehicles might carry different types of cargo from one trip to the next. An empty holder doesn’t necessarily mean the truck isn’t carrying hazardous materials, though. Federal regulations don’t require placards for every hazardous material or quantity.

When trucks do need placards, PHMSA requires them on both sides and both ends of the vehicle. Carriers must also keep the signs secure, readable, and visible. Federal regulations also prohibit misleading signs that resemble official hazmat placards. The rules specifically mention “Any sign, advertisement, slogan (such as ‘Drive Safely’), or device” that could be confused with an official warning placard.

A bare metal diamond, however, isn’t a hazard warning by itself. It’s simply a holder for the appropriate sign when the truck needs one.

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As you plan the tablescape upon which your Thanksgiving dinner will be presented, look to autumn’s stunning natural bounty and colors for inspiration. Earthy green, orange, and red tones can help set the scene, but natural elements like leaves, flowers, pinecones, and foliage, are what will really deliver the “natural abundance” vibe. The best part? Decor that you bring in from outdoors is compostable and inexpensive, if not free.

If you don’t have a ready supply of real leaves, consider creating some of your own, like DIY Candy does. These were made with stencils and thin sheets of cork (both of which you can purchase at craft supply stores). In addition to adding style, these leaves also serve as handy, decorative trivets. You can also purchase premade cork leaf coasters if you don’t want to make them.

Short on time? According to A Beautiful Mess, a beautiful centerpiece can be assembled quickly from items found in the produce department at the grocery store: Group colorful fruits, like oranges, tangerines and pomegranates. Sprinkle green pistachios and sprigs of fresh rosemary along the middle of the table to create the illusion of a decorative runner. When dinner is over, invite your guests to partake of the fruit and nuts as a post-feast treat, or save the tastiest morsels and place them in your kitchen fruit bowl.

The curves of a pumpkin’s stem makes it a natural choice for tabletop decor. Give your simple squash an unexpected twist, as A Night Owl blog does, by attaching a piece of eucalyptus and a nametag to the stem and fashioning a place card. You can purchase faux eucalyptus stems to use for your DIY decor year after year.

Butternut squash is probably in season now at your local farmers market. Bring this culinary hero to the table by featuring it in a Thanksgiving centerpiece, as blog A Piece of Rainbow does here. When placed in a nest of moss and pinecones, it makes a rustic statement.

This simple yet stunning idea from Cherished Bliss isn’t the typical way of serving Thanksgiving cranberries, but it’s certainly stylish. Float a tea light candle atop a handful of fresh cranberries in a water-filled vase. For extra pizzazz, add a sprig of eucalyptus to the water and dip the base of the vase in metallic paint. Or, skip the extras and let the bright berries shine on their own!

The autumn harvest days spent at the local apple orchard might be behind us, but America’s favorite fruit still has a place in your Thanksgiving festivities. Place apples (always in groups of three) of any variety at different places along your table runner, and fill in with pillar candles and faux or real greenery for a rich display.

If you’re burned out on pumpkin-themed decor and pumpkin spice-flavored everything, take a cue from Cupcakes and Cashmere blogger: Swap out the ubiquitous squash for an unexpected edible. Persimmons, for example, are of a similar size, shape, and color but bring a beauty to the table that is distinctly their own.

Cristina Garay at RemodelaCasa uses pears as a beautiful addition to a natural Thanksgiving tabletop display. Add it to an edible centerpiece or place it atop your guest’s place, on its own or with a name card, as an extra touch of hospitality. If, by lucky coincidence, someone has sent you some Harry & David pears for the holiday, why not put them to work before eating them?

Russet, crimson, mustard, and brown: These colors typify the Thanksgiving tablescape, but that doesn’t mean you can’t think outside the box when it comes to your holiday centerpiece. Follow the lead of the blog It All Started with Paint and paint seasonal squash in the color palette of your choice to marry tradition with contemporary style for a look that captures your personality. Or, purchase a set of painted faux pumpkins to use for your holiday table settings every year.

Nature offers an abundance of color this time of year, so use it to your advantage. At the StoneGable blog, napkins are topped with golden-hued leaves, which you can buy online or pluck from your lawn. The centerpiece of tall and short vases and white pumpkins carry through on the theme.

Design Dazzle’s basket of seasonal bounty may look like a headache to assemble, but many of the makings of this Thanksgiving display can be found in your own garden beds. If you do choose to forage in your backyard for your tabletop display, be sure to shake, wash or brush off the greenery, then let it sit for a couple of days before placing it on the table.

Normally hung on a door this time of year, Indian corn can be a beautiful addition to the Thanksgiving Day table. Here, the corn is placed atop plates, along with a seasonal card, to bring color and life to neutral stoneware.

The squirrels in your backyard already know the secret: Acorns are everywhere at this time of year, so there’s no reason not to bring them to the harvest table. Use them as fillers in glass containers or, if you are ready to recreate this DIY craft from Hello Little Home, make acorn napkin ties like those shown here.

Golden-hued wheat is certainly a symbol of the season and the Thanksgiving table. Create miniature sheaves bound with ribbon, as did the blogger at Carolyn’s Homework, or simply use the wheat to create a casual centerpiece of candles, gourds and fruit.

A pie pumpkin, placed atop a dinner plate, makes a wonderful place marker for the Thanksgiving table. Using a paint marker, write your guests’ names on the front of a pumpkin, and set it carefully at each person’s place. It’s a simple gesture but makes for a natural gift they can take with them when they leave and enjoy again, when added to their own homemade centerpieces.

The traditional holiday bird won’t be the only scene stealer this season, when you add feather and cork place cards to your Thanksgiving table. Feathers, corks, and ribbon can be purchased at your local craft store; bind them together to create the look, then watch the expression on everyone’s faces when they marvel at your crafty tablescape.

Bright and cheery, let a sunflower bloom greet each guest when they sit down at the table. Place one inside a folded napkin atop each guest’s plate. For less formal buffet dinners, float a couple flowers in a bowl of water, then place the bowl on a tray filled with rolls of silverware. When your guests go through the line, they’ll see the sunny arrangement and smile.

For a touch of whimsy, sprinkle a handful of fallen leaves over your tablescape. Not for neat freaks, this fanciful display evokes a walk in the woods. However, if you’re playing host to grandma (who never did quite approve of your slapdash cleaning routine), nix this one from your Thanksgiving idea file.

Branches create a natural centerpiece, and a dramatic statement in this country chic home. If you still have trees and shrubs with autumn-colored leaves, consider pruning a selection to decorate your Thanksgiving Day table. Just remember to keep them a reasonable height for dining, or remove them when the meal is served.

Evoke the beauty of nature, without giving the kids ammo with which to torture their cousins: This Thanksgiving printable from Kiki & Company makes an adorable addition to the kids’ table and lends a little fanciness to the little ones’ big meal.

This modern take on a table runner proves that order and symmetry might be overrated. Ruch and wrinkle your runner just so, and nestle vases of bright flowers and little pumpkins among the folds of the fabric for a perfectly imperfect arrangement.

Even after Halloween, pumpkin-carving season persists. Make these clever little votive holders by hollowing out a mini pumpkin and placing a tea light inside. Leave the outside of the pumpkin natural, or gild it with gold-colored paint. The 36th Avenue has the tutorial.

Sometimes simple is best. This understated table setting pairs a single pinecone with dinner plate and charger for an autumnal display that’s perfect for Thanksgiving.

Pumpkins and gourds make great table decorations at a big fall meal. That includes white pumpkins, too!  Here, a grouping of faux white pumpkins and other natural-hued elements set a distinctive Thanksgiving Day table, but it would look just as nice with naturally white (or painted) pumpkins.

Walnuts and pecans are back on the menu at this time of year, so add them to your Thanksgiving table settings for a festive touch. A handful of walnuts gives a name card a boost on this rustic display.

Illumine the simple beauty of natural (or faux) foliage with an arrangement of white pillar candles of varying heights. When the candles start to drip on the kraft paper tablecloth, you’ll know it’s time for pie.

A wooden charger brings a rustic sensibility to a Thanksgiving table of crystal and silver. You can make your own from wood rounds available at most craft stores. Apply wood stain to the rounds or leave them plain for a touch of woodland whimsy.

Another edible arrangement, this one brings together winter seasonal vegetables and fruit (like cabbage and pomegranates) with other colorful picks like bell peppers, globe grapes, and red radishes. Place your produce in a wooden trough or long basket and fill in with parsley and greenery for a unique centerpiece that you can turn into next week’s salad.

Who says evergreens are only for Christmas? Break out the boughs early and fashion them into a delightful place marker. This one from In Honor of Design is made from a couple sprigs of rosemary tied with string.

Nature and artifice combine in this stunning Thanksgiving tablescape. Clear and copper candle holders are complemented with white pumpkins adorned with stripes copper-colored tape, while a patterned table runner continues the theme.

A study in sturdiness, this table runner from Blooming Homestead is nothing more than a pine board stained an elegant dark brown. When laid atop the Thanksgiving table and topped with pinecones, adornments, and a vase full of wheat, it evokes and warmth and cheer.

Mums are the official flower of fall, so give them a spot at the Thanksgiving table. Place small vases of the blooms all along the length of the table for a short centerpiece that’s easy to peer over but still makes a big—and beautiful—statement.

Flowers don’t always have to be arranged in a vase. San Diego-area florist Native Poppy recommends laying a mini-bouquet of dried flowers at every place setting, which guests could then take home as favors. Fresh-flower bouquets are just as pretty, as are single stems in a seasonal color. Placing flowers at each place setting also eliminates the problem of trying to hold a conversation over a tall centerpiece—and probably costs a lot less than that tall centerpiece, too.

#7881. Some Surprisingly Tolerant Judges out There in Pennsylvania

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Commonwealth v. Outlaw, decided Thursday by Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice David Wecht, writing for a unanimous court:

In June 2022, Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington was holding a hearing on a motion to suppress evidence in Marquis McClain's criminal case. Seated in the gallery of the courtroom was McClain's acquaintance, Basile Outlaw. After Judge Covington announced that she would be denying McClain's suppression motion, Outlaw stood up and said "the judge is a cocksucker" loud enough for Judge Covington to hear. Judge Covington responded, "What did you say?" Outlaw replied: "Never mind. I'm leaving." Outlaw then exited the courtroom.

A deputy sheriff and a court employee began searching the building for Outlaw. The trial court recessed the suppression matter to allow McClain's defense attorney to confer with his client in the wake of the court's suppression ruling. The court subsequently adjourned, but Judge Covington asked McClain's attorney to "stick around for another moment … just in case." Around this time, Outlaw came back to the courtroom on his own, at which time he was taken into custody for direct criminal contempt.

Outlaw was tried and sentenced "to fifteen to thirty days' incarceration"; he served thirty days. But the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the conviction:

Specifically at issue here is Subsection 4132(3) [of the Pennsylvania Crimes Code]. A conviction under that Subsection "requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt: (1) of misconduct, (2) in the presence of the court, (3) committed with the intent to obstruct the proceedings, (4) which obstructs the administration of justice." This Court has held that, "[f]or conduct to constitute an obstruction of the administration of justice, it must significantly disrupt judicial proceedings." This means that "[r]emarks that are injudicious, or even disrespectful, will not, without more, justify a summary conviction for contempt of court." To illustrate these principles, consider Williams v. Williams, where a pro se attorney in a custody dispute reacted injudiciously to a trial judge's evidentiary ruling:

Opposing Counsel: I heard him say that you are such a fucking asshole. I heard it as an officer of the court. And the stenographer is nodding her head. That's exactly what he said, "He is such a fucking asshole." And he said it under his breath. And as an officer of the court, I am standing here, and I am testifying that that's exactly what he said.

The trial court held Williams in contempt. On appeal, however, this Court held that Williams' remark did not obstruct the administration of justice because, although "there was a momentary break in the proceedings" due to Williams' comment, "the hearing resumed quickly," "[t]he entire incident encompassed just three and a half pages of hearing transcript," and "[s]uch a transient delay is not an obstruction of justice." Expounding upon the statutory requirement that the contemnor must "obstruct[t] the administration of justice," we explicitly stated that "[i]nappropriate and even ill-mannered conduct which does not obstruct or delay the trial falls short of the misbehavior punishable under 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132(3)."

Consistent with Williams is Behr v. Behr, where a pro se litigant brought to family court a box of documents that had the word "DEATH" scrawled on it in faint orange highlighter. The box remained under the litigant's table for the entire hearing, and only after the proceeding concluded did anyone notice it. The trial court held the litigant in contempt, but this Court reversed, concluding that the litigant's conduct did not significantly disrupt the judicial proceeding. We also rejected the trial court's suggestion that a significant disruption occurred when the presence of the box triggered an investigation and subsequent contempt hearing. We called this "circular reasoning" because, if we accepted the argument, it would mean that "any time a court reconvenes a hearing to investigate alleged misconduct, the alleged contemnor has automatically obstructed the administration of justice." …

The circumstances of this appeal are analogous to those in Williams. The insult that Outlaw directed at the court here ("the judge is a cocksucker") is offensive in a manner similar to the remark made in Williams ("He's such a fucking asshole."). Both comments fall well below the expected standard of courtroom decorum, and both contemnors made their comments in response to judicial rulings with which they disagreed. Furthermore, the delay to the proceedings in this case was limited to the judge asking Outlaw "What did you say?", followed by Outlaw responding "Never mind. I'm leaving." This is the exact sort of "transient delay" or "momentary break in the proceedings" that we held in Williams cannot serve as the basis for a conviction under Subsection 4132(3). …

[A]t common law, judges had broad authority to impose contempt for insulting remarks that undermine the court's authority with the public. This sweeping authority continued to be enforced well into the twentieth century. In Appeal of Levine (Pa. 1953), for example, we affirmed the contempt conviction of a District Attorney who responded to a scheduling misunderstanding by saying to a trial judge: "that's the way with this court, always mixing things up; everything is set on one day." Upholding the contempt conviction, this Court described the inherent contempt powers possessed by trial courts in extremely broad terms, saying that: "[g]enerally speaking, one is guilty of contempt when his conduct tends to bring the authority and administration of the law into disrespect."

Appeal of Levine represents perhaps the zenith of judicial contempt authority in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. The Appeal of Levine Court itself admitted that the judicial power to punish all disrespectful conduct committed in the court's presence is "arbitrary in [ ] nature and liable to abuse." Following Appeal of Levine, the judicial contempt powers were codified and limited by the General Assembly's enactment of 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132. Our decisions interpreting that statutory codification, including Williams, Behr, and Campolongo, retreated from Appeal of Levine's maximalist approach and stressed that "[i]nappropriate and even ill-mannered conduct which does not obstruct or delay the trial falls short of the misbehavior punishable under 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132(3)." These decisions also emphasized that "trial judges are supposed to be persons of fortitude who are able to thrive in a hardy environment, and they must be on guard against confusing offenses to their sensibilities with obstruction of the administration of justice."

The OAG's [Office of the Attorney General's] argument cannot be squared with these contemporary precedents. Under the OAG's proposed approach, virtually all disrespectful remarks or profane language would be contemptuous, so long as the comment can be said to risk undermining the court's authority in the minds of the public. Indeed, the OAG maintains that "spewing" vulgar language of any kind while court is in session constitutes an obstruction to the administration of justice (even if it does not delay the proceedings) because such language "weakens the public's faithful adherence to a court's judgments and rules of decorum." The OAG's view of the law is not compatible with this Court's precedent, which holds that there can be no obstruction of the administration of justice within the meaning of the Judicial Code absent a significant disruption to the judicial proceeding. …

Justice Sallie Updike Mundy concurred, joined by Justices Kevin Dougherty and Kevin Brobson:

[W]e have not been asked to reconsider our holdings in [cases such as Williams], and absent such a request, this Court must adhere to these decisions…. I write separately to emphasize my agreement with Chief Justice Emeritus Saylor's dissent in Williams:

While not every intemperate remark will cross the line which separates zealous advocacy from contemptuous conduct, in my view the vulgar and insulting language at issue was appropriately punishable summarily as direct contempt. [Williams'] remarks were not only injudicious and disrespectful-the epithets directed at the Court were an affront to the authority and dignity of the tribunal and thus alone sufficient to constitute interference with the due and orderly administration of justice.

Like my esteemed former colleague, on a clean slate, I too would have found Williams' conduct punishable under Section 4132(3).

In fact, I find the use of the word "significant" throughout the majority in Williams, amongst other cases, when discussing disruptions that constitute "obstruction of the administration of justice" to be nebulous and subject to disparate interpretations. Merriam-Webster defines "significant" as, inter alia, "having meaning[,]" "large enough to be noticed or to have an effect[,]" and "having or likely to have influence or effect." Clearly, the trial court found the interruption caused by Outlaw's vulgar outburst to be "large enough to be noticed[.]"While I understand "that trial judges are supposed to be persons of fortitude who are able to thrive in a hardy environment," I find the act of calling a judge a "cocksucker" to be an "affront to the authority and dignity of the tribunal[,]"which was historically adequate to support a finding of contempt….

Keisha Nicole Hudson and Aaron Joshua Marcus (Defender Association of Philadelphia) represent Outlaw.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7880. Why Do Construction Barricades Come in Different Colors? The Colors Decoded

Red, yellow, and orange barricades don't always mean the same thing. Learn what common safety colors signal and when to stay clear.

Yellow caution tape is a pretty familiar sight, whether it’s blocking off a wet floor or keeping people out of a construction area. Orange barriers along the highway and red warning signs at job sites are just as common. But barricade colors aren’t random, and they don’t all mean the same thing.

In the U.S., OSHA has rules for certain workplace safety colors, while ANSI provides guidelines for signs and warning tape. Road construction follows a different set of standards. Depending on the location, the same color might serve a different purpose.

Learn what the most common barricade colors mean, where people are likely to see them, and what to watch out for.

There’s a reason red is a common choice for warning signs. OSHA uses it to identify danger, emergency stops, and fire protection equipment. At a construction site, a red “Danger” sign might warn of exposed electrical equipment or another hazard that could cause serious injury. OSHA’s general-industry rules also call for red warning lights at barricades and temporary obstructions.

Of all the safety colors, yellow might be the one people see most often. It shows up on caution tape, warning signs, and around areas where crews are working. OSHA uses yellow to warn of physical hazards, including falls and falling objects. A damaged walkway or an area undergoing maintenance might have yellow tape around it.

There’s no shortage of orange around construction sites. On workplace warning signs, the color often identifies hazards that could cause serious injury, particularly around machinery or equipment undergoing repairs. Orange also makes road construction easier to spot. Crews use orange barriers and signs to warn drivers about upcoming work, lane changes, or other temporary traffic conditions.

Instead of warning people away from something, it usually helps them find safety equipment. A green sign might point toward a first aid station, identify emergency equipment, or provide instructions for workers. It’s especially useful in workplaces where people need to find these resources quickly.

Blue signs typically provide information about workplace equipment or procedures that don’t directly involve a hazard. For example, a blue notice might explain that a machine is temporarily out of service. Unlike red or yellow warnings, blue notices generally provide information rather than warn of immediate danger.

Purple isn’t a color people encounter very often on construction barricades, but it does have a specific safety use. OSHA requires certain radiation warning signs to feature the familiar radiation symbol in purple or magenta against a yellow background. These signs warn people about radiation hazards, including areas where access may be restricted.

Those orange-and-white striped barricades lining roads and highways aren’t quite the same as the warning signs used inside workplaces. The Federal Highway Administration has separate rules for these barriers, which crews use to close lanes, block roads, and direct traffic around construction.

There’s also a purpose behind the diagonal stripes. When a barricade directs drivers around an obstruction, the stripes slope down toward the side where traffic should pass.

OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.144, Safety Color Code for Marking Physical Hazards” OSHA, “29 CFR 1926.200, Accident Prevention Signs and Tags” ANSI, “Z535.1-2022: Standard for Safety Colors” ANSI, “Z535.5-2022: Safety Tags and Barricade Tapes” OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.1096, Ionizing Radiation” FHWA, “Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, 11th Edition with Revision 1”
