#7879. ISIS-Inspired Terrorist Sentenced for Attacking Guards While Serving Sentence for Separate NYC Terror Plot

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

#7877. Bonfire Season Is Here — Here Are the Dos and Don’ts for Staying Safe

How to not to expose yourself to toxic fumes, burn down the neighborhood and injure the kiddos, plus other tips for enjoying a stress-free bonfire.

Cool fall evenings naturally put our minds on the merits of bones-warming bonfires. And while many create cherished family memories and set the backdrop for festive community events, some end up in tragedy, with emergency room visits and property damage.

“Every season there are always the same preventable mistakes made that lead to injuries,” says attorney Kevin Henrichson. “Falling into the fire, using gasoline, adding fuel when you shouldn’t, failing to supervise children and consuming alcohol all raise the stakes of something bad happening.”

Ahead, experts walk through exactly what to do and not to do to stay safe while enjoying a bonfire.

Notify your local fire department of your plans and ask them for guidance concerning:

“One phone call to the fire marshal’s office takes two minutes,” says fire and home safety expert Eugene Klimaszewski. “Otherwise, the consequence of burning without a permit on a restricted day is a fine, and if it gets away from you, it’s your liability.”

Look for a flat, open spot away from fences, barns, houses, trees and ground vegetation. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) recommends keeping bonfires at least 25 feet from the house and other structures.

“That number isn’t arbitrary,” says Klimaszewski. “Radiant heat and drifting embers are what ignite a deck railing, a vinyl fence or the mulch bed against the house. Every ember that lands on a roof or in a gutter full of dry leaves is a coin flip. Most go out. The one that doesn’t becomes a structure fire.”

Build the fire downwind of your home and close all windows and doors on the fire side, to prevent smoke from getting in.

“Even a small amount of smoke reaching an indoor smoke detector is enough to set it off,” says Klimaszewski. If you have a monitoring system, that could trigger a call to the fire department. “At best that’s an embarrassing conversation with the engine company. In towns that charge for repeat false alarms, that’s a bill on top of the embarrassment,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you have an older home, which isn’t airtight, put your alarm system on test mode or notify your monitoring company about your bonfire plans.

Wind can carry embers up to a mile, which means a bonfire on a windy day can easily end with a wildfire or house fire. If your planned bonfire day turns out to be windy, reschedule it. And even if there isn’t a breeze, plan for one by clearing all debris from around the fire pit and building rocks or bricks up higher on the windy side, which protects the fire from the wind plus radiates heat toward you for extra warmth.

Kiln-dried wood is the best. Seasoned hardwoods like oak, cedar and hickory are particularly good because they burn cleaner, longer and hotter than soft woods like pine and aspen (though a little soft wood kindling makes starting a fire a lot easier).

Steer clear of gasoline or other accelerants, as they too often lead to burn injuries, out-of-control fires and noxious fumes. (One year, my neighbor used so much gasoline to start a bonfire that the resulting shock wave from the explosion knocked pictures off of people’s walls three blocks away).

“A lot of people think they can use gas or lighter fluid to get the fire started or revive it, but please never do that because the vapors can flash back and get everyone nearby,” says Henrichson. “Gasoline is particularly dangerous and should never be used to start or revive a fire.”

Pro-tip: If you struggling to start a fire, build up a good kindling base and use a campfire starter or small bit of tightly twisted newspaper. Ample kindling will help you get a hot coal-bed established, which will burn larger logs more effectively plus lessen smoke.

Avoid newspaper, cardboard and other paper products, which tend to break down into large flying embers. Also, never burn anything with adhesives, plastics and other chemicals. The health risks of this are obvious, but plastics and chemicals are hiding in many items you might not realize, including: dryer lint, food packaging with shiny ink, glossy magazines, pressed woods including butcher block, varnished furniture and clothing made with synthetic fibers.

Before lighting the fire, set up a water source in case embers become a problem. That will also make it easier to put it out completely when you’re done. NFPA actually requires a hose, bucket or extinguisher be on hand for all recreational fires, and for fires to be attended at all times.

“A fire that’s left alone for ten minutes while everyone goes inside for more drinks is the one that ends up on the local news,” says Klimaszewski. “And an unattended fire that spreads is the homeowner’s liability, full stop.”

Assign someone to supervise the flames at all times to prevent the fire from getting out of control, and to keep kids and pets from standing too close. Equip the supervisor with proper protective clothing, including a fire-resistant glove, long-handled poker tool, shovel, closed-toe shoes and eye protection.

“The most common injuries I’ve seen are from people falling into the fire, and young children are vulnerable to this because they may want to play in the area where everyone is hanging out by the fire,” says Henrichson. “There should be a no-enter zone that is explained to children every single time, and the person tending the fire should not have any alcohol.”

Watch for loose sleeves, blankets, boots and other combustibles that are too close to the fire. “Those fun marshmallow-roasting memories are great to make, but shaking a burning marshmallow can cause trouble, and if you use metal skewers, they can burn you too,” says Henrichson.

Also, know what to do beforehand if something ends up catching fire. “The old advice that we were told years ago is still true: stop, drop, and roll if your clothes catch fire,” says Henrichson. “Repeat this as necessary every time kids approach, because they don’t always know to stay back.”

Embers can easily reignite hours or even days later, so the best practice for putting out a bonfire is to drown it, stir the ashes, and then drown it again until everything is cold to the touch. Don’t cover embers with dirt, as that actually insulates them, leaving open the possibility for them to reignite if they’re uncovered by a stiff wind.

Pro-tip: Put ashes in a metal container with a lid, on a non-combustible surface, away from the house, garage and deck for several days before they go in the trash, says Klimaszewski. Never put them in a plastic bin or next to the house.

#7876. Quartz May Be On Its Way Out—and Here’s How Kitchen Designers Would Replace It

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:06 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Quartz countertops have long been a favorite choice of homeowners and interior designers alike due to their strength, nonporous nature, modern look, and uniformity. However, recent discoveries and legal challenges regarding the material’s potential health hazards to fabricators have caused quite a stir and are now reshaping the industry.

The main issue is with crystalline silica that’s a natural mineral found in quartz. When particles are inhaled, they can penetrate deep into a person’s lungs, causing damage that can lead to serious respiratory diseases like silicosis, lung cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). And many workers have become ill from breathing in dust containing crystalline silica while fabricating quartz countertops. Australia has already banned many engineered-stone products, while California is pursuing policy rules that would prohibit fabricating engineered stone containing more than 1 percent crystalline silica.

As a result, more and more people are looking for safer countertop options to use in place of quartz. “We have found some homeowners shying away from quartz surfaces,” says Kaycee Conallen, owner of Kaycee Conallen Design Studio in Swarthmore, Pennsylvania. There are many alternatives to quartz countertops, and designers have helped us identify three top options for your new home or next remodel.

Note: There is no evidence indicating a health concern with already installed quartz countertops, so if you already have one, you don’t need to rip it out.

One alternative to quartz countertops is eco-friendly, silica-free alternatives like recycled glass and paper composites. Both eliminate silica risks while providing unique designs ranging from bold, contemporary glass patterns to sleek, solid-color paper finishes.

Recycled glass countertops incorporate post-consumer or post-industrial glass fragments bound in cement or resin, offering distinct visual textures from fine-ground particles to large, jewel-like shards. Notable glass brands include IceStone, Vetrazzo, Curava, GEOS, and Compac Obsidiana Zero. Glass surfaces are effective at resisting cuts, scratches, and heat, though stain-resistance and maintenance depend on whether a resin or cement binder is used.

Paper-based composites work well for those gravitating towards a solid color and solid surface materials, such as PaperStone, Richlite, and Fenix brands. Surprisingly durable, these heavy-duty panels are made from layers of post-consumer recycled paper or paper from FSC-certified forests, which are compressed under heat and pressure with a silica-free and petroleum-free phenolic resin.

While heat resistant to about 350 degrees Fahrenheit, minor scratches and stains may appear, but can be sanded out. “Fenix is a man-made resin and paper combination originally developed in Italy, and we love that it has a beautiful matte finish, feels soft to the touch, and is very durable,” explains Conallen.

“Sintered stone is another strong option for its resistance to heat, scratches, and stains,” notes Blima Ehrentreu, founder and CEO of The Designers Group (TDG) in New York City and other locations. Using a high-tech process, natural minerals like porcelain and glass are combined under immense heat and pressure to replicate metamorphic rock with minimal to zero crystalline silica.

The non-porous nature of sintered stone makes it resistant to staining, scratches, intense heat, and color-fading from UV exposure. Brands that make this type of surface include Lapitec, Dekton, Neolith, Florim, Sapienstone, and Caesarstone, which are actively eliminating or reducing silica content. In addition, many of these surfaces contain recycled content.

Conallen also loves the look of authentic materials like soapstone. “Each slab of stone carries unique characteristics, personality, and porosity,” she explains. Composed mostly of talc, this metamorphic rock is free of crystalline silica and has a distinctive, velvety feel. Soapstone offers design versatility, as it ranges in color from subtle grays and muted greens to charcoal or deep black, sometimes accented by marble-like veining. Not only does it offer a classic, understated elegance to modern spaces, but it is also a sustainable option given its low-energy extraction process, nontoxic nature, and recyclability.

From a functional standpoint, soapstone is very durable. It withstands heat, so you can set hot cookware directly onto the surface without trivets. It’s also nonporous so it doesn’t get damaged by acidic etching, spills, or bacterial growth. The only drawback is that it’s a softer material than most of the other options mentioned, so it can show minor scratches.

#7875. Firing for "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" Post Upheld

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

In Johnston v. County of Gila (D. Ariz.), Judge Dominic Lanza rejected, on procedural grounds, plaintiff's challenge to a Gila County Personnel Commission decision upholding his firing from his job as "a legal secretary with the Gila County Attorney's Office"; here's the factual and legal analysis from the Commission decision (see exhibit 10):

On September 10, 2025, at around 2:00 p.m. Arizona Time Appellant posted "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" on/via his Facebook account.

Multiple GCAO employees, including some who are not Appellant's Facebook friends and/or who do not personally use Facebook, saw and otherwise learned of Appellant's post on September 10 and in the days that followed. Multiple GCAO employees discussed the post with each other and complained about the post to GCAO's Chief Deputy Joseph Collins as well as to Gila County Attorney Bradley Beauchamp.

Beauchamp believed that the post appeared to condone murder based on the victim's political viewpoints and statements and became concerned that this post and perception would reflect on GCAO in the public's eyes and thereby undermine the public's trust in GCAO's official duty to prosecute homicides without bias and without regard to a victim's views, statements, or affiliations. Several other GCAO employees shared the perception that Appellant's post appeared to condone the murder of someone based on their statements and views and shared the concern that this would reflect poorly on GCAO and undermine public trust.

Multiple GCAO employees reported being offended or otherwise bothered by the post. Appellant's post resulted in immediate meetings and changes to office practices due to concerns of disharmony within the office and the effects it would have on GCAO operations.

Appellant's Facebook account was reportedly set to 'private' which Appellant believed would limit his post to only being seen by his existing Facebook friends and that all his friends had to do if they were upset by his post was 'unfollow' him. Notwithstanding Appellant's Facebook account setting and his belief as to the setting's effect on post-exposures, his post apparently reached multiple witnesses within a short timeframe, including some who either were no t his Facebook friends or did not use Facebook at all….

The evidence introduced in this matter demonstrated that Respondent's decision to dismiss Appellant for Appellant's social media post "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" was based on the following:

Accordingly, Respondent's reason for dismissing Appellant did not appear to have been decided at random or on a whim, to be founded in prejudice, or to lack a reasonable basis.

With regard to Appellant's assertions that his dismissal violated his rights under the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution, the evidence presented in this hearing did not support Appellant's claim, particularly in light of the close direct nexus between the central mission of Respondent's office—the fair and impartial prosecution of all criminal matters without regard to a crime victim's personal views, opinions, or affiliations and Appellant's post about a public homicide victim, Appellant's role in the office and exposure to members of the public, Respondent's concerns regarding inferences the public would make based on Appellant's post, the fact that almost immediately multiple parties complained regarding Appellant's post and their perception that it condoned murder and reflected poorly on the office, the immediate disruption it caused in Appellant's office, and the immediate and widespread knowledge of Appellant's post.

Here's a slightly adapted version of my analysis of the general First Amendment issue that I posted right after the Kirk shooting:

In such cases the government is acting as employer, and in that capacity it has more latitude to discipline and fire employees than it does to imprison or fine them. Generally speaking, the government may discipline an employee based on the employee's speech if

There is no categorical exception even as to government employment for speech that praises violence; indeed, Rankin v. McPherson (1987) (which Johnston cited in his arguments to the Commission) held that the First Amendment was violated by the firing of a law enforcement clerical employee for saying, after President Reagan was wounded, "if they go for him again, I hope they get him":

[The statement] plainly dealt with a matter of public concern. The statement was made in the course of a conversation addressing the policies of the President's administration. It came on the heels of a news bulletin regarding what is certainly a matter of heightened public attention: an attempt on the life of the President. While a statement that amounted to a threat to kill the President would not be protected by the First Amendment, the District Court concluded, and we agree, that McPherson's statement did not amount to a [punishable] threat … or, indeed, that could properly be criminalized at all.

The inappropriate or controversial character of a statement is irrelevant to the question whether it deals with a matter of public concern. "[D]ebate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open, and … may well include vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks on government and public officials." "Just as erroneous statements must be protected to give freedom of expression the breathing space it needs to survive, so statements criticizing public policy and the implementation of it must be similarly protected."

But Rankin stressed that the speech actually didn't create much upset or disruption for the office, whether because of an internal reaction or an external one. To quote the concurrence by Justice Powell,

There is no dispute that McPherson's comment was made during a private conversation with a co-worker who happened also to be her boyfriend. She had no intention or expectation that it would be overheard or acted on by others…. The risk that a single, offhand comment directed to only one other worker will lower morale, disrupt the work force, or otherwise undermine the mission of the office borders on the fanciful.

Interference with work, personnel relationships, or the speaker's job performance can detract from the public employer's function; avoiding such interference can be a strong state interest…. [But w]hile McPherson's statement was made at the workplace, there is no evidence that it interfered with the efficient functioning of the office…. Constable Rankin testified that the possibility of interference with the functions of the Constable's office had not been a consideration in his discharge of respondent and that he did not even inquire whether the remark had disrupted the work of the office.

Nor was there any danger that McPherson had discredited the office by making her statement in public. McPherson's speech took place in an area to which there was ordinarily no public access; her remark was evidently made in a private conversation with another employee. There is no suggestion that any member of the general public was present or heard McPherson's statement.

Nor is there any evidence that employees other than [her boyfriend] who worked in the room even heard the remark. Not only was McPherson's discharge unrelated to the functioning of the office, it was not based on any assessment by the Constable that the remark demonstrated a character trait that made respondent unfit to perform her work.

Here, the Personnel Commission found that there had been disruption, based on "Testimony from multiple witnesses attesting to staff disharmony and disruptions occurring almost immediately after, and in the days following, Appellant's post—including staff complaints, colleagues being bothered and offended by Appellant's post, an office meeting, and an immediate change to office standards regarding political debate to avoid further disharmony and staff complaints." And the post, unlike McPherson's statement, was made to a considerable number of people; even if it was a Facebook page set to private, a lot more people were aware of it.

If one looks at later lower court cases, they have routinely turned on whether the speech created enough controversy, with the public or with coworkers. When the government is administering the criminal law or civil liability, such a "heckler's veto" is generally not allowed: The government generally can't shut down a speaker, for instance, because his listeners are getting offended or even threatening violence because they're offended. But in the employment context, the Pickering balance often allows government to fire employees because their speech sufficiently offends coworkers or members of the public. (The analysis may differ for public university professors, though it's not clear how much; see this post for more.)

This conclusion by lower courts applying Pickering might, I think, stem from the judgment that employees are hired to do a particular job cost-effectively for the government: If their speech so offends others (especially clients or coworkers) that keeping the employees on means more cost for the government than benefit, the government needn't continue to pay them for what has proved to be a bad bargain. Maybe that's mistaken. Maybe it's so important to protect public debate, including on highly controversial matters, that public employers should have to keep on even the most controversial employees (see this article by Prof. Randy Kozel, which so suggests in part). But that appears to be the rule.

We see this, for instance, with statements that are allegedly racist, sexist, antigay, antitrans, etc.: If they cause enough public hostility, or seem highly likely to do so, then courts will often allow employees to be fired based on them. But if they largely pass unnoticed except by management and perhaps just a few people who file complaints, then courts are much more likely to hold that the firings may violate the First Amendment (see, e.g., this post and this post, though there are many other such examples).

There are other factors that courts consider, to be sure: For instance, if the employer can show that a person's speech shows they are unsuited to the job, that makes it easier for the employer to prevail. (That seems to be part of the county attorney's justification here.) But even there the magnitude of public reaction is relevant, because one common argument is that one trait required for certain employees is the ability and willingness to instill confidence and respect in coworkers and clients, rather than to produce outrage and hostility.

And while some have tried to distinguish, say, racist speech from other speech on the grounds that it shows the speaker is likely to unfairly treat clients or coworkers who belong the groups he condemns, one can say that about many kinds of speech: Speech praising the killing of people who publicly advocate for certain views may be said to show the speaker is likely to unfairly treat members of the groups. (Such unfair treatment may often be illegal, especially by public employees, but in any event will often be unethical and contrary to the employer's mission.) As a result, the magnitude of the public reaction, which is often measurable rather than speculative, ends up playing a major role.

This creates an unfortunate incentive: Like any heckler's-veto-like rule, it rewards would-be cancellers, whether among the public or just among coworkers, if they only speak out often enough and with enough outrage. But rightly or wrongly, that is how these cases generally shape up.

Ashley E. Caballero-Daltrey, Derek Ryan Graffious, and Michele Molinario (Jones Skelton & Hochuli PLC) represent the County.

Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7873. I Thought I Wanted a Single-Family Home. Turns Out, I Missed the Rental Income

We thought we wanted a single-family home, but adding an ADU made it the perfect place for us.

I’ve always had benchmarks for knowing when I’ve “made it” in life: a car with power windows and locks, a refrigerator with a water dispenser and owning a single-family home. The last one stems from the fact that my wife and I always owned two-family homes. We lived in one unit and rented out the other for over a decade before we finally had the means to move into a single-family home.

But the funny thing was, when we finally got there, something was missing. Our single-family home didn’t feel as rewarding as I thought it would. Ahead, I share why this long-sought-after dream house didn’t quite feel like one and how a new Massachusetts law allowed us to add the missing piece to our family’s forever home.

After 10 years of renting, my wife and I wanted to buy a home. We decided on a two-family property because we were nervous about taking on too much financially. A single-family home seemed like a luxury that was out of reach, but the rental income from a two-family home made homeownership seem feasible and financially safe. Collecting that first rent check was an amazing feeling, and it cut our mortgage payment in half. We were hooked. Being landlords wasn’t always stress-free, but regular rental income gave us so much financial freedom.

Seven years later, we moved into another two-family home that better suited our growing family and kept the first one, too. We continued to work and save for another five years. As we approached 40, buying a single-family home felt like the next logical step. It was the ultimate end goal, right? So we bought a single-family fixer-upper in a nice neighborhood and started making repairs. Our kids settled into a new school district, and we made friends with the neighbors.

At first, it all felt great, but living in a single-family home wasn’t everything we’d hoped it would be. Mostly, we found we really missed the rental income we were used to in our two-family homes. It felt foolish to have a house that only took money out of our bank account without putting any back in. We didn’t want to move, and soaring home prices made buying another property out of the question. To find ways to generate income from our property, I tried renting out our in-ground pool, second garage, and backyard to dog owners. None of those ideas panned out, leaving us without a way to recreate the two-family experience we missed.

Then, in August 2024, Massachusetts enacted a new law to encourage homeowners to build accessory dwelling units (ADUs), or in-law apartments, to ease the state’s housing shortage. These secondary, self-contained living spaces, complete with kitchens and bathrooms, can house extended family members or paying tenants.

My wife and I immediately knew this could be the solution we’d been looking for. Instead of moving to a two-family home, we could add a small apartment to our existing home. We considered our options and decided that converting a portion of our house into a one-bedroom apartment was the most cost-effective.

We researched town and state ordinances and building codes, then applied for a building permit and submitted plans for the proposed project. Because we weren’t changing the footprint of our home, the process went very smoothly. We started the work in August and had everything completed and inspected by December 2024. We received a certificate of occupancy from the town, and our first tenant moved in on January 1, 2025.

Nearly two years later, we have absolutely no regrets about our ADU conversion project. The rental income has been a fantastic addition to our monthly budget, and we’ve had amazing tenants from the start. It has been the missing piece of our dream home and is making a more secure financial future possible for our family.

If you’re considering adding an ADU to your home or property, here are a few things to keep in mind:

While we had been happy in a two-family home, we mistakenly thought we could do better. But after moving into what was supposed to be our perfect, single-family home, we realized we had made a mistake. Our “dream” house began to feel like a financial burden that only sucked up money and never gave anything back. Staying put and adding a small apartment has given us so much more breathing room and transformed our forever home from a burden into a boon.

#7871. We Tested Ryobi’s $129 Pressure Washer — Here’s What It Can (and Can’t) Do

Can this portable power washer possibly compare to the real thing? We put it to the test.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Nothing sets you up for a better spring than taking some time for some seasonal cleaning in the fall, and one of the best tools for autumn home cleanup is a classic pressure washer. If you’ve got a surface or a screen you need sprayed, a pressure washer can deliver enough pressure for all kinds of scrubbing.

But even the most avid pressure washer advocates would tell you they’re also pretty cumbersome tools that require a lot of setup and garage storage space. That’s exactly why I wanted to try out this portable pressurized washer from Ryobi. The concept is intriguing, promising users a fraction of the size, cost and power of a standard pressure washer. I was very curious whether this tool would actually provide more cleaning power than a standard garden hose nozzle.

The first thing I noticed when unboxing the Ryobi One Plus Electric Power Cleaner was how substantial the tool felt. I was expecting it to feel a little flimsy, but the tool felt well-built in my hands. It all assembled easily in just a few clicks, taking only a small fraction of the time it would’ve taken to set up a full-size pressure washer. And if you’re worried about water ruining your battery, don’t be. The entire battery chamber is enclosed by a tightly sealed plastic housing.

For this test, I decided to replicate a classic fall cleanup task: hosing down screens. I wanted a big surface to clean, so I pulled the screen door off the back door and set it up in the backyard. Then, I applied a light coating of flour to the middle of the screen and a light mist of water to lock the flour in place.

From there, I just had to finish setting up the Ryobi pressure washer. It comes with three different nozzles: two flat angled nozzles and one “turbo nozzle” that sprays the water in a speedy spiral. All I had to do was attach the pressure washer to a garden hose, and the tool was ready to go. Then I just set myself up in front of the screen with the pressure washer the recommended distance (1-2 feet) from the screen. ‘

All that was left to do was let it rip. The first thing that stands out when you use this portable pressure washer is that it feels a little underwhelming when you pull the trigger- especially if you’ve ever used a full-sized pressure washer. There’s not much kick, and the water leaves the nozzle at a steady but uninspiring speed. For a few seconds, I was worried the 700psi of pressure wouldn’t be enough to clean up the floury mess I’d created.

But my worries lessened the longer I used the tool. It was gentler than the pressure washers I’d used before, but it provided a consistent stream that quickly started knocking the flour loose from the screen. Things started going even better once I switched to the turbo nozzle. The spin action really helped compensate for the lack of PSI pressure. Within another minute, I had knocked off a ton of the sticky flour from the screen.

A post shared by Family Handyman (@familyhandyman)

So enough waffling… what’s the verdict? It’s pretty clear, as soon as you start using this tool, that the Ryobi tool isn’t going to fully replace a full-sized pressure washer… especially if you need to really blast something. But there are many use cases for a pressure washer where consistency is more important than power. And if you’ve ever accidentally damaged something with a pressure washer, the reduced power of this tool might even be something you consider a pro.

It took a while, but eventually the screen was sparkling clean- so clean, in fact, it was nearly invisible in the doorway. I should also point out that real-world conditions are rarely as messy as the sticky flour mess I created. If you just need to get dust off a screen or mud off a sidewalk, this tool is a significant upgrade over a simple stream from a garden hose. Ultimately, you’re trading power for portability, and whether that works for you will depend on the job you have to tackle. If it’s only needed for routine seasonal cleaning, this pressure washer could be perfect for you.

Just don’t expect it to peel paint off a pole.

#7869. Firing of R.I. Governor's Staffer for Pro-Gaza-Ceasefire/"End to the Occupation" Post Violated First Amendment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Sanchez v. Almond, decided Wednesday by Judge John McConnell (D.R.I.):

Mr. Sanchez began working at the office of Rhode Island Governor Daniel J. McKee in May 2021 as a "constituent services" staffer. The office is "the first point of contact with the public for the Governor's office" where employees handled calls, emails, letters, walk-ins, constituent problems, requests, and questions about the Governor's positions.

Mr. Sanchez was not a member of senior staff, and did not formulate policy, or policy developments. While the scope of his employment is shaded differently by the parties, they all agree that his duties involved, among other things, helping Rhode Islanders access public benefits and triaging their concerns by referring them to the appropriate departments. The office received roughly 500 calls and 400 emails per month.

Mr. Sanchez's direct supervisor was David Barricelli, who reported to Joseph Almond, Senior Deputy Chief of Staff, who in turn reported to Antonio Afonso, the Chief of Staff in charge of hiring and firing in the Governor's office, including Mr. Sanchez. Mr. Sanchez's performance was never called into question, and he was never disciplined before his termination….

Sanchez was also a Providence City Council member (and his superiors had not objected to his running for local office).

On October 7, 2023, Hamas attacked Israel killing roughly 1,200 people and Israel responded with fierce military actions in Gaza, whose population is overwhelmingly Palestinian. That day, the Governor's office issued a statement condemning "the abhorrent acts of terrorism by Hamas against innocent civilians in Israel" and expressed solidarity with Israel.

The same day, Mr. Sanchez posted on his personal social media a call for "respect of all human rights, especially the Palestinian people who faced atrocities for decades[,] and at the same time condemn all attacks on civilians." Ten days later, Mr. Sanchez posted that the United States was "actively aiding in a genocide" and called for "immediate deescalation and cease-fire."

On October 22, 2023, while off duty, he posted on the platform "X" (formerly known as "Twitter"):

"prov did not disappoint … yesterday, I marched with thousands of people calling for an immediate ceasefire and a [sic] end to the occupation"

The video attached depicted scores of people marching in Providence, Rhode Island. Some members of the Governor's staff thought that rally participants had chanted "from the river to the sea." That said, nothing suggests that Mr. Sanchez adopted or repeated that phrase nor is there evidence to suggest he endorsed that chant, or is in favor of violence. {No one disputes Mr. Sanchez's account "@MSanchezPVD" represents his employment as a City Councilman not his employment at the Governor's office suggesting that he was acting outside his capacity in the Governor's office.}

The post led to concern at the Governor's office, and to media questions:

On October 23rd, the Governor's Director of Legislative and Intergovernmental Affairs, Rico Vota, counseled Mr. Sanchez not to make new posts reflecting his opinion, to keep a low profile, to speak to Mr. Afonso, and to tell the communications team about any media inquiries. He did not, however, ask him to remove the posts. Mr. Vota notified Matthew Sheaff, the Governor's Senior Advisor for Communication, who likewise recommended that Mr. Sanchez keep a low profile, which Mr. Sanchez did.

That same day, two media outlets, NBC 10 WJAR and The Providence Journal's Katherine Gregg, asked the Governor's office about the rally but did not mention Mr. Sanchez or his posts. In response, the Governor issued a statement that he "unequivocally condemn[ed] the despicable acts of war and terror perpetrated by Hamas against the people of Israel."

The next day Ms. Gregg asked the Governor's communications team to confirm that Mr. Sanchez worked for the Governor and Mr. Sheaff replied that "… [a] member of our senior staff has spoken with the individual, and the situation is under review." Ms. Gregg also contacted Mr. Sanchez, but he did not respond to her and instead told Mr. Sheaff about her inquiry, apologizing for "dragging you guys into this."

On October 25th, Ms. Gregg published an article identifying Mr. Sanchez as a Constituent Services associate; NBC 10 WJAR and a WPRO radio host then asked the office about him, and NBC 10 reported on the post. A state legislator asked Mr. Vota whether the employee in the article "worked downstairs."

On October 26th, Mr. Barricelli reported to Mr. Almond that Constituent Services had received three emails and two phone messages about Mr. Sanchez's post, all after Ms. Gregg's article. Mr. Almond did not consider these "to be a lot," and they did not interfere with the office's operations. Mr. Almond testified that addressing such matters was within his own regular duties, and Mr. Barricelli testified that fielding such comments is the associates' job.

Afonso and Almond demanded that Sanchez take the post down, but he refused; he was then fired. Sanchez sued, and the court held that Sanchez's First Amendments rights were violated (and so clearly that the defendants weren't entitled to qualified immunity):

The First Amendment protects the right of a public employee to speak on matters of public concern, and that right "is not lost when an individual chooses to work for the government." Public employees' speech on matters of public concern, on their own time, is speech long understood to "occup[y] the highest rung of the hierarchy of First Amendment values." Nonpolitical public employees do not "surrender" their First Amendment rights by accepting government employment. …

The Court "must balance the interests of the employee, as a citizen, in commenting upon matters of concern and the interest of the State, as an employer, in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees." "This balancing act is commonly referred to as the Pickering balancing" after the Supreme Court's decision in Pickering v. Board of Ed. (1968)….

On Mr. Sanchez's side, speech on public issues occupies the greatest of First Amendment protection, and the stronger the speech interest, the stronger the justification the employer must offer. {The interest by the employee and the public is heightened when the employee is also an elected official, as was Mr. Sanchez.} …

On Defendants' side, legitimate interests include avoiding unnecessary disruption and inefficiency, maintaining discipline and harmony in the workplace, and protecting close working relationships that depend on loyalty and confidence. A reasonable prediction of disruption receives significant weight, and an employer need not wait until disruption becomes manifest before acting. Courts are more willing to credit such a prediction where some disruption has occurred….

Defendants contend that the post sent "a mixed message on the Governor's public stance." Mr. Afonso testified that some constituents conflated Mr. Sanchez's view with the Governor's. Even so, there was little room for genuine confusion. Mr. Sanchez's account identified him as a city councilor and never mentioned the Governor. The press, not the post, connected him to the Governor's office.

Crediting Mr. Afonso's testimony, nothing in the record shows that constituents conflated Mr. Sanchez's position with the Governor's that was traceable to the post itself. Mr. Sanchez's account cannot be reasonably understood as speaking on behalf of the Governor such that it would cause confusion in either the Governor's office or the public's perception….

[As to actual disruption, c]rediting Defendants' version of the record, in the five days between the post and the termination, the Governor's office received: one Providence Journal inquiry following up on the social media posts; three emails and two telephone messages from the public; a question posed by a state legislator in the elevator to Mr. Vota; and a few other questions from NBC 10 and a WPRO radio host. The Court also credits Ms. Darocha's recollection that the Governor was asked about Mr. Sanchez at press gaggles that week; Mr. Sheaff's testimony that the matter "encompassed [his] day"; testimony that time spent on the matter was time not spent elsewhere; and the decision not to put an optional event on the Governor's calendar.

Mr. Almond testified the inquiries were not "a lot" and "did not interfere with the operation of the office" and Mr. Barricelli testified that handling such communications was essentially his associates' job. By its own account, that office spends roughly "85 percent" of its time responding to current events and media inquiries. Better said by Mr. Sheaff, "[i]t's very common that the Governor gives a statement or his thoughts on news of the day …[;] [i]t's just part of the job of being a governor." This is the ordinary business of a governor's office and nothing in the record suggests that the post affected the Governor's own work, his relationship with his staff, or the office's ability to serve constituents in an unusual way. Balancing these facts, and considering the Defendants' burden on this issue, the Court settles this score firmly against Defendants.

{Defendants also point to Mr. Sanchez's later acknowledgment that he had "put[ ] the [G]overnor in a tough situation" and that, "given my day job, these kinds of things can get messy quickly." Though affecting the Court's calculus, an employee's recognition that his speech is affecting his employer does not supply Defendants with the artillery they think it does.} …

Brian W. Haynes (Casner & Edwards, LLP) and Edward H. Trent, Gene C. Schaerr, and Miranda Cherkas Sherrill (Schaerr Jaffe LLP), and James A. Ruggieri (Higgins Cavanagh & Cooney, LLP) represent plaintiff. Note that I'm a part-part-part-time academic affiliated with Schaerr Jaffe LLP, but I didn't work on the case, and was indeed unaware of it until it came up in a Westlaw query of mine; no-one asked me to blog about it.

NEXT: Firing for "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" Post Upheld

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7868. How Old Is Too Old To Use a Chainsaw?

Understand the risks associated with operating a chainsaw as you age with expert-backed advice and safety tips.

While you may take great pride in your ability to take care of things around the house, be careful when it comes to using a chainsaw as you age. Unlike other powered lawn equipment, chainsaws carry a significant risk of personal injury— and can be deadly in the wrong hands.

Ahead, learn how to evaluate when you may be too old to operate a chainsaw and should call in a pro instead, with help from physical therapist Dr. Ron Miller and manual therapist Doug Bertram.

Chainsaw injuries can happen in a fraction of a second and are often due to losing control of the saw during operation. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports roughly 36,000 chainsaw injuries each year, resulting in serious lacerations, traumatic brain injuries, limb loss or death.

While chainsaws are dangerous to operate at any age, the risks are even higher for older adults. “As we grow older, our ability to control our balance, grip strength, reflex times, eyesight and physical stamina dramatically decreases,” Miller says. “This makes it difficult to operate chainsaws.” It’s crucial that you have the strength and stamina to handle a chainsaw in all conditions to avoid injury.

If you’re not ready to put down the saw yet, consider these tips to do it safely.

Cut smaller logs and branches that are safely on the ground and avoid cutting while on a ladder or felling trees. Hire larger jobs out rather than tackling them yourself.

Consider using a lightweight, electric saw that is easier to control. Regardless of the saw, always make sure the chain is sharp and properly tightened before use.

Wear protective gear: Wearing eye and hearing protection, gloves and sturdy footwear is always sound advice, but don’t overlook chaps too, Miller says. Worn over pants and designed to stop a chainsaw chain, chaps can be the difference between a fatal injury and a superficial wound.

Never cut alone: Always have a cutting partner who remains nearby to help identify dangerous situations and call for help in the event of an accident.

Avoid working to fatigue: “Take breaks to stay awake and alert while operating a chainsaw,” Miller says. Stay well hydrated and fueled to keep your mind sharp during operation and stop when you start to feel tired.

“There’s no age that makes you too old to use a chainsaw,” Bertram says. “[But] you need adequate grip strength, adequate balance and good mental acuity.” It’s less about a specific number and more about your general health and ability. Conduct these physical fitness tests at home to gauge your grip strength, balance, leg and back strength, coordination and endurance. How you perform on these tests will give you a good idea of your functional fitness levels and whether handling a chainsaw is a good idea or not.  When in doubt, hire a pro.

For smaller limbs and logs up to 12-in. in diameter, a bow saw or reciprocating saw with a pruning blade are lower risk options.

Federal law prohibits anyone under the age of 18 from operating a chainsaw in a work setting, but there are no age limits for private chainsaw use on a residential property.

Though some may prefer ice melt that comes in a bucket or ice melt shaker, we found the durable bag-style packaging of this Snow Joe eco-friendly ice melt easy to reach into and move around. Be aware, however, that if the open bag gets wet, the contents will bind together and consolidate into a giant rock. We kept ours in the garage, and it was fine.

Get the Snow Joe Enviro Blend ice melt (various sizes) at Amazon, The Home Depot, Walmart, Best Buy, or Snow Joe.

Since almost all ice melt formulations contain salt or chlorides, this salt-free option from Safe Paw is quite unique. It’s a great choice if your household is sensitive to salts or if using anything corrosive is not viable (such as around a classic car, near expensive equipment, or on a newly paved surface). It’s also nonconductive, making it safe around electrical components.

This product comes in a granular form and doesn’t have sharp edges like rock salt. Thanks to its nonabrasive texture, our dogs had zero issues walking through it. They even played right where we tested this product and showed no adverse effects. That’s also likely partly due to the blend’s chemical composition, which isn’t as aggressive as other formulas. While that means it doesn’t melt ice as quickly as some of the heavier hitters we tested, it’s still effective.

In addition to melting a bit more slowly, it also doesn’t work at quite as low temperatures. In our tests, it melted ice in as low as 15 degrees Fahrenheit but struggled if it was colder. Though the label claims it works at -2 degrees Fahrenheit, the manufacturer only guarantees it down to 10 degrees Fahrenheit. We think 10 degrees is accurate—any lower than that, and we’d say all bets are off. So long as you know when and where to use it, you can rely on this salt-free formula around your sensitive family members and in spaces where you want to ensure the integrity of your equipment and surfaces.

What our tester says: “We really liked testing this product because it spread quite easily. We used an old cup to scoop and spread it without worrying about getting it on our skin. In fact, it spread nicely and didn’t cause a reaction even when we used our hands instead of the cup.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Safe Paw ice melt (various sizes) at Petco.

Don’t let this ice melt’s small bag fool you: This Redmond’s Nature’s Blend is packed with concentrated dye-free, urea-free, and polymer-free nontoxic ice melt chemicals that effectively bust ice and slush over an up to 400-square-foot area. The all-natural blend is certified by the Organic Materials Review Institute (OMRI), making it one of the best snow melts for use around children, pets, vegetation, and waterways. It’s safe and easy to apply via hand, shovel, or cup.

This pick’s unique formulation can melt snow quickly in temperatures approaching 0 degrees Fahrenheit. It works a bit more slowly at more extreme temperatures, but we were impressed by its overall melting capabilities in our tests. The fact that the mild formula is also easy to handle and safe around snow blowers, vehicles, and other sensitive items makes it ideal for residential use.

The Redmond Ice Slicer works well in climates with occasional storms and freezes. If you need something for a more extreme environment, you’re better off choosing another product, as overapplication of this melter can lead to red spots and smears on driveways and walkways. While we didn’t notice any spotting or staining during testing, Redmond’s more aggressive commercial- and industrial-grade ice melts might be better in colder and snowier climates.

Get the Redmond ice melt at Amazon or Ice Slicer.

When people think about removing snow from roofs, they often imagine doing so manually. That’s because few ice melt products are made to address ice buildup on roofs—which is what makes this ice melt such a unique product. The tablets are composed of calcium chloride and designed to be thrown onto roofs to prevent snow and ice buildup from wreaking havoc on gutters and adding weight to vulnerable areas. For those living in areas with heavy snowfall where ice dams often form, they are a worthy investment.

During testing, we aimed for problem spots and tossed the tablets up. While snow began to slough off the roof relatively quickly, we struggled to verify the exact rate at which the tablets melted the ice since we couldn’t see it happening from the ground. Still, for their intended purpose, they worked well.

The Roof Melt tablets aren’t granular or spreadable, so they aren’t compatible with larger surface areas like driveways. You could probably use them on the ground where drainage is constricted and problematic, but other options will be more economical for that purpose. If you deal with dangerous ice dams on your roof, however, these tablets are worth having around to quickly and easily resolve the issue.

The best way to determine how effectively various ice melts perform is to fully test each product. As residents of Montana, we began our testing in the aftermath of a winter snowstorm that turned bitter cold. We applied the products to gravel, pavement, and grass in temperatures as low as -6 degrees Fahrenheit.

As the snow went through several melt/freeze cycles over the coming days, it formed icy spots under our rooflines and in several low spots. We tested the ice melts in freezing temperatures on water drips and overnight freezes that created walking hazards each morning. We analyzed how long it took to apply each product, how quickly they melted ice and snow, their degree of pet friendliness when used around our dogs, and a number of other hands-on factors. Lastly, we compared pricing, packaging, and ease of application.

Ice melt products are designed for use either before or after snow or ice has fallen. Their application prevents ice from forming or melts it into a slush that’s easier to clear with a standard snow shovel. Each type of ice melt will perform differently depending on its form and chemical composition. Other variables, such as temperature, ground type, melting time, and environmental impact are essential to consider before purchasing an ice melt product.

Ice melt is available in solid and liquid formulations, each with pros and cons. Solid ice melt typically comes in pellets and granules. It works well for many applications and is typically the go-to solution for road crews dealing with icy and snowy weather. Pellets and granules are generally less expensive and easier to store than liquid formulas, and they add a “crunchy” texture on surfaces that adds grip for walking and driving. Their main downsides are that they scatter more easily across icy surfaces, making them harder to apply with precision, and that they tend to be slower acting and more likely to clump together, which sometimes makes them less effective.

Liquid ice melt is a wise choice for lower-temperature situations and times when faster results are necessary. That said, some products must be applied before ice forms rather than after. When applied, liquid is less likely to scatter, staying in place for longer-lasting results. Liquid de-icers, which tend to cost more, can be more challenging to transport and store because of their weight. Plus, if heavy rain ensues, the product can get washed away.

Self-heating ice melt, which comes in pellet and granular form, generates its own heat when in contact with ice and snow—a process known as an exothermic reaction. Unlike other products that must absorb moisture to create a brine to melt the ice, self-heating ice melt can get right to work.

Ice melts work by absorbing the moisture on the top of the ice, creating what’s called brine, and working its way down to break the bond between the ice and the surface. This creates cracks and flakes that are safer to walk on and easier to remove. All of these products have a temperature limit. If temperatures plummet beyond a product’s ice melting point, the chemicals will no longer be effective. Here’s what to expect from the various ice melt types available:

Many of the chemicals in ice melts can potentially damage surfaces, so it’s important to consider where the product will be used. The most common areas—driveways, sidewalks, decks, and porches—can be composed of different materials, such as concrete, asphalt, wood, and metal. Packaging and product descriptions of the best ice melts will reveal what materials they can be used on safely, so be sure to read this information prior to purchase. It would be unwise to apply a product that could corrode concrete, rust metal, or damage wood on those surfaces around the home.

The quest for comfort and convenience in frigid weather has led to the invention of such products as heated jackets, heated gloves, and electric snow shovels. Similarly, certain ice melts have been developed to work in colder climates. Some products won’t work in temperatures lower than 20 degrees Fahrenheit. This is acceptable if the temperature in an area seldom gets that low, but these products won’t get the job done if you live in a colder spot. For locations where temperatures can reach less than 20 degrees Fahrenheit, you’ll want to purchase a product specifically made for lower temperatures.

The time it takes a product to melt ice and snow depends on several factors. Liquid ice melters and self-heating ice melters act fairly quickly. Unlike solid melters that take time to absorb moisture and create the brine, liquid products are already a brine. Self-heating ice melters have a similar advantage: Instead of absorbing moisture, the pellets will heat up more quickly and melt the ice and snow faster than other ice melters. Regardless of which form you choose, there will still be some downtime while you wait for it to work, which you put to good use cleaning your windows with an ice scraper.

Longevity refers to an ice melt’s ability to keep working beyond the initial application period. A long-lasting ice melter is especially helpful when snowstorms or icy rain continue throughout the day. Although long-lasting ice melt tends to be more expensive, the cost can even out since smaller amounts of product tend to get the job done.

The chemicals in some ice melters can be hazardous to pets and plants. According to Alex Blutinger, Medical Director of Veterinary Emergency Group in Greenwich, Connecticut, “Melting ice can be very dangerous to animals, specifically because of the harsh ingredients in ice melt products. Ingestion of these chemicals can cause stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea. It may also irritate the paw pads and exposed areas of the limbs.” Dr. Blutinger says that, if you suspect your pet has been exposed to unsafe deicing chemicals, you should wipe your pet’s paws with a damp cloth or baby wipe to minimize ingestion through liking and reduce the risk of skin irritation. While using a pet-safe ice melt is smart, you can also reduce exposure using paw was or booties.

Certain elements in ice melters can also do environmental damage, such as killing wildlife that may ingest the pellets or aquatic life if the chemicals reach waterways. Many people are concerned about the impact of using large amounts of these products outdoors, so it’s important to read product information carefully to understand the dos and don’ts of using ice melt.

To ensure you get the best performance out of your purchase (or even a homemade ice melt), try the following de-icing tips and tricks.

If you’re not keen to try to melt ice without salt and want more information about ice melts, here are answers to some commonly asked questions.

Ice melters absorb moisture and create a brine that then melts snow and ice. This eventually breaks the bond between the ice and the surface, creating a slush.

Both. Applying ice melt before and after it snows allows the product to work at its best.

A solid, noncorrosive choice for concrete is the Natural Rapport ice melt. This ice melt is made with calcium chloride, which will not corrode concrete no matter how many times it is applied to outdoor surfaces.

It depends. Some but not all ice melt products are formulated to avoid damaging wood, so read product descriptions carefully.

Generally speaking, calcium chloride is better for ice melt. It’s effective at low temperatures, is a good choice for concrete, and comes in pellet, granule, and liquid forms. Since both types can be unsafe for use around plants or waterways, you may want to refer to the Type section above for more information, especially if you intend to use them around pets or kids.

What would the holidays be without Christmas lights? While nothing brightens a dark winter night quite like a twinkling display, finding the right set can feel overwhelming when strands with so many bulb shapes, lengths, and extra features are available,

To help you find the right options, we researched dozens of popular sets, eventually choosing the JMEXSUSS 33-Foot 100 LED Indoor String Lights as our favorites for their energy efficiency, gorgeous warm white glow, and built-in memory function. Read on to learn more about these and the rest of our picks for the best indoor Christmas lights.

The top picks listed here feature different styles and types of Christmas lights. Durable enough to last several holiday seasons, they fall within different price ranges. These lights meet the criteria previously listed, but they are also attractive and offer a positive user experience.

We researched more than 90 indoor Christmas lights from almost as many brands. Specifically, we looked at user experience, reliability, and durability. LED lights were more likely to make this list because of their energy efficiency and ability to work with smart technology. Finally, we considered design. Bulbs, both large and small, globe and novelty, made the list, but they had to have the durability and reliability to warrant their inclusion. We tried to represent a wide range of options and brands to fit different preferences.

Everything from the string length to the bulb size and power source can affect the look and feel of Christmas lights. The following considerations are important to take into account before starting to browse for the best indoor Christmas lights for the home.

Traditional incandescent bulbs work by creating enough heat to make a filament inside the bulb light up. Consequently, these lights use a lot of energy and release a significant amount of heat. However, they’re less expensive than LEDs and have a warm white glow that LEDs don’t.

LED Christmas lights have diodes that emit light via the movement of electrons within the semiconductor. LED bulbs are significantly more energy efficient and durable than traditional incandescent bulbs. They also release far less heat. LED bulbs are used in most smart lights, offering up to several million color choices.

Distance to a power source is a concern when buying and installing Christmas lights. For indoor lights, power must come from electricity or batteries. Lights with an electric plug require access to an electrical outlet or an extension cord. Electricity provides consistent power that never runs out (unless the power goes out). Several strings can connect to each other to use power from a single outlet. However, outlets can get crowded with all the light plugs.

Battery-powered Christmas lights are less common, though they are convenient. They can hang almost anywhere without proximity to an outlet. However, battery-powered lights have a short runtime and will dim as the power runs out.

Wire lengths vary from short 10-foot strings to 66- to 100-foot strings. A longer cord means fewer outlets and connection points between strings; however, experts recommend using strings in lengths appropriate for the decor job at hand. Use a tape measure to estimate the distance required to wrap around the tree or run down the banister.

Bulb size should be to scale with the rest of the holiday decor. Delicate ornaments may get overpowered by large bulbs. If unsure of the right size, mini lights blend into the background no matter the style or theme.

White, single-color, and multicolor sum up the Christmas light color options. Whites can be warm (yellowish) or cool (bluish), and single colors can be red, green, blue, orange, purple, and various hues in between. Pick a color or several colors that complement holiday themes. White makes an ideal neutral when unsure of which color to choose.

Shapes range from globes and small teardrop lights to vintage bulbs shaped like candleholders or snowmen. The shape should complement the rest of the decor, just like the color and style.

A few lighting modes include twinkle flash, slow glow, chasing flash, slow fade, and steady on. Smart LED Christmas tree lights offer the most lighting options. Some allow the user to set the colors by section or offer variable brightness adjustments. Lights that feature lighting modes may cost more than a typical string of Christmas lights, especially if they’re smart lights, because they usually cost more.

Choosing the right lights with the perfect length, color, and style isn’t an easy decision. We’ve answered the most common questions to help make your choice easier and get those twinkling Christmas lights up and running.

The Christmas lights used by professionals are usually LED lights with coaxial connectors, which are a little more hard-core than domestic lights. The wiring may be different, but the lights are not.

Color depends on the decor theme and personal preferences. White offers a clean, classic look, while a single color adds mood. Cheerful multicolor lights bring fun to the holidays. Think about the look you want to create, and go with a color that supports your decor.

Incandescent bulbs are approved for safe use on Christmas trees. However, LED Christmas lights don’t get as hot, which probably makes them a safer option for a live tree.

Remove each bulb one at a time, placing a piece of foil in the socket after removing the bulb. If the lights turn back on, you’ve found the bad bulb.

Longevity and durability vary by brand, but incandescent bulbs typically last two or three seasons, and LED bulbs typically last six or seven seasons. Both can last longer if cared for and stored appropriately. Certain conditions, such as living near the ocean or in an area that experiences extreme heat, can shorten their lifespan.

#7865. 4 Common Tools With a Hidden Second Function Most People Never Use

Some everyday tools hide useful features in plain sight. These four have built-in cutters, openers, and other functions worth knowing about.

A pair of pliers can sit in the same toolbox for years without its owner ever noticing the cutting edge near the hinge. The same goes for measuring tools, utility knives, and even gadgets in a kitchen drawer.

Some everyday tools have other tools built in, but those extra features are easy to overlook. Anyone who has spent time on home improvement projects knows how frustrating it can be to search for a tool, especially when the one already in hand could do the job.

Of course, features vary by model, but these four familiar tools have some useful extras worth knowing about.

Some pliers have built-in wire cutters near the hinge, just behind the gripping jaws. These can trim soft wire without needing a separate pair of cutters. Not every pair has this feature, though. It’s also worth checking whether the tool has wire strippers, which remove insulation without cutting through the wire itself.

Some wire strippers have small, threaded holes near the handles that allow users to shorten machine screws. The screw goes into the appropriately sized hole, and squeezing the handles cuts it to length. This feature can come in handy when installing electrical fixtures or other hardware that requires shorter screws.

Some manual can openers have a bottle opener built into the handle or near the cutting mechanism. Depending on the design, it may look like a small notch or hook in the metal. Other models have magnets that help lift cut lids from cans without touching the sharp edges.

Many nail clippers have a small metal file that folds out from beneath the lever or sits along the body. It helps smooth rough edges after trimming. Some models also have a pointed tip for cleaning beneath nails, although the design and placement of these extra features vary.

#7864. My New Dispatch Article on the Legal Case Against Trump's Section 338 Tariffs Targeting Canadian Imports

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

It explains why the Section 338 tariffs are illegal, and part of a broader pattern of tariff power grabs.

Today, The Dispatch published my new article on the case challenging Trump's Section 338 tariffs against Canada. Here is an excerpt:

Courts have already ruled against two avenues President Donald Trump used to impose his tariff regime. That hasn't stopped his efforts to attempt to deploy obscure or outdated trade law provisions to justify new import levies.

His latest tool is the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, the notorious legislation that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression.

Section 338 of that law is the basis of Trump's massive 50 percent tariffs on a variety of Canadian imports, including motor vehicles, furniture, dairy products, and more. On October 20, Gellert Global Group Corp., a major food importer and producer based in New Jersey, filed the first lawsuit challenging those tariffs before the U.S. Court of International Trade, the federal court with jurisdiction over tariff cases.

Gellert, which imports Canadian cheese subject to the tariffs, is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, a public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). It resulted in the tariffs' invalidation in February by the Supreme Court, which not only ruled that IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs but also emphasized that tariffs are a congressional power, and that the president does not have the power to "impose tariffs on imports from any country, of any product, at any rate, for any amount of time." The Section 338 tariffs are a similar power grab.

They are illegal for multiple reasons, part of an ongoing effort by this administration to usurp Congress' constitutional authority over tariffs. In addition, they harm the U.S. economy and poison relations with a key ally. Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act has never been used by a president to enact tariffs before; Philip Zelikow, a conservative trade policy expert and former Bush administration official, has shown that Section 338 was superseded by legislation enacted in 1962 and 1974.

Even if Section 338 is still operative, Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods violate its requirements. As the complaint explains, the Canadian trade measures cited by Trump as justification for the new tariffs do not discriminate against U.S. goods; Section 338 can only be used against discriminatory policies. Some of the Canadian measures retaliate against previous tariffs imposed by Trump. Most do not actually treat U.S. goods less favorably than imports from many other countries. In addition, the Section 338 tariffs go well beyond "offsetting" Canadian measures, violating another requirement of the law….

The administration's interpretation of Section 338 also runs afoul of the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to "speak clearly" when authorizing the executive to make decisions of "vast economic and political significance." Under Trump's approach, Section 338 can be used to impose 50 percent tariffs whenever a trading partner imposes any restrictions on U.S. goods, or simply chooses not to buy them. And the resulting tariffs need not be calibrated to those they are supposed to "offset." This is a blank check to impose massive tariffs against almost any imports at any time—exactly the kind of power the Supreme Court, in its ruling on the IEEPA case, determined the executive cannot have…

If Section 338 is still valid and does grant the kind of nearly unlimited authority Trump claims, that would violate the constitutional "nondelegation" doctrine, which restricts delegation of legislative power to the executive…

The Section 338 tariffs are part of an ongoing series of import taxes Trump has instituted in the wake of the IEEPA decision, seeking to again usurp the unlimited tariff authority the Supreme Court denied him. He previously tried to use Section 122 and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to essentially replicate the IEEPA tariffs. In both cases, he sought to transform a narrowly limited tariff authority into a blank check to impose massive tariffs at will…

In addition to illegally usurping Congress' authority under the Constitution, these tariff actions raise prices for consumers, greatly reduce economic growth, would impose some $700 billion in new taxes on Americans over a 10-year period, and have failed to increase manufacturing employment, despite Trump's claims that they would achieve that goal.

The tariffs against Canada—combined with Trump's repeated threats to make Canada the "51st state"—have also poisoned U.S. relations with a key ally. The percentage of Canadians with a favorable view of the U.S. has fallen from 54 percent in 2024 to only 33 percent this year—a worse rating than even China's authoritarian regime…. Alienating a key ally and trading partner doesn't make America "great again." It makes us weaker, poorer, and more isolated.
